ko-news-notices-192-8372c75064.title: New Tide-Gauge Station to Be Established on Geoje Island
ko-news-notices-192-8372c75064.text:
New Tide-Gauge Station to Be Established on Geoje Island
2022-03-02
Wave-height observations will also be conducted there for the first time.
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Jong-rok Park) announced that it will establish a tide-gauge station at Dojangpo Port on Geoje Island to monitor sea-level changes caused by global environmental change, including warming, and to observe wave heights during typhoons.
Geoje Island is home to well-known tourist destinations such as Oedo, Haegeumgang, and Maemuldo. Its complex seabed topography, strong tidal currents, and frequent vessel traffic have created a need for tide observations to provide accurate tidal information.
Construction of the Geoje Island tide-gauge station is scheduled to begin in mid-August this year. It will observe sea-level changes (tides), seawater properties (temperature, salinity, and density), and marine weather conditions (air temperature, wind direction, wind speed, and atmospheric pressure). The results are to be provided in real time through the agency’s website (www.nori.go.kr).
An agency representative said that Geoje is affected by typhoons every year and that, unlike other tide-gauge stations, a wave gauge will be installed near this station to monitor wave heights during typhoons and severe weather. The resulting data are expected to help forecast wave-related hazards and support disaster-prevention agencies, providing important information for preventing marine disasters.

ko-news-notices-193-8372c75064.title: Environmental Impact Assessment Report Preparation Fees Expected to Rise Next Year
ko-news-notices-193-8372c75064.text:
Environmental Impact Assessment Report Preparation Fees Expected to Rise Next Year
2022-03-02
“Fees for preparing environmental impact assessment reports are expected to rise next year.”
The increase is not expected to be large, and industry views will be taken into account.
Fee standards for preparing environmental impact assessment reports are expected to be raised beginning next year. The Ministry of Environment said the current standards are low and raise concerns about poor-quality reports. It also cited the growing emphasis on the environmental performance of development projects as a reason to raise the standards.
By October, the Ministry of Environment plans to review its March 2001 “Notice on Standards for Calculating the Cost of Preparing Environmental Impact Assessment Reports” and develop improvements to the calculation of direct costs, overhead expenses, technical fees, and additional costs.
In particular, it plans to revise staffing requirements and cost-estimation standards for assessment categories such as topography and geology, water quality, and cultural heritage, taking account of the content of each assessment.
A ministry official said, “Labor costs have continued to be adjusted in line with changes in prices, so the increase will not be large, but we plan to reflect industry views. We will adjust the fee standards based on the cost, difficulty, and quality of preparing an environmental impact assessment report.”
The notice will also apply under the Price Stabilization Act overseen by the Ministry of Finance and Economy and the Engineering Technology Promotion Act overseen by the Ministry of Science and Technology. The ministry plans to consult with the relevant ministries before preparing a final proposal.
An official from the Environmental Impact Assessment Association said, “As the scope and difficulty of environmental impact assessments increase with changing social conditions, the fee standards urgently need to be brought into line with actual costs.”
Reporter Jang-hee Jeong, Korea Construction Newspaper (h2hideo@)

ko-news-notices-194-8372c75064.title: National Oceanographic Research Institute Surveys Water Movement around Hallyeohaesang National Park
ko-news-notices-194-8372c75064.text:
National Oceanographic Research Institute Surveys Water Movement around Hallyeohaesang National Park
2022-03-02
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director General Jong-rok Park, announced that it would survey water movement in the waters around Hallyeohaesang National Park from that month through early October.
For the survey, the institute deployed 10 buoy systems, including surface current meters, in the waters around Hallyeohaesang National Park, from Geoje Island to Namhae Island. It said it would observe seawater movement continuously for more than a month.
The waters around the park attract many visitors for their scenic coastline and lie along routes to Yeosu and Samcheonpo. Harmful red tides occur there and repeatedly damage nearby fish farms. Accurate information on water movement is therefore essential for marine tourism, safe navigation, and forecasting the spread of red tides.
An institute official said, “These observations will enable accurate tidal-current forecasts for major shipping routes and passages around Hallyeohaesang National Park, contributing to maritime economic activity and protection of the marine environment.” The official also asked vessels passing near the survey area to help protect the observation buoys so the survey could be carried out successfully.

ko-news-notices-268-8372c75064.title: Updated Nautical Chart Published for Onsan Port
ko-news-notices-268-8372c75064.text:
Updated Nautical Chart Published for Onsan Port
2022-03-02
Updated with precise 3D seafloor survey data
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Yu-seop Jeong) announced that it has published a revised nautical chart incorporating the latest information on the waters of Onsan Port, Ulsan, to support safe navigation.
The newly published chart, at a scale of 1:10,000, incorporates precise 3D seafloor survey data collected using advanced survey equipment, including a multibeam echo sounder and satellite positioning equipment. It records changes to water depths, coastlines, navigational hazards, and other features.
The updated area is the approach channel to Onsan Port, where vessel traffic is frequent. It is important to port operations, including extension of the No. B subsea crude-oil pipeline, dredging of a reef inside the port, and construction of Ulsan New Port.
An agency official said the new chart is expected to help vessels navigating the waters off Onsan Port travel safely. The agency plans to continue producing and distributing charts with information needed for maritime safety and fishing activities.

ko-news-notices-270-8372c75064.title: 3D Seafloor Visualization Planned for Waters South of Jeju
ko-news-notices-270-8372c75064.text:
3D Seafloor Visualization Planned for Waters South of Jeju
2022-03-02
The seafloor in the southernmost waters of Korea’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ) will be presented in an immersive 3D visualization.
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Yu-seop Jeong) announced that it will invest KRW 100 million from April through November to create a 3D seafloor visualization of the southern waters off Jeju.
The project will reprocess seafloor topography data that the agency collected from 2000 to 2002 under the National Basic Ocean Map Survey Project and render it in 3D. The source material covers a total survey length of 91,000 km and amounts to 25 GB.
The visualization will clearly show the seafloor around the Korea-China-Japan exclusive economic zones, about 300 km from Jeju Island, including Ieodo, where a comprehensive ocean science station was built for ocean forecasting and marine-disaster prevention.
An agency official said the 3D visualization will make the underwater seafloor easier to see in detail and will serve as an important resource for maritime administration and help raise public awareness of the ocean.

ko-news-notices-272-8372c75064.title: Seafloor Survey to Begin in the Central Waters off the Southern Coast
ko-news-notices-272-8372c75064.text:
Seafloor Survey to Begin in the Central Waters off the Southern Coast
2022-03-02
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency’s Southern Sea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Office (Director Jae-seop Lee) announced that it will conduct a detailed hydrographic survey for five months beginning in May in the waters south of Yokjido, Tongyeong, Gyeongsangnam-do.
The survey vessel Namhae-ro, equipped with a multibeam echo sounder and satellite positioning equipment, will conduct a comprehensive survey of the seafloor, including its topography and sedimentation.
Three-dimensional analysis of features such as submarine hills will support the preparation and publication of detailed and electronic nautical charts. The results will also provide basic data for marine-industry development, including future mapping of the seafloor across the southern coast and exploration for submarine mineral resources.
Navigational hazards such as sunken vessels and reefs found during the survey are expected to be promptly reported as navigation information, helping improve maritime traffic safety.

ko-news-notices-275-8372c75064.title: “Will a Public Sea-Sand Extraction Area Destroy the Southern Coast’s Fishing Grounds?”
ko-news-notices-275-8372c75064.text:
“Will a Public Sea-Sand Extraction Area Destroy the Southern Coast’s Fishing Grounds?”
2022-03-02
Critics warn that the government’s plan to designate a public aggregate (sand) extraction area, intended to curb indiscriminate sea-sand extraction off the southern coast, could instead damage the marine environment.
According to relevant ministries, including the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and the Ministry of Construction and Transportation, the Korea Water Resources Corporation plans to apply to the Ministry of Construction and Transportation on the 25th for designation of a public aggregate extraction area covering 27 km² in 10 sections, 50 km south of Yokjido, Tongyeong, Gyeongsangnam-do.
After consulting with the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries on use of the sea area, the Ministry of Construction and Transportation plans to authorize sand extraction as early as August.
About 72 million m³ is slated for extraction over five years for national port-development projects, including Busan New Port, Ulsan New Port, and Gwangyang Port.
Industry groups and local residents oppose the plan, saying the government is encroaching on private business and harming the marine ecosystem. Private companies have long extracted sand at a site only 11 km from the waters the government proposes to designate.
Fishermen and some environmental groups argue that developing another large extraction area would cause vibration, noise, and turbid water, alter fish migration routes, destroy spawning and habitat areas, and damage the foundations of the fishing industry.
Tongyeong City Council adopted a resolution opposing designation of the public extraction area and sent it to the Blue House and the National Assembly.
Views within the government are divided. One official said individual companies had extracted sea sand indiscriminately, prompting allegations of preferential treatment, while post-extraction environmental management had been inadequate. The official said the Aggregate Extraction Act was amended in 2004 to introduce a public aggregate-management system so the public corporation Korea Water Resources Corporation could manage designated areas systematically.
Another official countered that the law allows designation of public extraction areas only on a limited basis, when they would otherwise cause serious disruption to the national economy. The official said there was no immediate shortage of aggregate and no need for the government to encroach on private business.
Reporter Bae Geuk-in bae2150@donga.com

ko-news-notices-281-8372c75064.title: 2006 Marine and Fisheries Development Implementation Plan Finalized
ko-news-notices-281-8372c75064.text:
2006 Marine and Fisheries Development Implementation Plan Finalized
2022-03-02
KRW 5.7464 trillion to be invested in 214 projects across seven areas
The “2006 Implementation Plan for Marine and Fisheries Development,” aimed at the rational development and conservation of marine resources, was finalized after approval at a Cabinet meeting on the 27th.
The annual plan details implementation of “Ocean Korea 21,” a 10-year medium- and long-term plan established in 2000. It was jointly prepared by 12 central government agencies, including the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Energy, and the Ministry of Environment.
This year, KRW 5.7464 trillion is planned for 214 projects across seven areas, including creating a marine domain for life, production, and livelihoods; building a foundation for sustainable fisheries; and establishing Northeast Asia as a center for shipping and logistics. By ministry, the allocations are: Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, KRW 3.9663 trillion (69%); Ministry of Environment, KRW 673.4 billion (11.7%); Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, KRW 349.5 billion (6.1%); and Ministry of Culture and Tourism, KRW 123.9 billion (2.2%).
Key priorities this year include strengthening management of marine territory, including Dokdo, uninhabited islands, and the EEZ; building the fisheries-industry base through fisheries technology and fishing-village business models; and pursuing a strategy to become a high-value international logistics hub.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries is working on a “Future Ocean Strategy,” targeted for finalization in September. The strategy is intended to respond to trends in leading maritime nations and neighboring countries that are strengthening their maritime policies, and to advance national ocean policy from the perspective of policy users and the public.
The strategy is to set out policies for Korea to become one of the world’s five leading maritime nations within the next 10 years.
Based on the strategy, the ministry plans to prepare a rolling plan linked to the Basic Plan for Marine and Fisheries Development and finalize it as a national plan in the first half of next year.
A ministry official said that this year marks the 10th anniversary of the ministry’s launch and that it plans to update the Basic Plan for Marine and Fisheries Development based on the Future Ocean Strategy and prepare a roadmap for the next stage.

ko-news-notices-283-8372c75064.title: Latest Nautical Chart Published for the Area around Daesan Port
ko-news-notices-283-8372c75064.text:
Latest Nautical Chart Published for the Area around Daesan Port
2022-03-02
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Yu-seop Jeong) announced that it has published a revised chart with updated information for the waters around Daesan Port in Seosan, Chungcheongnam-do, and Taean Port in Taean County to support safe navigation.
The chart (No. 357, scale 1:35,000) incorporates precise bathymetric data and port geographic information collected using advanced equipment, including a multibeam echo sounder and satellite positioning equipment.
It shows changes in water depth and navigational hazards along the channels, anchorages, and areas around the dolphins at Daesan and Taean Ports, where vessel traffic is heavy. The updated chart is expected to support port management and vessel operations in the area.
Daesan is a major port being developed with multipurpose berths for general cargo and container ships to establish a maritime logistics hub in the central West Sea. Port construction to provide berthing facilities is active, making current port information particularly important.
An agency official said it will continue producing and distributing up-to-date charts to support maritime traffic safety and provide information needed for marine development and conservation.
Charts are available from authorized chart vendors at 02-701-9981 and 051-466-0760, and through the vendor’s website, www.chartkorea.com.

ko-news-notices-284-8372c75064.title: KHOA Launches Marine Survey and Research Office
ko-news-notices-284-8372c75064.text:
KHOA Launches Marine Survey and Research Office
2022-03-02
Creating high-quality marine information through scientific research and analysis
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Yu-seop Jeong) launched a Marine Survey and Research Office on July 3, 2006, to apply scientific methods to marine surveys and produce higher-value marine information.
When the agency began operating as a comprehensive marine survey institution alongside the launch of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries on August 8, 1996, it began accumulating extensive marine survey data using advanced equipment and vessels. However, it faced substantial limitations in systematically and scientifically analyzing the data to produce high-value marine information that could meet the public’s diverse needs.
Since the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea entered into force in 1994, the concept of maritime territory based on a 12-nautical-mile limit has expanded to a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone. Competition among Korea, China, and Japan to gain an advantage in establishing this “new maritime territory” through marine surveys and research has intensified. The agency therefore launched the office to carry out this national responsibility effectively.
The Marine Survey and Research Office is responsible for research on EEZ and continental-shelf boundaries; developing technology to monitor and forecast storm surges and other marine-origin disasters; providing baseline data for marine-resource development through analysis of marine and seabed geological structures; and developing marine prediction technology to minimize loss of life and property in marine accidents.
The newly launched office has six doctoral-level staff specializing in marine and fisheries fields: one senior research officer and five research officers.

ko-news-notices-286-8372c75064.title: Environment Ministry Calls for Review of Large-Scale Aggregate Extraction Plan off the Southern Coast
ko-news-notices-286-8372c75064.text:
Environment Ministry Calls for Review of Large-Scale Aggregate Extraction Plan off the Southern Coast
2022-03-02
(Tongyeong = Yonhap News) Reporter Lee Jeong-hoon — The Ministry of Environment said the Korea Water Resources Corporation’s plan to designate a large-scale aggregate extraction area in the waters off Yokjido, Tongyeong, Gyeongsangnam-do, should be reviewed again because of its potential adverse effects on the marine ecosystem.
On the 12th, the Tongyeong–Geoje Environmental Movement Federation and Tongyeong City said the Ministry of Environment had recently notified the Ministry of Construction and Transportation that the project should be reviewed again. The notice concerned preliminary environmental review materials submitted by the Korea Water Resources Corporation for its proposed aggregate extraction area in the EEZ south of Yokjido.
The ministry said large-scale sea-sand extraction would alter the seafloor and significantly affect marine plants and animals. It also expected fishermen to seek compensation for damage to fishery resources and their livelihoods.
The ministry further noted that the public had not been given sufficient opportunities to comment through briefings and hearings, and that the cumulative environmental effects of concentrated large-scale development had not been adequately assessed, particularly since aggregate extraction was already taking place nearby.
The ministry clarified that its notice did not amount to outright non-consent to the extraction project. It said renewed consultation under the relevant provisions of the Environmental Impact Assessment Act could still be considered after the identified problems were resolved.
The Korea Water Resources Corporation is pursuing a plan to extract 73 million m³ of sea sand from this year through 2011 in the EEZ about 50 km south of Yokjido, to ensure a stable aggregate supply for new-port construction.

ko-news-notices-287-8372c75064.title: Joint Effort Planned to Improve Water Quality off Incheon
ko-news-notices-287-8372c75064.text:
Joint Effort Planned to Improve Water Quality off Incheon
2022-03-02
(Incheon = Yonhap News) Reporter Shin Min-jae — Incheon City, Seoul, Gyeonggi Province, and the central government are considering jointly funding projects to improve water quality off Incheon.
At a briefing on a study of pollution sources and cost-sharing options, held at Incheon City Hall on the afternoon of the 19th, the city discussed how to divide KRW 62.7 billion needed for water-quality improvement and marine-litter cleanup over the five years from next year through 2011.
In April 2001, the city signed a four-year agreement, running through the end of this year, to share KRW 28.5 billion in the cost of handling litter carried into the waters off Incheon by the Han and Imjin Rivers. The shares were Incheon 50.2%, Gyeonggi 27%, and Seoul 22.8%.
With Seoul’s and Gyeonggi’s contribution payments due to end at the close of this year, Incheon commissioned the Incheon Development Institute to provide a basis for a new agreement.
The study found that the existing agreement covered only marine-litter cleanup. Under a new agreement, the parties would also need to share the costs of treating contaminated sediments to improve marine water quality and of monitoring and investigating marine pollution. The city plans to pursue this broader cost-sharing arrangement.
The city also plans to ask the central government to contribute. The existing framework limited responsibility for pollution off Incheon to the three metropolitan-area local governments, but the area benefiting from cleanup is wider.
For the next five years, the city proposed sharing the total KRW 62.7 billion—KRW 42 billion for marine-litter cleanup and KRW 20.7 billion for water-quality improvement—as follows: Incheon 34.0–35.2%, Seoul 22.1–25.2%, Gyeonggi 28.2–32.6%, and the central government 11.3–11.4%.
Based on the study, the city plans to hold working-level consultations and consult the Seoul Metropolitan Area Administrative Council, then sign a cost-sharing agreement by the end of the year.

ko-news-notices-288-8372c75064.title: Submerged Breakwater Found to Help Protect Sand at Songdo Beach
ko-news-notices-288-8372c75064.text:
Submerged Breakwater Found to Help Protect Sand at Songdo Beach
2022-03-02
(Busan = Yonhap News) Reporter Park Seong-jin — A monitoring study found that the submerged breakwater installed off Songdo Beach in Busan has helped prevent sand loss.
On the afternoon of the 19th, Professor Do-sam Kim of Korea Maritime University presented the results of a monitoring study at Busan’s Seo-gu Office. He said the amount of sand had increased due to the submerged breakwater off Songdo Beach.
According to Professor Kim, 190,093 m³ of sand was placed on Songdo Beach in July last year. When measured in December, 164,935 m³ remained, indicating erosion across the beach.
From December last year through February this year, however, sand accumulated overall, and the beach’s sand volume rose to 211,619 m³.
Professor Kim said that measurements at individual locations showed an overall decline in sand volume from summer erosion and an increase during winter deposition. Although the overall change was within the margin of error, the measurements showed deposition.
He said the submerged breakwater, built as part of the Songdo Coastal Comprehensive Development Project launched in 2000, appeared to have prevented sand erosion.
In 2004, Busan’s Seo-gu Office installed the submerged breakwater through the Songdo development project. It is 40 m wide and 300 m long, positioned 300–350 m offshore from the beach at the depth reported in the source as 50 m. It was intended to reduce wave strength substantially and minimize sand loss and damage to nearby businesses from summer typhoons.

ko-news-notices-290-8372c75064.title: Jeju–Udo Subsea Water Main Planned
ko-news-notices-290-8372c75064.text:
Jeju–Udo Subsea Water Main Planned
2022-03-02
(Jeju = Yonhap News) Reporter Kim Seung-beom — A subsea water-main project is being planned to connect Udo, a popular “island within an island” tourist destination in Jeju City, with Jeju’s main island.
The Jeju Special Self-Governing Province Water Resources Headquarters said on the 24th that it plans to conduct a feasibility study and basic design in 2008, then invest KRW 10 billion over three years, from 2010 to 2012, to lay the water main. The project is intended to address Udo’s recurring water shortages during the summer tourist season.
The pipeline would be 18.5 km long in total, including a 3.1 km subsea section between Jongdal in Gujwa-eup and Udo. The province is considering a long-lasting installation using specialized polyethylene pipe to minimize corrosion from salt, as well as damage from waves, storm surges, and trawlers.
From 1999 to 2001, Udo built a facility capable of desalinating up to 1,000 tonnes of brackish groundwater per day at a cost of KRW 3.5 billion. This meets the needs of about 1,800 residents, but in summer as many as 3,400 tourists visit per day, causing a daily shortfall of about 500–600 tonnes.
On Jeju Island, a 75 mm subsea water pipe was laid in 1972 along a roughly 700 m stretch between Hyeopjae in Hallim-eup and Biyangdo, supplying 38 tonnes of tap water per day.

ko-news-notices-291-8372c75064.title: Fishermen Outside the Saemangeum Seawall Demand Compensation
ko-news-notices-291-8372c75064.text:
Fishermen Outside the Saemangeum Seawall Demand Compensation
2022-03-02
(Jeonju = Yonhap News) Reporter Lim Cheong — Fishermen living outside the Saemangeum Seawall have begun demanding compensation from Jeollabuk-do Province and the central government for various losses.
About 10 residents of islands outside Saemangeum, including Yami, Sinsi, and Seonyu, held a press conference at the provincial government office on the 26th. They urged the government to compensate residents of all island communities in the Gunsan area whose ports lost their function because of the seawall construction.
They said that they had endured the hardship caused by construction of the Saemangeum Seawall as a national project, but that even after its completion the government and Jeollabuk-do Province were ignoring the losses suffered by residents outside the seawall.
The fishermen also called on the government to convert their restricted fishing permits to general permits and provide business-closure compensation for their fishing boats. They said about 4,000 residents outside the seawall would fight forcefully to protect their livelihoods if their demands were not met.
Residents inside the Saemangeum Seawall have continued to seek compensation. The government and the Uri Party have recently been preparing livelihood support for inside-the-seawall hand-gathering fishers. Attention is focused on how the collective opposition from residents outside the seawall may affect the situation.
Jeollabuk-do Province said the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries manages fishing permits and the central government is responsible for livelihood support, leaving the province with no clear measure of its own. It said it would convey the outside fishers’ requests to the central government and political leaders and work to have them accepted.
