ko-news-notices-292-8372c75064.title: Low-Salinity Water from the Yangtze Raises Concerns for Jeju’s Waters
ko-news-notices-292-8372c75064.text:
Low-Salinity Water from the Yangtze Raises Concerns for Jeju’s Waters
2022-03-02
Freshwater from China’s Yangtze River is expected to flow into the waters southwest of Jeju, affecting the marine environment and fisheries and potentially reaching waters near the island. The source says countermeasures are urgently needed.
On the 25th, the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency announced results of a marine survey it had conducted jointly with the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute and the National Institute of Fisheries Science since the 18th. The survey took place in the East China Sea west of Jeju and near the Ieodo Ocean Research Station to investigate circulation in the Yellow Sea.
The survey found that the summer influence of low-salinity water from the Yangtze—known to affect Korea’s marine environment and fisheries—was clearly visible as far as the seafloor southwest of Jeju. Cold bottom water from the Yellow Sea was also evident as far as the seafloor northwest of Jeju.
The Yangtze low-salinity water is also expected to move into waters near Jeju.
The article reported that completion of the Three Gorges Dam, built across a gorge in the middle and upper reaches of the Yangtze and described as the world’s largest, would result in a large freshwater discharge that could substantially affect Korea’s marine ecosystem, including waters around Jeju in summer.
In light of earlier research finding that harmful algal blooms can occur in large numbers when Yangtze River outflow approaches Jeju and the southern coast, the survey results were assessed as potentially having a major effect on the marine ecosystem.
The East China Sea fishing grounds are important to Jeju’s cutlassfish and tilefish fleets. Because ecosystem changes directly affect their catches, the low-salinity conditions raised concern about deaths of fish and shellfish.
In 2002, water with salinity of 25.2–26.7‰ was detected at ports and communal fishing grounds in northwestern Jeju, causing some losses of conch and abalone for local fishers.
Earlier, in August 1996, low-salinity water of 19–25‰ reached communal fishing grounds, killing 184 tonnes of abalone, conch, and sea urchins and causing KRW 5.9 billion in losses.
When seawater salinity falls below 28‰, some marine organisms develop physiological disorders; below 25‰, fish and shellfish die.
The agency plans to analyze by the end of this year the East China Sea survey data on current direction and speed, water temperature, salinity, and plankton. It will use the results to clarify Yellow Sea circulation and assess the effects of the Three Gorges Dam on the waters southwest of Jeju.
Jeju Ilbo (Reporter Hyeon Bong-cheol)

ko-news-notices-293-8372c75064.title: Development Pressures Threaten the Han River Estuary’s Tidal Flats
ko-news-notices-293-8372c75064.text:
Development Pressures Threaten the Han River Estuary’s Tidal Flats
2022-03-02
The Han River estuary is the only one of Korea’s four major river estuaries that remains largely undeveloped, in part because it straddles the Military Demarcation Line. It is now under threat. Tidal-power and new-town proposals, bridge and road construction, and aggregate extraction are putting the estuary ecosystem at risk. Development is accelerating without a lead ministry responsible for balancing development and conservation in the Han River estuary.
“People say the tidal flats at the southern tip of Ganghwa are being considered as a site for a tidal power plant. Hundreds of thousands of migratory birds travel between Southeast Asia, Australia, and Siberia each year to feed and rest there. I worry this could be an ecological disaster.”
Dr. Ki-seop Lee of the Korea Institute of Environmental Ecology said this while walking through the Seonduri tidal flats south of Ganghwa, on the Han River coast. Through a telephoto lens, a juvenile black-faced spoonbill, a Korean Natural Monument (No. 205), bobbed its head at Gaksi Rock and begged its mother for food. In the first part of the month, far eastern curlews hurried across the mud in search of crabs; gulls searched for lugworms among stands of saltwort; and cormorants were feeding in the busy tidal flat.
Dr. Lee said Gimpo’s tidal flat had already become a landfill and the Songdo and Sihwa tidal flats had also been reclaimed. He asked whether the only remaining tidal flat in the Han River estuary should not be protected.
The tidal-power proposal, shelved several years ago amid opposition over damage to the ecosystem, resurfaced this year because of energy shortages. An official from the then Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, the lead ministry, acknowledged that the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute was conducting a feasibility study this year.
The official said alternative energy development was needed to address rising oil prices and international pressure to make greenhouse-gas reductions mandatory under the Kyoto Protocol beginning in 2013. The West Coast, where the tidal range reaches 9 m, was considered suitable. The proposed power plant corridor was reported to link Ganghwa, Jangbong, Yongyu, and Yeongjong Islands, which would effectively enclose the tidal flats on both sides of southern Ganghwa.
Changes in water circulation would inevitably alter the tidal-flat topography. Professor Gyeong-nam Han of the Department of Oceanography at Inha University called for a detailed study, saying that slower water flow east of the Yeongjongdo reclamation area had increased sediment deposition, while faster flow to the west was eroding the tidal flats—effects already associated with development.
Development of inland estuarine wetlands was accelerating as well. Large housing developments were proceeding in Gimpo, Paju, and other areas.
Two additional bridges are planned across the wetland-protection area, in addition to the already approved Ilsan Bridge. Aggregate extraction—the estuary’s “gold mine”—was also being pursued as part of inter-Korean economic cooperation, prompting concerns that fishery resources in the West Sea would decline. The species expected to be hit first by these environmental changes include the black-faced spoonbill, considered a flagship species of the Han River estuary ecosystem, in summer; shorebirds in spring and autumn; and the white-naped crane, a Korean Natural Monument (No. 203), in winter. If these species cannot survive, other migratory birds—including herons, egrets, swan geese, and bean geese—will also struggle to survive.
Dr. Chang-hee Lee of the Korea Environment Institute said estuary development was advancing and being planned rapidly, while environmental impact assessments were conducted only for individual projects. There was no integrated monitoring of development’s cumulative impacts.
The article argues that a master plan coordinating the Han River estuary policies of the then ministries responsible for construction and transportation, maritime affairs and fisheries, environment, and agriculture and forestry is needed before inter-Korean economic cooperation becomes more active.
〈Reporter Choi Min-young min@kyunghyang.com〉

ko-news-notices-295-8372c75064.title: Oxygen-Depleted Water Mass Threatens Fisheries in Masan and Jinhae Bays
ko-news-notices-295-8372c75064.text:
Oxygen-Depleted Water Mass Threatens Fisheries in Masan and Jinhae Bays
2022-03-02
An oxygen-depleted water mass has formed in Masan and Jinhae Bays in Gyeongsangnam-do, raising concern about losses for aquaculture operators.
The Marine Environment Research Division of the National Institute of Fisheries Science said on the 28th that a survey conducted in the area on the 27th aboard the survey vessel Tamgu No. 17 found an oxygen-depleted water mass with dissolved oxygen levels below 3 mg/L. The area affected is expected to expand after the monsoon rains end and sunlight increases, potentially causing greater losses of fish and shellfish. Aquaculture operators should take precautions.
The low-oxygen water mass forms near the seabed and gradually rises toward the surface. It was detected at a depth of 10 m. With increased sunlight, it may rise as far as the thermocline at 5–6 m, where it could harm net-pen farms and suspended-culture operations raising oysters and sea squirts.
Jin Hyeon-guk, a senior research officer on the institute’s Environmental Management Team, said that when an oxygen-depleted water mass occurs, suspended aquaculture stock should be folded into a U shape and lifted closer to the surface.
Kookje Newspaper (Reporter Kim Dong-su)

ko-news-notices-296-8372c75064.title: Tensions Rise between Fishermen and the Maritime Affairs Ministry over Proposed Sand-Mining Area off the Southern Coast
ko-news-notices-296-8372c75064.text:
Tensions Rise between Fishermen and the Maritime Affairs Ministry over Proposed Sand-Mining Area off the Southern Coast
2022-03-02
Fishermen and environmental groups are escalating their opposition to the government’s plan to designate a large aggregate extraction area in the southern-coast exclusive economic zone. They warn that it could damage marine ecosystems and deplete fish stocks, and the dispute is intensifying.
Fishing organizations and fishermen in Tongyeong are demanding that the designation plan be withdrawn. They say that placing an extraction area near Yokjido, the southern coast’s largest fish-spawning ground, would destroy the marine ecosystem and take away fishermen’s livelihoods.
On the 27th, the then Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries met in Tongyeong with representatives of fisheries cooperatives and fishermen to discuss the proposal. The parties restated their positions but reached no agreement.
Cho Yong-jae, chair of the committee opposing sand extraction near Yokjido, said that two meetings had only confirmed the sharp disagreement between the ministry and fishermen, leaving no room for further negotiations. He said the committee would soon convene a full meeting to hear fishermen’s views and consider every possible means of protecting their livelihoods.
The opposition committee plans to step up its campaign, including a protest visit to the ministry and large-scale demonstrations at sea using fishing vessels.
Experts have also voiced concern about the government’s unilateral designation plan.
Professor Ki-seong Bae of the Department of Ocean Civil Engineering at Gyeongsang National University said seabed sand extraction is unlike work on land and that the seafloor cannot return to its original state. He warned that altered seabed conditions and suspended sediment generated during extraction could drive migratory fish, including anchovies, away.
The then Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries had called for supplementation followed by renewed consultation, and the Ministry of Environment said the plan needed further review. On the 28th, the Ministry of National Defense stated that the area could not be designated.
Lee Seong-hoon and Kang Byeong-gyun (lee777@busanilbo.com)

ko-news-notices-297-8372c75064.title: Pilot Red-Tide Barrier Screens Planned for Fish Farms
ko-news-notices-297-8372c75064.text:
Pilot Red-Tide Barrier Screens Planned for Fish Farms
2022-03-02
Local governments in Busan, Ulsan, and Gyeongsangnam-do are preparing measures to prevent harmful algal blooms. After a series of meetings on preventing red-tide damage, they have announced steps including distributing supplies for testing for red-tide organisms and installing barrier screens.
On the 30th, the Busan Regional Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Office said it would provide Müller gauze for testing for red-tide organisms to 20 fish farms. Installing the gauze where seawater enters the farms will make it possible to detect immediately whether red-tide organisms are present.
Gyeongsangnam-do plans to pilot red-tide barrier screens and preemptive release of fish at offshore net-pen farms, which are especially exposed to red tide. The province plans to spend KRW 250 million to enclose five net-pen farms in Tongyeong with barrier screens, connect oxygen-supply equipment inside them, and release 60,000 rockfish in advance. Jeong Un-hyeon, the aquaculture official in the province’s Fisheries Production Division, said Gyeongsangnam-do had suffered red-tide damage every year except 2004 and was seeking alternatives to spreading loess. If the method worked well this year, he said, the province could expand it and sharply reduce damage to fish farms.
When a red-tide advisory is issued, Ulsan plans to station a small, high-speed monitoring vessel and staff in offshore waters around Seosaeng-myeon, Ulju-gun, where exposure risk is high. As soon as red tide is detected in an area, the city will set up a local operations room and begin round-the-clock monitoring.
Busan has not suffered red-tide damage since 2002, but it is continuing its prevention work. Hong Seok-tae, head of the city’s Fisheries Promotion Division, said Gijang County would buy red-tide control materials such as powdered loess using KRW 60 million in national and local-government funds plus KRW 20 million from its own budget. The Coast Guard had also promised helicopter support for monitoring. He said the city would do its utmost to avoid damage for a fifth consecutive year.
Kookje Newspaper (Reporter Kim Dong-su)

ko-news-notices-298-8372c75064.title: 43 Tonnes of Shellfish Died after Completion of the Saemangeum Seawall
ko-news-notices-298-8372c75064.text:
43 Tonnes of Shellfish Died after Completion of the Saemangeum Seawall
2022-03-02
After the 33km Saemangeum seawall was completed, seawater circulation was restricted and the number of shellfish deaths exceeded 40 tons.
According to the Saemangeum Project Division of the Korea Rural Community Corporation on the 2nd, after the seawall construction was completed in late April, seawater distribution was restricted to two drainage locks, and shellfish mortality rapidly progressed, centering on the mudflats of Geojeon Port, Jinbong-myeon, Gimje-si, and 43 tons were collected.
From May to July, the Saemangeum Project Group mobilized approximately 1,800 people to collect dead shellfish and dispose of them at a waste disposal site, with some of them being stored in the open air.
The reason why such a large number of clams died is because the seawall blocked the circulation of seawater, creating an extensive mud flat with almost no seawater inside the seawall.
For this reason, a fisherman claimed, “Considering that about 40 tons of shellfish died in the Geojeon Port area, hundreds of tons of shellfish will disappear if we consider the entire area of ​​Saemangeum,” and added, “The bad smell of waste shellfish is also a problem.”
The Saemangeum Project Group said, “It is a natural phenomenon that occurs when the inflow and outflow of seawater is restricted,” and added, “As fishing has stopped inside the seawall, we will collect all of it to prevent problems such as environmental pollution.”
Reporter Hong In-cheol ichong@yna.co.kr (Gimje = Yonhap News)

ko-news-notices-300-8372c75064.title: Haeundae's white sand beach has decreased by 30% in 60 years...
ko-news-notices-300-8372c75064.text:
Haeundae's white sand beach has decreased by 30% in 60 years...
2022-03-02
The sandy beach of Haeundae in Busan, the largest beach in Korea, has shrunk by more than a third over the past 60 years, and this is believed to be mainly due to the development of surrounding areas, including tourist hotels. This means that the coastal environment can be severely damaged not only by direct development of the coast, such as the construction of breakwaters and ports, but also by development of surrounding areas. Researcher Yang Ji-yeon of the Busan Development Institute and Professor Choi Cheol-woong of the Department of Satellite Information Science at Pukyong National University recently published a paper in the Journal of the Korean Society of Geographic Information titled ‘Analysis of Coastal Topography and Land Cover Changes at Haeundae Beach’ and revealed that the sandy beach of Haeundae has decreased by more than one-third over the past 60 years.
Researchers analyzed changes in the area of ​​Haeundae's sandy beach and land use in the surrounding area of ​​2.71 million m2 between 1947 and 2005 using satellite images. As a result, in 2005, the forest area near Haeundae decreased by 50% compared to 1947, while the built-up area and bare land increased by 66% and 55%, respectively. The area of ​​sandy beaches decreased by 35% from 88,658 m2 in 1947 to 57,893 m² in 2005.
Regarding the reason for the shrinking of the sandy beach, the researchers said, “This is because a large amount of soil in the forest area was washed away as the land was dug up for development in the area around Haeundae, while the inflow of sand was blocked by covering the Chuncheon Stream around Haeundae.” In fact, in 1947, the amount of soil lost annually was only 81 tons, but in 1970, when full-scale development began, the number increased five-fold to 410 tons. In the academic world, it has been assumed that the main causes of coastal changes are natural factors such as erosion and direct coastal development such as breakwaters and ports, rather than development of surrounding areas.
Professor Choi said, “This is the first time to prove that the coastline can change due to development of the surrounding area,” and added, “Artificial development has a greater impact on shrinking the coastline than natural change.” He warned against reckless development around the coast, saying, “This means that if beach development is severe, it could lead to the disappearance of the sandy beach.”
Reporters Yoo Ji-hye and Seo Jae-hee (s123@seoul.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-302-8372c75064.title: Environment Minister Lee opposes further tidal flat reclamation
ko-news-notices-302-8372c75064.text:
Environment Minister Lee opposes further tidal flat reclamation
2022-03-02
(Seoul = Yonhap News) Reporter Kim Seong-yong = Minister of Environment Lee Chi-beom said, “The development-oriented mudflat (public waters) management policy originated from a legal problem that allowed the development department to establish plans autonomously, without the control of even the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, the responsible ministry,” and added, “There should no longer be indiscriminate tidal flat reclamation.”
Minister Lee revealed this in an interview with Yonhap News on the 20th and emphasized, "Currently, all related organizations, including the Sustainable Development Commission, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, and the Ministry of Environment, are participating in preparing fundamental measures to prevent the indiscriminate development of tidal flats." He added, "It is time to establish broad policy principles to prevent tidal flat reclamation."
Minister Lee's comments are interpreted as expressing his will to put the brakes on the Janghang wetland development issue, which has recently been causing controversy surrounding development, and to manage the Saemangeum project through as strict an environmental impact assessment as possible. Attention is focused on whether and how the government's mudflat reclamation policy will change in the future.
Regarding the issue of changing the use of the Saemangeum project, Minister Lee emphasized his position on phased use designation, saying, "I think it would be desirable to first designate a use for only some areas rather than determine a use for the entire Saemangeum area, and then leave the rest as is and use it later as needed."
In the case of the Saemangeum project, if the land use plan changes by more than 15% of the total site, it is subject to change consultation. If a tourist complex (300,000㎡) or an industrial complex (150,000㎡) is created instead of farmland, a separate environmental impact assessment consultation process will be conducted for each project. The joint land use service of five organizations, including the Korea Research Institute for Human Settlements and the Environmental Policy Evaluation Institute, is scheduled to be completed in December.
Minister Lee announced that the unification of water management, which has caused controversy over duplication and excessive investment, is being discussed among ministries on the issue of establishing a water management committee and the Basic Act on Water Management, and that the Ministry of Construction and Transportation and the Ministry of Environment are considering a method of handling it by preparing a bill through joint legislation and unifying the relevant National Assembly standing committees into the Environment and Labor Committee.
Minister Lee expressed his will to discuss discussions with the Ministry of Construction and Transportation on integrating ministries or policies, saying, "I understand that a plan to integrate national land development and environmental conservation policy functions will be prepared by the end of this year through the Government Innovation and Local Decentralization Committee. I will actively reflect the position of the Ministry of Environment in the process of discussing the integration plan, and will also actively contact and discuss with the Ministry of Construction and Transportation when necessary."
Minister Lee also said, "We are pushing for the establishment of the Waterside Ecological Zone Management Corporation under the Ministry of Environment in order to resolve operational problems and systematically manage the four major river waterfront areas. Although there are differences of opinion with some local governments, the establishment of the Corporation is urgently needed for comprehensive management, including ecological surveys for each watershed and establishment of conservation and restoration plans."
He expressed his position, saying, "It is undesirable to argue that a dam should be built without an accurate investigation into the cause of flood damage. Dam construction should be promoted with social consensus as a last resort, and even in this case, the construction of large dams should be actively avoided."

ko-news-notices-303-8372c75064.title: Ministry Broadens Marine Observation Activities
ko-news-notices-303-8372c75064.text:
Ministry Broadens Marine Observation Activities
2022-03-02
Domestic coastal ferries will also be used to monitor changes in the marine environment, including harmful algal blooms and cold-water events.
On the 18th, the then Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries said it had instructed its regional offices nationwide to cooperate with the National Institute of Fisheries Science (NIFS), enabling NIFS to use coastal passenger ferries to monitor marine-environment changes. Until then, marine observations had been conducted only from NIFS survey vessels.
By next month, NIFS plans to equip the Hyundai Seolbong, which sails between Busan and Jeju, to monitor changes in the Tsushima Warm Current and the formation of oceanic fronts in the Korea Strait.
It also plans to monitor conditions along the routes served by the Sunflower ferry between Pohang and Ulleungdo, the Hankyoreh between Mukho and Ulleungdo, and the Mandarin between Incheon and Baengnyeongdo.
The previous month, NIFS had installed equipment on the Hanil Car Ferry No. 2, which travels between Wando in Jeollanam-do and Jeju, and was conducting trial observations of sea conditions, including red-tide formation and spread and jellyfish movement.
Coastal ferries follow regular, fixed routes, making it possible to build a continuous record for those waters and detect and respond to changes promptly. This is the main reason they are useful for marine observations.
Disruptions to survey-vessel operations caused by the sharp rise in fuel prices are another reason for using ferries.
NIFS expects observations from coastal passenger ships to help analyze unusual sea conditions, including cold-water events, low-salinity water, and typhoons.
A ministry official said the data could also support short-term forecasts to protect coastal fisheries and aquaculture areas. If observation methods are established in cooperation with private companies, the routes covered could be expanded to international services and the kinds of observations diversified.
Reporter Lee Gyeong-sik (Kookje Newspaper)

ko-news-notices-304-8372c75064.title: Companies Preparing Deep Seawater Products Get Ready for Full-Scale Production
ko-news-notices-304-8372c75064.text:
Companies Preparing Deep Seawater Products Get Ready for Full-Scale Production
2022-03-02
Companies that have been preparing deep-seawater businesses expect to begin full-scale operations next year, as the Deep Seawater Development and Management Act is expected to be introduced to the National Assembly’s Agriculture, Forestry, Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Committee on the 20th.
According to the then Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and industry sources on the 18th, the bill submitted by the ministry to the National Assembly in February was all but certain to be referred to the standing committee on the 20th. Companies preparing products including bottled water, salt, tofu, soy sauce, beer, and cosmetics were therefore hurrying to prepare for full-scale production next year.
Industry sources estimate the deep-seawater market could exceed KRW 200 billion a year. Companies that had completed prototypes and their products included: Kooksoondang—Baekseju; Aekyung Industrial—cosmetics; Sempio Foods—soy sauce; Dongwon F&B—sea-green-tea beverage; Hyundai Pharm—ion beverage; Gangneung Chodang Tofu—tofu; Doosan—refined rice wine (cheongju); and Daehakchon (Kyungpook National College of Science)—fermented beverages.
The government plans to introduce a licensing system for deep-seawater development and a fee on its use.
Reporter Lee Dong-hyeon (Busan Ilbo)

ko-news-notices-305-8372c75064.title: Electronic Video System for Maritime Accident Inquiries to Be Introduced for the First Time
ko-news-notices-305-8372c75064.text:
Electronic Video System for Maritime Accident Inquiries to Be Introduced for the First Time
2022-03-02
An electronic video system developed with Korean technology is to be introduced into maritime-accident inquiries, a first worldwide according to the source article.
On the 20th, the Central Maritime Safety Tribunal under the then Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries decided to adopt an advanced information and communications technology system to determine the causes of maritime accidents scientifically. Full operation is scheduled to begin next month.
Choi Jang-hyun, head of the Central Maritime Safety Tribunal, said the system had not been used by comparable domestic administrative adjudication bodies, including civil courts and patent tribunals, or by foreign organizations that investigate and inquire into maritime accidents. He said the system would make it possible to establish causes scientifically and objectively and thereby increase confidence in inquiries in Korea and internationally.
The process, previously conducted offline with paper documents and statements, will move to an advanced, science-based inquiry system incorporating information and communications technology.
Previously, hearings consisted of one-way questions and answers among the investigator who examined an accident and requested an inquiry, the inquiry officer responsible for determining its cause, and the people involved in the accident. With the digital video system, investigators and inquiry officers and the people involved will be able to give statements to one another interactively.
The system can record and preserve the inquiry proceedings, supporting transparency. Inquiry materials can be reviewed at any time, and faster proceedings are expected to shorten the inquiry period and make the process more convenient for members of the public.
The system comprises software such as a 3D ship-collision simulator and interactive video-hearing support, as well as advanced hardware including a ship-navigation display, radar imagery, and a document camera.
Within this year, the Central Tribunal plans to install the system at four regional maritime safety tribunals—in Busan, Incheon, Mokpo, and Donghae. Starting next year, it plans to connect the central and regional tribunals in an integrated network so they can share inquiry materials and hold remote video hearings.
Reporter Lee Dong-hyeon (Busan Ilbo)

ko-news-notices-306-8372c75064.title: Fishing Industry Reacts Strongly to Mandatory VMS for Fishing Vessels
ko-news-notices-306-8372c75064.text:
Fishing Industry Reacts Strongly to Mandatory VMS for Fishing Vessels
2022-03-02
The fishing industry is in an uproar over the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries’ notice requiring installation of vessel monitoring systems (VMS)—automatic vessel-position reporting devices—on fishing vessels. Captains and fishing masters fear the system could expose fishing-ground information they have held for decades, and seafarers’ unions have joined the opposition. (The issue was reported on page 16 of the newspaper’s July 19 edition.)
On the 14th, a public hearing on VMS installation convened by the ministry at the Busan Joint Fish Market was derailed at the outset by opposition from industry representatives and the National Democratic Seafarers’ Union.
Fisheries-industry position: On the 20th, the union issued a detailed response disputing the ministry’s stated basis for the VMS notice and asked, “Whom is this policy for?”
The union argued that the ministry says VMS is intended to prevent casualties in maritime accidents, but most deaths and missing-person cases result from safety accidents, not an inability to locate a vessel, so this does not justify mandatory installation.
Industry groups also oppose the installation costs and say revealing information such as fishing-ground locations would infringe their intellectual property.
An official from the large-vessel bottom-trawl sector said that installation on about 30,000 vessels nationwide could cost more than KRW 100 billion. Even with 50% government funding, the cost would be a major burden for fishers facing high fuel prices and declining catches. The official also said the government could face criticism for spending public money on a measure with uncertain benefits.
Ministry’s position: Given domestic conditions in which about 120 of the roughly 170 annual casualties from maritime accidents involve fishing vessels, the ministry plans to install VMS on fishing vessels to enable prompt rescue.
On intellectual-property concerns, the ministry said VMS data would be kept strictly confidential except when used for rescue, and would not be transmitted to other countries; it described industry concerns as unfounded. It also said the industry was comparing the proposed equipment with expensive VMS units used on large commercial vessels.
Ministry official Jeong Seon-mun said the fishing-vessel VMS under development would cost KRW 500,000–700,000 per unit, making installation on about 30,000 vessels possible for roughly KRW 18 billion. The government was considering covering most of that cost.
The ministry attributed some industry opposition to longstanding outside factors, such as conflicts among fishing sectors over fishing grounds. It decided to revise details, including the implementation schedule and vessels covered, after review by the Policy Deliberation Committee and the Central Regulatory Review Committee.
Reporter Lee Sang-yoon (Busan Ilbo)

ko-news-notices-307-8372c75064.title: Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, “Opposes reclamation of Geumgang Janghang mudflat”
ko-news-notices-307-8372c75064.text:
Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, “Opposes reclamation of Geumgang Janghang mudflat”
2022-03-02
Regarding the Janghang National Industrial Complex development project at the Geumgang Estuary, which is causing controversy over mudflat damage like Saemangeum, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries expressed its opinion that it is opposed to mudflat reclamation.
Lee Eun, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, said at a regular briefing on the 27th, “It is the opinion of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries that the Janghang mudflats should not be reclaimed.” Vice Minister Lee said, “As a result of the field investigation, it has been revealed that the Janghang mudflats have high conservation value as a migratory bird habitat,” and added, “Large-scale reclamation projects should no longer be carried out on the west coast, which is one of the five largest mudflats in the world.”
Regarding the fact that compensation for fishing rights, land expropriation, and road construction have already been made to build an industrial complex, he said, “National resource management should not be dragged down by existing investments,” and added, “We must seek ways to revitalize the economy of the area without reclamation of mud flats.”
Vice Minister Lee said, “The final decision (on the reclamation of the Janghang mudflats) will soon be made through consultation with relevant ministries.”
The Janghang National Industrial Complex project was decided in 1989 to create an industrial complex by filling 3.74 million pyeong of mud flats (1.5 times the area of ​​Yeouido and 1/33 the size of Saemangeum reclaimed land) in the western part of Maseo-myeon and Janghang-eup in Seocheon-gun, Chungcheongnam-do, which is the northern end of the Geum River Estuary.
South Chungcheong Province and Seocheon-gun are insisting that the construction of an industrial complex, which has been in the works for 17 years, should be completed as soon as possible to revitalize the local economy, while fishermen and environmental groups are opposing reclamation for the sake of fishermen's right to survive and the preservation of mudflats.
This project was continuously postponed due to lack of demand for industrial complex land, but began to be promoted in earnest in 2004 when the environmental impact assessment began. Currently, the third environmental impact assessment consultation is in progress. Hongseop Cho, environmental reporter ecothink@hani.co.kr

ko-news-notices-308-8372c75064.title: The southern coast is ruined - the sea is dying due to marine pollution.
ko-news-notices-308-8372c75064.text:
The southern coast is ruined - the sea is dying due to marine pollution.
2022-03-02
Not only is the coastline around the southern coast damaged by indiscriminate reclamation of public waters, but the clean waters are losing their characteristic blue color and dying because of the various wastes and wastewater flowing into the sea. The bleaching phenomenon is progressing rapidly at the bottom of the sea along the southern coast. The 'ocean desertification phenomenon' is in progress, where white calcareous substances stick to the rock like moss, causing algae and corals to disappear and the food chain to collapse. Additionally, coastal waters are turning into underwater garbage dumps due to household waste being secretly thrown away.
#Tongyeong Coast, the heart of Hallyeohaesang National Park
Hallyeohaesang National Park, including the waters of Hansando in Tongyeong, Gyeongsangnam-do and parts of the southern coast, including Namhae and Geojedo Island. The heart of this place is Gangguan in Tongyeong. The sight of waves rolling in from the sea and crashing against the long breakwater boasts a spectacular view that is reminiscent of a painting.
However, the bottom of the Gangguan sea, which the reporting team explored with the special task force of the Tongyeong Marine Police Station on the 28th of last month, was suffering from various trash thrown away by people, contrary to appearance.
Scuba divers who dived to the coast at a depth of 6 to 7 meters appeared after about 5 minutes. When two divers pulled the line, a rusty oxygen tank came up. After a while, they picked up various trash, including crab pots. The coastal area was full of discarded nets, various fishing gear, and household waste. Household waste secretly thrown away from land is covering the sea.
Police officer Oh Gyeong-hoon (30), who completed the exploration, said, "This is high tide time, so visibility under the sea should be good, but I couldn't see even 30 centimeters in front," and added, "The sea bottom around the Gangguan coast is heavily polluted."
The situation on the coast of Misu-dong, Tongyeong, was not much different. Divers who went into the sea pulled up a rusty children's bicycle about 20 minutes later. Even under the sea here, you can't see 30cm in front of you.
# Eogu Coast in Dundeok-myeon, Geoje, and the coast of Samcheonpo Port
After leaving Tongyeong’s Gangguan, we arrived at the coast of Eogu in Dundeok-myeon, Geoje, Gyeongsangnam-do. As we approached the coast where oyster farms were concentrated, suspended materials that appeared to have originated from the farms were floating here and there. The scene in the sea at a depth of about 10 meters was even more miserable. Oyster shells from the oyster farm were scattered here and there. While oyster farms were cultivating more oysters than the appropriate amount to increase profits, the oysters, unable to withstand their weight, fell, died en masse, and became entangled in white rocks.
Because of this, seaweed and microorganisms growing on rocks are disappearing, and as a result, the lowest level of the aquatic ecosystem food chain is collapsing, turning the sea into a dead sea where fisheries resources cannot live.
Superintendent Ko Young-hwan (36), who inspected the bottom of the fish farm, explained, "Due to the nature of algae, in the summer when the water temperature rises, oysters that fall due to overcrowding rot and become a cause of pollution," adding, "It was difficult to secure visibility under the fish farm."
A fish farm a few kilometers away from the oyster farm. This place, with a depth of about 15m, looked a little different from the sea we explored earlier. We explored for about 10 minutes, but unlike the fishing gear coast, visibility under the sea was good, perhaps due to the normal current flow, and no special contaminants were found.
Professor Kim Seong-jae (majoring in marine environmental engineering) at Gyeongsang National University's College of Marine Science said, "Pollution near coastal oyster farms and cage farms is serious, and in particular, various secretions are deposited, causing eutrophication and polluting the ocean." Professor Kim explained, “Indiscriminate construction of breakwaters that disrupt the flow of tidal currents also causes loss of natural purification ability,” adding, “Even when constructing breakwaters on the coast, construction methods that reduce waves and smooth the flow of water should be applied.”
#Addu Island Coast, Sacheon City
Addu Island was designated as a natural monument by the Cultural Heritage Administration on the 20th of last month. This island, located in Sinsu-dong, Sacheon-si, is entirely a source of dinosaur fossils and is where sedimentary structures from the Cretaceous period were discovered.
However, the coast of this island was also littered with various types of trash. Household waste, including beverage bottles and cans and discarded fishing gear, was strewn everywhere. On the 25th of last month, about 100 volunteers from the Sacheon Environmental Movement Federation, the city, and the Samcheonpo Fisheries Cooperative worked tirelessly to collect trash, but there was no end in sight.
The Korea Federation for Environmental Movement analyzes that the largest amount of trash discarded here comes from beach tourist attractions, accounting for 60% of the total. Additionally, it is estimated that approximately 33% of waste comes from fishing and maritime transportation. Garbage carelessly thrown away by vacationers during the summer is said to be the main culprit of marine pollution. In the sea near Samcheonpo Port, abandoned motorcycles and handcarts were even found. Garbage in the sea is difficult to collect, and the exact situation is not even known.
Jin Han, team leader of the Sacheon Environmental Movement Federation, said, "We carry out purification activities near Samcheonpo Port every year, but so much household waste is thrown away that it is not enough to collect it."
# Tongyeong Coast Guard Lieutenant Koo Young-hwan
- "A nationwide movement to save the ocean"
“The sea off the southern coast is losing its blue color to the point where you can’t see even an inch ahead when you go under the sea.”
Lieutenant Koo Young-hwan (53, photo), commander of the special task force at the Tongyeong Coast Guard, which has jurisdiction over the waters of Gyeongnam, is a veteran with more than 30 years of diver experience since enlisting in the Navy Marine Rescue Unit (SSU).
Inspector Koo expressed regret, saying, “Just 30 years ago, the southern coast had a blue ink color like the beaches of Hawaii, but as time goes by, the color of the sea is becoming more turbid and pollution is getting worse.” He gave a clear example, saying, “The southern coast is rotting to the point that when ROVs (unmanned underwater vehicles) are deployed to investigate sunken ships, there is so much floating material under the sea that it is impossible to take proper pictures.” Inspector Koo pointed out that the main cause of marine pollution is lack of awareness of the sea, including the act of recklessly dumping various harmful substances into the sea. He advised, “The level of pollution in the coastal waters adjacent to the land is more serious than expected, but the more distant seas are still clean waters,” and added, “If sea pollution continues to be neglected, the next generation will no longer be able to see the blue sea.”
“It is my belief that ‘the sea is a national asset.’ We must return the benefits we have received so far to the sea before it loses its ability to purify itself.” Inspector Koo emphasized, “There are limits to how organizations can save the ocean,” and added, “We need to launch a large-scale ‘nation-wide movement’ at the national level.”
# Marine debris increases by 25,000 tons per year
- Side effects such as annual fishing loss of KRW 320 billion
It was found that the amount of various wastes, including waste nets and ropes, abandoned in the sea exceeds 400,000 tons, and 25,000 tons of new waste is generated every year.
According to the government audit data recently submitted by the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries to Grand National Party lawmaker Kim Myeong-ju (Tongyeong and Goseong, South Gyeongsang Province), 400,470 tons of marine waste, including 167,978 tons in the West Sea, 86,412 tons in the South Sea, and 86,080 tons in the East Sea, is dumped at the bottom of Korea's coast. In addition, 115,000 tons of sunken marine debris that interferes with fishery resources and the safe operation of navigation vessels is left unattended, and with 25,000 tons of trash generated every year, the amount of trash deposited on the coast of Korea is continuously increasing.
These marine wastes are mainly floating waste, discarded fishing nets, discarded ropes, etc., and have been found to not only cause safety accidents on ships, but also cause problems such as damage to marine-life spawning grounds and habitats and to coastal scenery caused by debris accumulated on the seafloor. In addition, it was found that the loss of fishing production due to the decrease in catch amounted to 320 billion won per year.
Rep. Kim said, “Not only is the marine ecosystem damaged by the increase in marine waste, but marine pollution is worsening, causing enormous damage to local fishermen,” and added, “There is an urgent need to increase the budget to smoothly carry out marine waste collection and disposal projects.”

ko-news-notices-309-8372c75064.title: Suspicions of environmental destruction and preferential treatment for aggregate collection at New Port
ko-news-notices-309-8372c75064.text:
Suspicions of environmental destruction and preferential treatment for aggregate collection at New Port
2022-03-02
Suspicions of environmental destruction and preferential treatment related to the extraction of aggregates such as sea sand required for the construction of Busan Port's new port were raised.
On the 16th, Uri Party lawmaker Cho Kyeong-tae pointed out in a government audit of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries of the National Assembly's Agriculture, Forestry, Oceans and Fisheries Committee, "The government granted exclusive permission to Busan New Port Co., Ltd. and Samsung C&T to extract aggregates for the first phase of the Busan New Port project, but the unit price for aggregate extraction and reclamation is only 8,467 won per ㎥ as of 2000."
Commissioner Cho said, “Considering the price of aggregates at the time, this was to sell aggregates at cost price, and through this, Samsung C&T was able to reduce costs by 120 billion won,” raising suspicions of preferential treatment related to aggregate extraction during the construction of the new port.
Rep. Cho said, "Among the numerous port construction projects, Samsung C&T is the only company that has received permission to extract aggregates. Please clarify why." He added, "The Minister of Oceans and Fisheries should conduct an audit on suspicions of preferential treatment related to aggregate extraction by Samsung C&T."
Rep. Cho said, "The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and Samsung C&T, while conducting a new port development project, collected more than 40 million ㎥ of sea sand from the EEZ (Exclusive Economic Zone) near Yokjido, Tongyeong-si, Gyeongsangnam-do, which is an act of self-destruction of the marine ecosystem." said.
He emphasized, "In most developed countries, the priority for reclaimed soil is the development of stone mountains in the landfill site, followed by dredged soil generated during the course of port dredging and recycled aggregates such as construction waste." He emphasized, "In the future, sea sand collection should be prohibited in port construction."
In addition, Rep. Cho said, "Despite the government supporting a huge amount of construction costs for port construction, construction companies are making huge profits by selling shares to foreign logistics companies at the end of the construction period. We must prepare legal measures to prevent this." Reporter Lee Dong-hyeon (Busan Ilbo)

ko-news-notices-311-8372c75064.title: If there was a radioactive leak, it would take 5 days for Gangneung to be contaminated.
ko-news-notices-311-8372c75064.text:
If there was a radioactive leak, it would take 5 days for Gangneung to be contaminated.
2022-03-02
“If there was a radioactive leak, it would take 5 days for Gangneung to be contaminated.”
Although it is unlikely, Cookie News reported that if radioactivity leaked from North Korea's underground nuclear test, the entire groundwater on the Korean Peninsula could become radioactively contaminated.
The Korea Institute of Nuclear Safety under the Ministry of Science and Technology, which monitors environmental radiation in Korea, said, “The closest area to the site of the nuclear test is Gangneung, about 320 km away. If radioactivity occurred, it is expected to take about 5 days for Gangneung to be contaminated, and we are currently operating an emergency response team to monitor radioactivity 24 hours a day.”
An official from the Korea Institute of Nuclear Safety explained, “Even if the underground nuclear test was perfect, it could not completely block radiation, resulting in about 0.1% of the total radiation. However, even assuming the worst case scenario, there will be no direct effect on the human body, and the radiation dose is expected to be significantly below the 0.1 millisievert (mSv) allowed per year for natural radiation under the Atomic Energy Act.”
However, some foreign media and experts are pointing out that the safety of North Korea's nuclear testing facilities cannot be trusted. Foreign countries conduct underground nuclear tests in areas without groundwater, such as deserts, but the area where North Korea's underground nuclear tests were conducted is different, and problems may arise.
China's Global Times warned that if North Korea goes ahead with nuclear testing, the entire groundwater on the Korean Peninsula could be contaminated with radioactivity. David Albright, director of the International Institute for Science and Security (ISIS), who served as a UN weapons inspector, said, “If there is a flaw in the design of the nuclear test site, not only can a significant amount of radioactivity leak out, but it can also blow up everything outside the test site.”
Satoshi Morimoto, a professor at Takushoku University and a Japanese security expert, also said, “There must be a 3,000㎦ desert to avoid groundwater contamination due to radioactive leaks.”
/ Chosun.com internetnews@chosun.com

ko-news-notices-312-8372c75064.title: ‘Contemplating measures’ for global temperature and sea level rise
ko-news-notices-312-8372c75064.text:
‘Contemplating measures’ for global temperature and sea level rise
2022-03-02
‘Contemplating measures’ for global temperature and sea level rise
There is much controversy as to whether global warming is the direct cause of abnormal climate, but scientists also acknowledge that the Alaskan glacier has shrunk significantly over the past 100 years, raising global sea levels by 10 to 25 cm and raising the average global temperature to about 0.3 to 0.6 degrees Celsius.
According to data released by the government in December 1994, Korea also reported that global warming is bringing about various changes in the fields of water resources, agriculture, forests, ecosystems, coastlines, and coastal structures, according to the ‘National Report on Climate Change Convention’.
#Global warming and weather changes
The global warming phenomenon is believed to be caused by the phenomenon in which solar radiation energy (ultraviolet rays) entering the Earth's atmosphere falls on the Earth without being filtered due to the destruction of the ozone layer in the stratosphere above the Earth's atmosphere due to the excessive use of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
As the global temperature rises due to direct solar irradiation of the Earth and the use of greenhouse effect gases such as carbon dioxide, methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), and aerosol particles, part of the solar energy reaching the Earth's surface from the troposphere (10 to 15 km from the surface) must be emitted back to the outside of the Earth through the tropospheric boundary in the form of infrared energy, but these gases act like a greenhouse in the upper troposphere of the Earth. This is a phenomenon that causes the temperature of the Earth to rise by forming a film and preventing the release of energy.
The Earth's greenhouse gases that cause global warming have the greatest effect through the actual water vapor in the troposphere, which is due to the influence of the entire Earth's energy flow and temperature system.
The most important thing is that carbon dioxide generated during human activities is 55%, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) 24%, methane 15%, and nitrous oxide 6%.
For a 1 kg emission and a 100-year assessment period, with carbon dioxide assigned a warming potential of 1, the article gives methane a value of 21, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) approximately 300–3,500, and nitrous oxide 1,500. Although their shares of total emissions are smaller, their warming effects are substantial.
Accordingly, the second report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in 1995 stated, ‘The impact of global warming and climate change on human activities is already being seen, and the main cause is the use of fossil fuels and the increase in greenhouse gases due to agriculture.’
Comparing the concentration levels of major greenhouse gases before the Industrial Revolution and in 1992, carbon dioxide increased from 280 ppm to 360 ppm, and methane increased from 770 ppb to 1,720 ppb.
When the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubles, the isotherm line shifts, affecting the existence of 1/3 of the Earth's forest area. Considering the tendency of forest destruction to occur during this change and greatly weaken the Earth's carbon dioxide absorption function, it can be estimated that a considerable amount of damage has been done in the past 100 years.
In particular, climate experts predict that by 2050, carbon dioxide will reach 575ppm, twice the level before the Industrial Revolution, and by 2100, it will reach 1,330ppm, resulting in a rise in global temperature by as little as 1.7℃ or as much as 5.3℃.
As a result, various weather changes occur throughout the Earth, with desert areas accelerating desertification and drying out many areas, while some areas turn into wet areas with a lot of rain.
There are concerns that these changes will change the distribution of arid areas, semi-arid areas and farmland, disrupt the ecosystem, and lead to the extinction of many plants and animals.
And the current biggest concern is the decline of glaciers in polar regions and alpine regions. Although accurate predictions are impossible, it is expected that sea levels will rise by 15 to 19 cm over the next 100 years, and in the worst case, the territories of low-lying countries where 20% of the world's population are concentrated will be flooded.
This is related to food production, and it is expected that the global food shortage will further worsen.
#International trends related to global warming
▲Climate Convention
In the late 1980s, direct evidence of global warming, such as increased carbon dioxide concentration and rise in global temperature, appeared around the world, and in the 1990s, signs of actual abnormal climate appeared.
In response to this, in 1988, the IPCC, an official intergovernmental organization responding to climate change, was first formed by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP), and finally, in 1992, the ‘Convention on Climate Change’ was adopted as a UN basic convention at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), the largest environmental conference of mankind.
The main goals of this Convention on Climate Change to prevent global warming, which came into effect in March 1994, are to prepare national reports on the greenhouse gas emissions and absorption status of each country, establish and implement domestic policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and reduce carbon dioxide emissions to the 1990 level by 2000 in developed countries.
At the COP, in which 168 countries participated, 38 developed countries, including the United States, agreed to reduce total greenhouse gas emissions by 5.2% on average between 2008 and 2012 compared to 1990, and by -8 to +5% by country.
It also emphasized efficient management of energy, protection and promotion of sinks such as forests that can absorb greenhouse gases, development of environmentally friendly technologies related to new and renewable energy, abolition of market imperfections, financial incentives, and subsidies that cause an increase in greenhouse gases, reform of policies and measures, and management of the transportation sector and waste.
In addition, at this meeting, for the first time, the ‘Joint Implementation System’ and ‘Emission Trading System’ were introduced as economic means to reduce carbon dioxide, and there was an attempt to submit an agenda for discussion on ‘Voluntary Agreements’ of each country to encourage the participation of developing countries, but it was met with strong opposition from several developing countries, including India.
*Emission Trading = As a policy tool that can be applied to a wide range of environmental issues along with the emission charging system, it is a property rights system designed to clearly define the rights and obligations for polluting activities or pollution prevention activities and achieve environmental quality at the minimum social cost through autonomous adjustment.
It is a system that sets the global warming gas emissions and gives each country a certain amount of emission limit. If it exceeds this limit, it purchases emissions rights, and if it falls below this limit, it sells the remaining amount.
*Joint Implementation = This is a system in which a country, such as a developing country, changes its inefficient energy industrial structure to a highly efficient industrial structure through the expansion of social overhead capital or the development of technology, and as the country's fossil fuel use decreases, the reduced amount is recognized as a reduction for any developed country that implemented this in return.
*Carbon tax = It is also called carbon dioxide tax (COP's official term, carbon-dioxide tax) or carbon burnt tax. The tax is imposed differently depending on the carbon content of fossil fuels, and the goal is to fundamentally suppress the consumption of fossil fuels.

ko-news-notices-314-8372c75064.title: Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Publishes Strategy to Manage Land-Based Sources of Marine Pollution
ko-news-notices-314-8372c75064.text:
Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries establishes land-based marine pollution source management strategy
2022-03-02
Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries establishes land-based marine pollution source management strategy
Source: Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries
(Seoul = Newswire) October 13, 2006-- A detailed action strategy has been established to protect the marine environment from land-based activities.
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries announced on the 23rd that, in collaboration with the Ministry of Environment, it has established a ‘National Action Strategy’ for land-based pollution source management, which aims to invest a total of $6.4 billion (approximately KRW 6.4 trillion) by 2010 in three areas: land-based pollution source management, marine ecosystem conservation, legal system improvement, and policy base strengthening.
This action strategy will be submitted to the 2nd intergovernmental meeting on the ‘Global Action Plan (GPA) for protecting the marine environment from land-based activities’ held in Beijing, China from the 16th to the 20th.
※ GPA: Global Program of Action for the Protection of the Marine Environment from Land-based Activities
According to the implementation strategy, coastal management regional plans of relevant local governments will be established early to ensure implementation of the integrated coastal management plan established in 2000. As of last year, 17 out of 80 local governments had completed establishment and 25 were in the process of establishment.
In addition, the role of the central committee on coastal management will be strengthened to review whether coastal development plans such as ports and fishing ports, coastal use activities according to individual laws, etc. are consistent with the integrated coastal plan.
The action plan also calls for the establishment of a joint management system between ministries, including the establishment of a comprehensive estuary management plan, jointly with related ministries such as the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, the Ministry of Environment, and the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry starting next year.
In addition, starting this year, the National Institute of Fisheries Science of the Ministry of Oceans and the National Institute of Environmental Research of the Ministry of Environment will jointly establish an ‘estuary monitoring system’ to lay the scientific foundation for estuary management.
In addition, in order to improve the marine environment, which is the final receptor for land-based pollutants, the polluter-pays principle will be introduced, with costs shared with upstream areas, and basin-level management will be established for waste carried into the sea through the Han and Nakdong Rivers.
In addition, the implementation strategy involves non-governmental organizations (NGOs) such as the Han River Citizens' Alliance and Sihwa Lake Environmental Watch group in national research projects to strengthen the pre-coordination function of policies such as collecting local opinions and promoting them, and networks with stakeholders through information systems such as the coastal information system, tidal flat information system, and waste marine discharge comprehensive information network are also activated.
In addition, we continuously provide training for honorary wetland guides and natural environment guides, and promote local residents' participation in environmental conservation by publishing guidebooks and holding seminars.
In order to strengthen the policy decision support system based on scientific data, a basic survey of the marine ecosystem will be conducted from this year to 2015, and a public-private cooperation program will be developed by activating private participation in marine environment monitoring projects such as estuary surveys and marine environment measurement network operation.
In addition, from this year to 2008, the ‘National Marine Environment Information Integration System’ will be established to integrate national data from the National Institute of Fisheries Science, Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency, Coast Guard, and Ocean Research Institute, thereby increasing the disclosure and accessibility of marine environment information produced by the nation.
In addition, next year, management priorities appropriate for marine characteristics, such as domestic sewage in Masan Bay and heavy metals and hazardous chemicals in Gwangyang Bay, will be set to efficiently use financial resources and establish a reasonable management plan.
In particular, a plan to apply the ‘emissions trading system’, which is being piloted for air pollution, to water pollution is being promoted as a long-term task.
The implementation strategy also plans to revise the Coastal Management Act to introduce the coastal use zoning system and the Coastal Total Pollution Load Management Act to introduce the Total Pollution Load Management System next year, and to suppress indiscriminate reclamation by revising laws related to reclamation, such as the Public Waters Reclamation Act and the Public Waters Management Act.
In addition, international cooperation will be strengthened, including continued cooperation in the field of marine environment conservation with neighboring countries such as China, Japan, and Russia, and the establishment of the Korea-US Environmental Cooperation Joint Committee with the United States.
In order to efficiently pursue this project, a total of $6.4 billion will be invested, including $320 million for ecosystem conservation and restoration, $5.83 billion for reduction of land-based pollutants, and $270 million for strengthening policy base.
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries has not received adequate evaluation from the international community despite Korea investing a large amount of budget to manage land-based pollution sources and implementing advanced management policies such as implementation of the Total Pollution Load Management System. However, the submission of this national action strategy is expected to significantly improve our image.
Meanwhile, GPA was adopted by 108 countries, including Korea, Japan, and the European Union, at the Washington Conference of the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) in 1995, and the first intergovernmental conference was held in Montreal, Canada in November 2001.
More than 100 countries will participate in this second intergovernmental meeting, and about 34 countries, including Korea and China, are expected to announce their national implementation strategies.
The GPA Intergovernmental Conference is held every five years and the secretariat is located in The Hague, Netherlands.
Media Inquiry

ko-news-notices-315-8372c75064.title: “Conserving the Marine Environment Is a Shared Responsibility of All People on Earth”
ko-news-notices-315-8372c75064.text:
“Conserving the Marine Environment Is a Shared Responsibility of All People on Earth”
2022-03-02
The Beginning of a New Marine Conservation Movement
“Conserving the Marine Environment Is a Shared Responsibility of All People on Earth”
2006/10/13
Reporter Yoon Mi-sook
On the 10th, the Marine Committee of the Korean Federation for Environmental Movement held an inaugural discussion in the small auditorium of the National Assembly Library on the theme “A Sea of Life, a Sea in Crisis.” This article summarizes presentations from the discussion. — Editor’s note
Since time immemorial, the sea has given generously to humankind. It has provided food, economic benefits, routes for exchange, comfort, and the foundation for survival. But as life on land changed greatly, the sea gradually began to deteriorate. Through reclamation, illegal dumping, oil spills, increasingly intensive fishing, and marine-sand extraction, people have damaged the health of the sea in ever more ways. These actions threaten marine biodiversity and sharply diminish people’s quality of life.
Reporter Yang Gye-tak
On the morning of the 10th, the Korean Federation for Environmental Movement held a campaign at Cheonggye Plaza in Seoul to mark the launch of its Marine Committee and call for “Protect Antarctica: A Living Continent in Crisis.” Models of penguins, elephant seals, minke whales, Patagonian toothfish, krill, and albatrosses symbolized the Antarctic ecosystem as the campaign explained the threats facing Antarctica and the need to protect it.
Inadequate response to the marine environment
Although Korea is a maritime nation surrounded by seas on three sides, its response to marine-environment issues has remained very limited. Localized campaigns and one-off events are common. The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, which should lead research and analysis of ocean health, has instead remained focused on port construction, while its budget has long been skewed and unbalanced. The pessimistic suggestion that responsibility for marine-environment conservation should be transferred to the Ministry of Environment may soon become a serious policy debate.
The consequences of human activity on land all affect the sea. Most marine debris originates on land and drifts out to sea; wastewater discharged on land also flows directly into the ocean. Toxic wastewater and difficult-to-dispose-of waste are dumped at sea under the seemingly plausible label of “ocean disposal.” Large-scale coastal reclamation continues despite its widely known damage, while the remaining natural coastline is disappearing under projects justified as tourist coastal roads or coastal improvement. Breakwaters are still being built in ways that leave water stagnating and putrefying inside bays. The contradiction of mining seabed sand to build ports—like biting into one’s own flesh—continues to play out in Korea’s seas.
Unable to rein in the drive to develop
The Coastal Management Act was enacted late and has proved insufficient to restrain local governments’ development ambitions. Some local governments mistakenly believe the law exists simply to let people manage and develop the coast, and pursue ambitious plans to create an industrial complex and build three or four coastal golf courses. Such outcomes reflect the lack of public information about national policy.
It may be late, but citizens are coming together to address problems that have long been postponed, even though the facts have been known. The work and methods of government and its research institutes, and the breadth of the issues they raise, may differ somewhat; the shared goal of protecting and restoring the health of the sea is the same. A serious marine-conservation movement can take root when government, research institutes, and civic groups divide responsibilities and communicate with one another.
Marine activism can be difficult for ordinary citizens to engage with. The sea is deep and vast; summers are hot and winters cold. Currents, waves, typhoons, eddies, storm surges, and exchange with the distant open ocean all pose challenges. Access has also been difficult because of limits on survey methods, the scale of the work, and its cost. Even so, the Marine Committee of the Korean Federation for Environmental Movement has been formed, bringing together the voluntary efforts of activists who have lived alongside the sea and want to view and engage with Korea’s seas and the world’s oceans in a new way.
Protecting a global common
With great effort, the group raised enough money to acquire a second rubber boat. Local training to adapt to marine conditions has begun, and it hopes to obtain a campaign vessel before long. Its commitment to caring for and loving the sea is firm; the remaining task is to proceed step by step, starting with accessible work, proposing alternatives, and joining efforts with others. Drawing on more than a decade of regional monitoring of marine problems, activists will continue to work together for a healthier, more beautiful sea. They will also strengthen cooperation with international organizations through the Antarctic Conservation Coalition, a whale-protection campaign with Greenpeace, and efforts to end ocean dumping under the London Convention.
The sea is a vast system connecting the world. It is a global common and a shared responsibility of all people on Earth. As a maritime nation surrounded by seas on three sides, Korea urgently needs to restore its identity by making a serious effort to conserve the marine environment and thereby uphold its sovereignty.
Yoon Mi-sook, member of the Marine Committee, Korean Federation for Environmental Movement

ko-news-notices-316-8372c75064.title: Mainland China struggles with water shortages
ko-news-notices-316-8372c75064.text:
Mainland China struggles with water shortages
2022-03-02
China's water shortage is becoming increasingly serious. Last year, one in four Chinese people suffered from water shortages. The amount of food production reduced due to water shortage amounts to 35 million tons, or 8.2% of total production.
As China's population peaks at 1.6 billion in 2030, the entire country is expected to suffer from the worst thirst.
▽Water at the mouth of the Yellow River has decreased by 91% in 40 years = According to the South China Morning Post on the 7th, the total amount of water flowing into the sea from the Yellow River in the 1960s averaged 49.6 billion tons every year. In the 1990s, it decreased to 14.1 billion tons, and after 2002, it decreased to 4.65 billion tons. This is a whopping 90.6% decrease compared to 40 years ago.
Currently, the water utilization rate of the Yellow River is about 60%. According to international standards, the utilization limit of river water is 40%. Exceeding this standard will have a serious negative impact on the surrounding ecosystem.
The water resource utilization rate of the Huaihe River and Liaohe River reaches around 60%. The Haihe River, which flows through Beijing to Tianjin, uses up 100% of its water before it reaches the sea.
▽World average of water resources per capita: 1/4 = According to data from the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), China's total water resources last year were 2.83 trillion tons, ranking 6th in the world after Brazil, Russia, the United States, Canada, and Indonesia. However, water resources per person are only 2,140 tons, which is only a quarter of the world average.
However, 1.7 trillion tons simply flows away during floods or flows underground, so the actual usable water resources are 1.1 trillion tons, which is only 840 tons per person.
According to China's Ministry of Water Resources, about 400 out of 669 cities across China are suffering from water shortages. Among these, 110 cities are in a serious situation. 320 million people, or 24.4% of China's population, are experiencing water shortages.
Due to the excessive use of scarce water resources, it is difficult for even plants to cover the surface of 4.42 million km², or 46% of the entire country, including Hebei, Shanxi, and Inner Mongolia autonomous regions.
▽Forecast = China’s total water use last year was 563.3 billion tons. In the future, water use is expected to increase every year, reaching 700 to 800 billion tons in 2030. This amounts to 89% of the total amount of water available for use at this time, which is 800 to 900 billion tons. This is only possible if the average use limit of 40% of the river water is exceeded.
To solve this problem, the Chinese government plans to invest 1 trillion yuan (approximately 120 trillion won) by 2010 to improve water facilities and prepare for water shortages.
However, since the average precipitation is only 600 mm, it is expected to be difficult to fundamentally solve the water shortage crisis.
At the annual academic conference of the Chinese Hydraulic Society held in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, Vice Minister Hu Siyi of China's Water Ministry warned, "As we currently have a water shortage of 40 billion tons every year, if we do not make thorough preparations 25 years from now when water shortage reaches its peak, a huge disaster could occur."
Source: Beijing = Ha Jong-dae, Donga Ilbo correspondent, orionha@donga.com |

ko-news-notices-317-8372c75064.title: Global warming and weather change
ko-news-notices-317-8372c75064.text:
Global warming and weather change
2022-03-02
If the average rises by 6 degrees, the Earth will be destroyed.
Chief writer Lee Wan-woo
Climate change due to global warming is emerging as a hot topic today. After the Tokyo Convention took effect, the smokestack industry, which contributes to global warming, improved its carbon dioxide emission facilities, and the oil refining industry mandated desulfurization facilities, but air pollution still exceeds the standard amount. On the London carbon market, companies that emit a lot of pollution are working hard to secure carbon dioxide emissions rights, but air pollution is already so widespread that each country cannot afford emissions rights.
The industry that has the greatest impact on global warming is the automobile industry. The exhaust fumes and carbon dioxide (CO2) emitted by cars driving down the road have the greatest impact on air pollution.
Recently, the U.S. state of California filed a lawsuit in state court seeking damages from automakers that have significantly contributed to global warming. The state of California filed a lawsuit against six auto companies, including General Motors and Toyota, seeking billions of dollars in damages, holding them responsible for global warming.
California has already spent billions of dollars on coastal erosion protection and flood control. They claim that this is due to abnormal weather conditions caused by global warming and that the automobile industry, which has affected global warming, should compensate. Even though regulations had already been established to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the automobile industry below the standard amount, the industry failed to implement them, leading to a lawsuit being filed.
As a result of the lawsuit, if the automobile industry loses the suit for damages, the automobile industry will inevitably incur a huge cost burden. Depending on the outcome of the lawsuit, it is expected that exports to the United States by domestic automobile industries such as Hyundai Motor Company and Kia Motors will be affected.
The effects of global warming can be seen throughout Earth's long history. 200 million years ago, at the end of the Permian period, the Earth, which was the home of various animals and plants, turned into ashes overnight. It was a disaster caused by a series of volcanic eruptions that erupted lava and caused the Earth's temperature to rise rapidly. Over the next 100,000 years, dark red acid rain fell from the sky, the sea spewed out terrible methane gas, and 95% of life on Earth became extinct.
The continued abnormal weather events this century are analyzed as the effects of global warming. A study was recently published in which an expert calculated that the temperature rise at the time was only 6 degrees Celsius. Additionally, if the current temperature rise trend continues, it is estimated that the Earth's temperature will rise by 6 degrees Celsius over the next few decades. It's no different from having a terrible outcome predicted.
The current average temperature of the Earth is about 15 degrees. The upper limit of the annual temperature increase rate is 2.5 degrees. In Europe and other Western countries, the unit of measurement for temperature is expressed in degrees Fahrenheit. Americans' favorite temperature is 70 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 21 degrees Celsius. The limit temperature for humans is 37 degrees Celsius. The average human body temperature is 37 degrees, so the optimal temperature of the atmosphere should not exceed 37 degrees. Survival is possible only when the temperature is maintained below 37 degrees. When the patient's body temperature reaches 40 degrees, he or she is in critical condition from the high fever.
The hottest time on Earth was last year, when temperatures in some parts of the United States soared to 115 degrees Fahrenheit. This is 46.1 degrees Celsius. It has already exceeded the human body temperature limit by 9 degrees. The temperature difference on Earth between winter and summer, and between cold and hot regions, is considered to be an average of 4 degrees. The theory is that if the temperature rises by just 6 degrees due to warming, humanity will not be able to withstand it and the Earth will perish.
As the ice sheet in Antarctica melts, global warming is accelerating, with sea levels rising and average temperatures rising by more than 0.1 degrees every year. The island nation of Tuvalu is submerged in water due to rising sea levels, and all citizens are migrating to neighboring countries. Conflicts due to global warming will occur everywhere. California's claim for damages from the automobile industry is only the beginning. The outbreak of war, launching rockets, nuclear tests, or using nuclear weapons affects global warming, and air pollution and water shortages due to depletion of water resources also affect global warming. Ultimately, a situation will arise where humanity will have to completely stop urban development, which is a convenience facility for life, in order to preserve forest resources that neutralize atmospheric temperature.
