ko-news-notices-319-8372c75064.title: Electronic Nautical Charts to Adopt License-Based Sales for the First Time among Government Publications
ko-news-notices-319-8372c75064.text:
Electronic Nautical Charts to Adopt License-Based Sales for the First Time among Government Publications
2022-03-02
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Yu-seop Jeong) announced that it will introduce license-based sales to encourage use of electronic nautical charts and provide services tailored to users’ needs.
Under the new service, purchasing an electronic chart will also grant the user one year of structured maintenance and update services. Several leading maritime nations already use this sales model.
Since 2000, the agency has provided 212 electronic nautical charts covering Korea’s coasts. Until now, each chart had a two-part pricing model: an initial purchase fee of KRW 20,500 and a renewal fee of KRW 9,600.
Users have increasingly called for lower prices. They have also faced the risk of maritime accidents from using outdated chart data, while differences in distribution models have made international circulation of Korean electronic charts difficult.
With the license model, a one-year license for each electronic chart will cost KRW 11,000. More effective user management is also expected to improve the quality of chart-update services.
An agency official said the license service would provide a basis for expanding distribution both in Korea and abroad. Lower prices and systematic quality management are expected to increase use of electronic charts and contribute substantially to navigational safety.

ko-news-notices-320-8372c75064.title: Establishment of comprehensive marine environment management foundation
ko-news-notices-320-8372c75064.text:
Establishment of comprehensive marine environment management foundation
2022-03-02
On the 22nd, three bills, including the Marine Environment Management Act, passed the National Assembly.
In the future, pre- and post-management of indiscriminate use of the ocean will be thorough, and monitoring of various sources of marine pollution will be further strengthened.
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries announced that the ‘Marine Environment Management Act’, which aims to comprehensively and systematically manage the marine environment and actively respond to new marine environmental demands, passed the plenary session of the National Assembly on the 22nd.
Accordingly, the ‘Sea Area Use Evaluation System’ has been introduced, and anyone who wishes to engage in marine use activities above a certain scale, such as collecting sea aggregates, must undergo a ‘Sea Area Use Impact Assessment’ after collecting opinions from stakeholders.
In addition, even after the impact assessment, if damage to the marine environment occurs due to violation of obligations by ocean users, the government may take necessary measures such as license cancellation, business suspension, and restoration to original condition.
In addition, a new reporting system for marine facilities will be established to strengthen preventive management of marine pollution sources.
A project management team for each sea area will also be established to intensively manage polluted sea areas such as Sihwa Lake and Masan Bay.
In addition, systematic investigations will be conducted on new sources of marine pollution, such as persistent organic pollutants, and the use of harmful anti-fouling paints that have a detrimental effect on the marine environment will be banned.
In addition, in order to produce accurate and reliable marine environmental data, a quality control system for marine environmental measurement and analysis institutions was implemented and a ‘measurement and analysis ability certificate’ was granted to suitable measurement and analysis institutions as a result of evaluations such as verification of data, thereby increasing the accuracy and reliability of basic marine environmental data.
The Korea Marine Pollution Control Association, which was established after the Sea Prince accident in 1996 and has mainly been in charge of oil control work, has been expanded and reorganized into the Marine Environment Management Corporation and is being fostered as a comprehensive marine environment specialized organization that can comprehensively carry out various projects necessary for the conservation and management of the marine environment in addition to oil control work.
With the enactment of this law, marine environment management has so far been limited to passive activities such as post-processing in the event of pollution accidents, but now we have various policy tools to carry out more active marine environment management.
In addition, amendments to the Fishery Products Quality Control Act, the Fisheries Promotion Act, and the Oil Pollution Damages Guarantee Act also passed the National Assembly on this day.
The Fishery Products Quality Control Act strengthens penalties for violators of false labeling of origin and genetically modified marine products to ensure the safety of marine products.
The Farming Fisheries Promotion Act transfers government affairs, such as the establishment of aquatic disease management offices, to mayors and county governors.
The Oil Pollution Damage Compensation Guarantee Act makes administrative procedures transparent, such as skipping entry and exit inspection when a ship owner submits relevant documents such as an insurance contract certificate, and requiring advance notice at the time of entry and inspection and notification of the results.

ko-news-notices-321-8372c75064.title: Establishment of Ulsan Port Authority in the second half of 2007, accelerating port privatization
ko-news-notices-321-8372c75064.text:
Establishment of Ulsan Port Authority in the second half of 2007, accelerating port privatization
2022-03-02
Ulsan Port Authority Establishment Planning Team begins operation from January of the new year
Ulsan Port Authority is expected to be established as early as July next year. On the 22nd, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries jointly formed the Ulsan Port Authority Establishment Preparation Committee with related ministries and Ulsan Metropolitan City, and announced that it would establish an Establishment Promotion Planning Team as a working body to support the committee and begin work on January 2 of the new year.
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries plans to establish the Ulsan Port Authority in July next year after six months of preparations, including evaluation of national property, investment, and organization and personnel composition.
The Ulsan Port Authority Establishment Committee is chaired by the Vice Minister of Oceans and Fisheries and consists of seven members, including the Director of the National Treasury of the Ministry of Finance and Economy, the Director of the Public Innovation Division of the Ministry of Planning and Budget, the Deputy Mayor of Ulsan Metropolitan City, the Director of the Economic and Trade Bureau, and the personnel of the Ulsan Development Research Institute. It will deliberate and decide on major matters related to the establishment of the Corporation, such as recommending the first president and appointing port members, until the Port Corporation is launched.
The Establishment Promotion Planning Team, which is established as a dedicated organization within the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, consists of a total of 9 people, including employees dispatched from Ulsan Metropolitan City and the Ulsan Regional Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Office. The planning team will carry out various tasks such as appraisal and investment of state-owned properties necessary for the establishment of the Port Authority, establishment and implementation of staff recruitment plans, registration of establishment, and establishment commemoration ceremony.
So far, Ulsan Port has been evaluated as a port that can successfully introduce Port Authority (PA), following Busan Port and Incheon Port, with stable port revenue and high financial independence among national trade ports.
As of 2005, Ulsan Port's cargo handling volume was 162 million tons, ranking third after Busan Port (217 million tons), and its port usage fee income was 41.7 billion won, which is evaluated as having a foundation for financial independence.
Once the Ulsan Port Authority is established, it is expected that it will be possible to lay the foundation for Ulsan Port to develop into a central port for liquid cargo in Northeast Asia through the introduction of private management techniques and marketing activities that reflect the characteristics of the port.
An official from the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries announced that they plan to gradually introduce PA and privatize ports that have a large impact on the national economy and have a high level of financial independence, such as Yeosu and Gwangyang ports.

ko-news-notices-322-8372c75064.title: Promotion of Joint Use of Marine Survey Vessels
ko-news-notices-322-8372c75064.text:
Promotion of Joint Use of Marine Survey Vessels
2022-03-02
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries has decided to promote joint use of marine survey vessels operated by its affiliated organizations and other related institutions, in order to use them more efficiently.
To support joint operation, the ministry plans to publish next year’s marine-survey-vessel operating plan on its website and encourage universities, research institutes, and other marine-related organizations to participate. Institutions with strong records of joint operation will receive incentives.
Over the longer term, the ministry also plans to establish institutional arrangements to encourage shared use of all survey equipment, including vessels. One proposal is a tentatively named “Marine Survey Vessel and Equipment Shared-Use Center.”
Potential joint-research work includes 71 projects such as fisheries-resource surveys by the National Institute of Fisheries Science; 21 projects such as surveys of currents along Korea’s coast by the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency; and 60 projects such as research on sediment transport and depositional environments by the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute.
The ministry’s affiliated survey fleet currently consists of 25 vessels: 15 operated by the National Institute of Fisheries Science, seven by the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency, and three by the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute. Their construction cost, calculated at the price of newly built vessels, totaled KRW 100 billion; annual operating costs reach KRW 10 billion.
The ministry estimates that shared use could save more than KRW 10 million per vessel per day.
This year, the ministry made its survey vessels available through its website for 42 projects involving companies, research institutes, universities, and individual researchers.

Following the briefing, President Roh moved to the Lotte Hotel and had lunch with 300 people, including local businessmen and civic groups, to collect various opinions from people from all walks of life on development plans for the Busan region.
The North Port Redevelopment Project is a large-scale national project with a total of 9.3 trillion won invested from 2008 to 2020. ko-news-notices-326-8372c75064.title: Tide Predictions and Sea-Parting Information Now Available in Car Navigation Systems
ko-news-notices-326-8372c75064.text:
Tide Predictions and Sea-Parting Information Now Available in Car Navigation Systems
2022-03-02
Drivers can now look up predicted high and low tides and sea-parting information for Korea’s coasts.
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Yu-seop Jeong) announced that it will provide predicted high- and low-tide times, sea-level heights, and sea-parting information for 47 major coastal ports through car-navigation systems.
Use of tide information is growing as rising living standards and the popularity of marine activities such as recreational fishing bring more people to the coast. These data need to be checked frequently in the field, but access had been limited because they were mainly available online.
To view tide forecasts and sea-parting information in a navigation system, users can buy one that includes the data or update an existing system through the map provider’s website. The data will be updated each year.
An agency official said that including the information in navigation systems would help overcome the limitations of internet-only access and could support wider distribution of marine and other information.
The agency is discussing with navigation companies how to expand tide information—which is currently included by only one navigation-software provider—to all systems during the first half of this year, along with a broader range of data.

ko-news-notices-327-8372c75064.title: Busan New Port Current Observations to Be Available Online in Real Time
ko-news-notices-327-8372c75064.text:
Busan New Port Current Observations to Be Available Online in Real Time
2022-03-02
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency announced on the 5th that it will begin publishing real-time observations of water movement around Busan New Port online this week.
The service uses two high-frequency radars (HF radars) installed along the coast of the new port and on Geoje Island. They observe water movement hourly from the entrance of Gadeok Channel to Busan New Port and provide the results online in real time.
Unlike conventional current-measuring equipment, the high-frequency radar transmits radio waves from a shore station toward the sea surface and measures the frequency shift in the reflected signal. This makes it possible to determine the speed and direction of water movement and continue observations at night and during sea fog or typhoons.
Vessel traffic at Busan New Port has increased since it opened in January last year, and cargo volumes are expected to rise substantially, making current information essential for the area.
An agency official said the real-time service was expected to support safe navigation for vessels entering and leaving Busan New Port, Masan Port, and Jinhae Port, and to be useful for oil-spill response, marine-accident response, search and rescue, and other purposes.
Current information for the new port is available in the Marine Data Room’s tidal-current section on the agency website: http://www.nori.go.kr.
Reporter Lee Sang-yoon

ko-news-notices-328-8372c75064.title: Marine Environment Technology Center Planned for Busan
ko-news-notices-328-8372c75064.text:
Marine Environment Technology Center Planned for Busan
2022-03-02
A tentatively named Marine Environment Technology Center is expected to be established in Busan to conduct marine-environment research and development, education and training, and public outreach.
On the 5th, Busan City said the Korea Marine Pollution Control Association—the organization expected to be succeeded by the future Marine Environment Management Corporation and the proposed center’s lead organization—had recently asked the city to survey potential sites in Busan by the end of this month. The request followed the full revision and promulgation of the Marine Pollution Prevention Act as the Marine Environment Management Act on the 19th of the previous month. The law provides for the establishment of the Marine Environment Management Corporation, with a technology center planned as an affiliated institution. Busan immediately began searching for a site. Candidate locations include Centum City in U-dong, Haeundae-gu; the Munhyeon Financial Complex in Munhyeon-dong, Nam-gu; and coastal areas of Gijang County.
The center is planned to cost about KRW 10 billion, entirely from national-government funds. It will occupy a 5,000-pyeong site, with a building footprint of 1,000 pyeong, one basement level, four above-ground floors, and a total floor area of 2,400 pyeong. Planned facilities include research and education buildings, residential quarters, a red-tide response training area, a coastal oil-spill response training area, and equipment-testing facilities.
Once the site is confirmed by the end of this month, the city plans to prepare a master plan and solicit design and construction proposals. It expects to select a contractor in the second half of this year, begin site preparation and construction in the first half of next year, and complete the center around December next year.
A Busan City official said that once completed, the center would enable the country to provide efficient response training for marine oil pollution and other incidents at the level required by international conventions.
(Segye Ilbo, Busan = Reporter Jeon Sang-hu)

ko-news-notices-334-8372c75064.title: [New Ocean Era] Uldolmok Tidal-Current Power Plant
ko-news-notices-334-8372c75064.text:
[New Ocean Era] Uldolmok Tidal-Current Power Plant
2022-03-02
The current is very fast due to the narrow channel and rocky seabed.
World's largest tidal power plant produces first electricity in November
“Uuu~shooaa~, rumbling~shooaa~”
It was definitely a cry. It sounded like the cry of a man with a deep voice, or the howl of an animal. Uldolmok, the strait between Jindo, Jeollanam-do and Hwawon Peninsula, Haenam-gun. There is a reason why it is called ‘Myeongryang (鳴梁)’ with the meaning of ‘the road where the sea cries’.
The current of Uldolmok seen from Jindo Bridge during low tide was still strong and unstoppable. The saying of the people here, “If people on the land look at the swirling currents of Uldolmok for a long time, they will get seasick,” was definitely not a lie.
A tidal-current power plant, a technology still unfamiliar to many, will be built at Uldolmok, known for its exceptionally fast currents. It will generate electricity by harnessing those currents.
The Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute (KORDI), which led the technology development, has completed fabrication of the turbines and generating structures for the world’s largest test tidal-current power plant, a 1,000 kW facility at Uldolmok scheduled to begin generating power in November. Only on-site structural installation and electrical and mechanical work remain. Following the announcement, KORDI has received repeated requests for technology transfer and joint research from coastal countries including Indonesia and Vietnam.
Lee Kwang-soo, head of the Coastal Development Research Division, said, “Our country has almost achieved technological independence, having completed the commercialization of the ‘helical turbine,’ a power generation experimental device, through tidal-current power experiments since 2002,” and added, “Countries such as the United Kingdom, which installed a 150 kW test power generation turbine one step ahead of us, are also paying close attention.”
The reason Uldolmok is able to demonstrate the value of fast water currents is because of its unique narrow channel and seabed topography. Uldolmok is narrow, about 294m wide, and the water level difference between the south and west widens by up to 2m during high and low tides. The seafloor has no sedimentary layers and is made up of highly curved rock. As a large amount of seawater tries to pass through the narrow strait, the current inevitably becomes faster.
In fact, the current speed of Uldolmok reaches an average speed of 5.5 m per second at the depth and a maximum speed of 6.5 m per second at the surface of the sea. Normally, when a flood occurs in the Han River, the current speed is about 2 to 3 meters per second, enough to wash away a car, which is an incredible speed.
However, the high current speed at Uldolmok also poses a challenge for tidal-current power generation. Because the current is so fast, it is not easy to install a water turbine power plant structure weighing 790 tons.
Above all, drilling work to insert six large iron pipes (137 cm in diameter), which formed the main frame of the structure, into the Uldolmok seafloor rock was impossible due to the high flow rate. Therefore, Hyundai Engineering & Construction, which was in charge of construction, changed the installation method by first putting down the structure, inserting a drilling machine into the iron pipe, drilling a hole to a depth of 8m, and then inserting another iron pipe to pour concrete.
Kim Joo-sik, head of the Uldolmok Experimental Tidal Current Power Plant construction site, said, “It was impossible to perform drilling work on a barge shaking at a high speed, so we changed the construction method. Although the changed installation method is the first to be attempted in the world, there is a good chance of success.” The structure will be installed at the end of April.
The test plant's annual electricity generation amounts to 1.2 GWh (1.2 million kW) per year. This is the amount of electricity that 300 households (based on average monthly consumption of 300 kW per household) can use for one year. However, this does not mean that the power originally expected can be stably produced. This is because a barrier must be installed on the structure to prevent marine debris such as refrigerators and TVs, which are swept away by the strong current of Uldolmok, from hitting the water wheel. Experts predict that power generation efficiency will drop by about 10% due to the installation of barriers.
So, why is tidal-current power generation at Uldolmok in the spotlight as a next-generation alternative energy source? First of all, unlike wave power, solar power, or wind power generation, long-term prediction of power generation is possible due to the periodicity of high and low tides.
In addition, it is the most environmentally friendly as it does not require dams like tidal power generation using the ebb and flow of the tides, and has a significant energy import substitution effect. In fact, if the 50,000 kW Uldolmok commercial tidal current power plant is built by 2012, it will produce 123 GWh (123 million kW) of electricity annually, which will not only replace energy imports worth 12 billion won (200,000 barrels of crude oil) each year, but also reduce carbon dioxide by 76,000 tons per year.
Park Jin-soon, a senior engineer at KORDI, explained, “In a situation where the environment and energy are changing toward coexistence, tidal power generation is the most suitable and economical method.”
Uldolmok, where the test tidal power plant will be built, will have a tremendous impact on the local economy. Jindo-gun is already full of expectations that Uldolmok Tidal Power Plant will create new wealth. In order to promote the tidal power plant and turn it into a tourist resource, the county decided to build a marine energy park on a 6,050 pyeong site in Nokjin-ri, Gunnae-myeon by 2009.
Jindo-gun predicts that the Marine Energy Park, which will feature an exhibition hall, an observatory, and amusement facilities where visitors can directly experience marine-energy systems such as tidal-current and tidal-range power generation, will bring about a production inducement effect of KRW 24.597 billion and an income inducement effect of KRW 6.849 billion.
Hwang Gyu-woong, head of Jindo-gun fishing village and fishing port, said, “Once the tidal power plant and marine energy park are built at Uldolmok, the battle site of Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s Battle of Myeongnyang, Uldolmok is expected to not only emerge as a historical tourist site and science education center, but also play a significant role in the local economy.”
Jindo (Uldolmok) = Reporter Ahn Gyeong-ho khan@hk.co.kr

ko-news-notices-335-8372c75064.title: Beach Nourishment Identified as the Best Method to Prevent Erosion at Jungmun Beach
ko-news-notices-335-8372c75064.text:
Beach Nourishment Identified as the Best Method to Prevent Erosion at Jungmun Beach
2022-03-02
A commissioned study has identified adding new sand to the beach as the most suitable method for preventing erosion at Jungmun Beach.
At a briefing on the project to establish a monitoring system for erosion changes at Jungmun Beach, held at Seogwipo City Hall’s First Building on the 21st, the study team assessed beach nourishment as the most suitable erosion-control measure for Jungmun Beach.
According to the study, the area behind Jungmun Beach consists mostly of coastal dunes. However, continued erosion has caused rapid changes, including the collapse of planted dune areas, loss of vegetation, and erosion-related collapse.
The analysis found that reinforcing the dune foundations is necessary to prevent dune erosion at its source, and that beach nourishment is a suitable way to reinforce them.
Beach nourishment protects the shore by adding sand to the beach to absorb incoming wave energy and reduce reflected waves. Compared with other methods, it costs less and directly widens the beach.
Its disadvantages are the need for ongoing maintenance and the difficulty of finding a suitable source of sand.
The study team also said that fences should be installed alongside nourishment to keep visitors away from the dunes.
Because visitor access is generally not restricted at Jungmun Beach, a wooden boardwalk was proposed as a way to protect the dune foundations.
The team added that longer-term monitoring is needed to understand how the beach changes. Detailed marine surveys should also examine external drivers of sandy-beach erosion, including weather, waves, and currents. %scoop@jejunews.com

ko-news-notices-336-8372c75064.title: Documentary Warning About Global Warming Draws on Al Gore’s Lectures
ko-news-notices-336-8372c75064.text:
Documentary Warning About Global Warming Draws on Al Gore’s Lectures
2022-03-02
An Inconvenient Truth is a documentary based on environmental lectures by former U.S. Vice President Al Gore.
The film shows Gore traveling around the world to warn audiences about the seriousness of global warming, as well as scenes from his daily life as an environmental activist. In that sense, Gore is the film’s central figure. It opened in the United States in May of the previous year and earned more than $24 million at the box office, an unusual result for a documentary. After his presidential election loss, the film gave Gore, who had been regrouping, an opportunity to attract public attention again. It opened in Korea in September of the previous year but was not a box-office success.
The film warns that if carbon dioxide emissions from burning oil and coal continue to rise as they have, the Earth will become excessively hot in the near future and face an environmental disaster. It vividly shows scenes such as the melting snow on Mount Kilimanjaro, made famous by an Ernest Hemingway novel, and collapsing polar glaciers. It also predicts that low-lying areas of Manhattan in New York and Shanghai will be flooded and that severe storms and droughts will strike in turn.
The film indirectly criticizes President George W. Bush for refusing to ratify the Kyoto Protocol, which was intended to reduce carbon dioxide emissions. It also urges viewers to use environmentally friendly products and vote for politicians who pursue environmentally friendly policies. Gore published a book of the same title the previous year. It was also translated and published in Korea under the subtitle “Al Gore’s Urgent Environmental Report.”
Los Angeles — Reporter Joo Jeong-wan

ko-news-notices-338-8372c75064.title: Beach Erosion of 10% Could Reduce Economic Value by 14%
ko-news-notices-338-8372c75064.text:
Beach Erosion of 10% Could Reduce Economic Value by 14%
2022-03-02
An estimate found that erosion of about 10% of a beach could reduce its economic value by about 14%.
On the 7th, the Korea Maritime Institute (KMI) said that it had reached this estimate in a report titled “Economic Assessment of Coastal Erosion Damage Caused by Marine Sand Extraction.” The study estimated the loss in value at Iilre Beach in Ongjin County, Gyeonggi Province, which had been cited as a case of coastal erosion associated with marine sand extraction.
KMI estimated that the average daily willingness to pay per person wishing to visit Iilre Beach was KRW 40,846–56,930, and that the average willingness to pay per 100 m² was KRW 45.9–64.
KMI cautioned that multiplying a per-unit value by the total area does not represent the total economic loss from beach erosion.
To estimate how erosion affects beach value, KMI analyzed how marginal erosion affects visitors’ willingness to pay. For Iilre Beach, when 10% of the beach was eroded, the maximum estimated daily willingness to pay fell from KRW 56,930 to KRW 48,985.
KMI said the results indicated that 10% erosion at a recreational beach could cause an approximately 14% loss in economic value.
Based on the Iilre Beach case, KMI estimated that erosion of 20%, 30%, and 40% would reduce a beach’s economic value by 27%, 39%, and 50.55%, respectively.
KMI said the amount of marine sand extracted from the waters around Iilre Beach—the basis for the analysis—was officially estimated at several thousand cubic meters, while the unofficial amount was thought to be enormous. Local residents argued that marine sand extraction was the main cause of erosion on the beach.
KMI noted that Korea relies more heavily on marine sand extraction than any other country and that developing alternative resources would be difficult in the near term. Since environmental concerns do not currently make a complete ban feasible, it said, a range of policy measures and alternatives would be needed.
KMI recommended creating a database of marine environmental assessment data, introducing cumulative environmental impact assessment, and strengthening monitoring of marine sand extraction.
Yonhap News (yulsid@yna.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-339-8372c75064.title: Seosan and Taean Divided Over Garorim Bay Tidal Power Project
ko-news-notices-339-8372c75064.text:
Seosan and Taean Divided Over Garorim Bay Tidal Power Project
2022-03-02
Seosan City and Taean County in South Chungcheong Province, once closely linked, are showing signs of conflict as their interests diverge over a proposed tidal power plant in Garorim Bay on the West Sea.
According to Seosan City on the 9th, it recently collected opinions from 13 fishing-village cooperatives in three local districts around Garorim Bay—Daesan-eup, Palbong-myeon, and Jigok-myeon—on construction of the tidal power plant. Eleven opposed it, as did the fisheries cooperatives and the Seosan-Taean Environmental Movement Federation.
Opposition has intensified in Jigok-myeon, where residents have begun a signature campaign to cancel the construction plan.
Residents fear that a tidal power plant would change the tidal range and the bay’s currents, reducing tidal flats and disrupting the ecosystem, damaging fish food chains and spawning grounds for fish and shellfish, reducing seafood production, and harming local livelihoods.
They also oppose the project because the deep bay is considered a suitable site for a new port, and building the plant would permanently rule out that opportunity.
Choi Jang-hwan, chair of the Jigok-myeon Development Council, said, “Garorim Bay is a spawning ground for fisheries resources such as crabs, octopuses, and prawns, and the basis of local residents’ livelihoods. A tidal power plant that threatens their right to make a living must not be built.”
By contrast, residents of Taean County privately hope the plant could help spur regional development.
The Iwon-myeon area of Taean, where Garorim Bay lies, has developed more slowly and has less development potential than southern Taean, including Anmyeondo Island. Residents therefore see the tidal power plant as a possible catalyst for development.
They also expect the plant’s breakwater to serve as a link between Daesan in Seosan and Iwon in Taean, improving access for tourists visiting Taean.
A Taean County official said, “A tidal power plant does not block the waterway like a tidal embankment, so it is not reasonable to assume that tidal power generation necessarily means environmental destruction. In particular, the breakwater would replace a bridge project costing KRW 170 billion and become a new environmentally friendly tourism resource.”
A Seosan City official said, “There are differences of opinion among regions and residents about building the plant, but it is difficult for the city to state an official position before the project plan becomes concrete. We will review public opinion comprehensively and decide how to respond.”
Garorim Bay has a large tidal range of 7–9 m and is considered one of Korea’s best sites for a tidal power plant, along with Sihwa Lake in Gyeonggi Province, where a plant is now under construction. Korea Western Power plans to close off the bay with a 2-km tidal embankment and build a 480-MW tidal power plant. Feasibility studies and environmental impact assessment procedures are under way.
Yonhap News (seokyee@yna.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-342-8372c75064.title: [New Ocean Age] The Mysterious Water: Deep Ocean Water
ko-news-notices-342-8372c75064.text:
[New Ocean Age] The Mysterious Water: Deep Ocean Water
2022-03-02
Off Ohori, Jukwang-myeon, Goseong County, Gangwon Province, a large intake pipeline about 2.45 km long runs along the seabed toward land. It is used to draw “East Sea water” from depths of 300 m and 500 m. The water brought up through the seabed intake pipe is no ordinary water: it is deep ocean water, the “mysterious water” that has remained in the deep sea for at least 300 years.

Growing interest for its many potential uses
Dr. Deok-su Moon of the Deep Ocean Water Research Center at the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute said, “Deep ocean water is a resource for the future, with enormous potential for use not only as drinking water but also in agriculture and fisheries, medicine, beauty care, and health products. It is an especially important national resource for Korea, which the United Nations classifies as a water-scarce country.”

Deep ocean water is seawater found at depths greater than 200 m, beyond the reach of sunlight. With no sunlight, its temperature remains at or below 2°C. Photosynthetic phytoplankton and seaweed cannot live there, so pathogens and organic pollutants associated with them are scarce.

By contrast, organic matter from the surface sinks and decomposes, releasing and accumulating nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus. The water is therefore rich in inorganic nutrients, and it also contains abundant minerals, including calcium and magnesium, that support cellular processes.

Deep ocean water has many uses. One major use is drinking water: once desalinated, it is clean water that can be consumed directly and can be made into a functional beverage rich in natural minerals. The salt recovered during desalination is also a clean salt, distinct from ordinary salt.

Developed and used in only five countries

Even after being brought ashore through intake pipes, deep ocean water remains at about 5°C, making it useful for air-conditioning and ice-making facilities. One hundred tonnes of deep ocean water can provide a full day of cooling for 8 to 16 households.

It is also rich in nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon, making it suitable for seaweed cultivation and aquaculture of cold-water fish. In laver cultivation, for example, growth is about twice as fast as with ordinary surface water.

In medicine, deep ocean water is used in treatments for conditions such as atopic dermatitis. In agriculture, it is used to prevent excessive growth when raising seedlings such as peppers and cabbage. Desalinated deep ocean water is also used in skin-care products, cosmetics, and food additives.

After use, deep ocean water is discharged into nearby waters with substantial nutrients, which can help restore and maintain the balance of the fishing-ground environment. The East Sea Fisheries Research Institute recently confirmed that, after deep ocean water was discharged continuously for a year off Jukdo near Ohori, Jukwang-myeon, the number of seaweed species in the waters north of Jukdo increased from 15 to 27. In short, deep ocean water is a resource with virtually nothing to waste.

Dr. Seung-won Lee of the research center said, “Only five countries—Korea, the United States, Japan, Norway, and Taiwan—have succeeded in developing deep ocean water. We are working with domestic universities and research institutes to identify ways to develop and apply this resource for multiple purposes in Korea.”

The East Coast: a trove of deep ocean water

Deep ocean water, a potential “gold mine of the sea,” is present in vast quantities in Korea’s East Sea. The international oceanographic community recognizes the East Sea as a naturally favorable region for deep ocean water. In the global circulation of seawater, water reaches Greenland’s glacial regions, cools and becomes denser, sinks to the seabed, and flows onward. It later rises to the surface in the northern North Pacific, cools again, and sinks. A full circuit of the globe by deep water takes about 2,000 years.

Although the East Sea is surrounded by the Korean Peninsula, the Russian coast, and the Japanese archipelago and has an average depth of 1,684 m, its four connecting straits are narrow and less than 200 m deep. As a result, little deep water is exchanged with neighboring seas, and deep water forms, circulates, and changes within the East Sea.

That is why researchers call it the “East Sea Proper Water.” The volume of deep water in the East Sea is currently estimated at 3 × 10¹⁹ tonnes, and its internal circulation period is estimated at 300 to 700 years.

Related bill has languished in the National Assembly for more than two years

Korea has abundant deep ocean water resources but has not yet been able to turn them into economic value. The “Act on the Development and Management of Deep Ocean Water,” which the government announced it would introduce to support systematic development, has not passed the National Assembly in more than two years. Japan and Taiwan do not have laws specifically governing deep ocean water, but Korea is pursuing legislation because of concerns about unregulated development and excessive competition.

Eight companies, including Kooksoondang (Baekseju), Aekyung Industrial (cosmetics), Sempio Foods (soy sauce), and Hyundai Pharmaceutical (ion drinks), have developed deep-ocean-water prototypes but have not been able to put them on the market. Developers, saying they can no longer wait, are now acting on the position that they will proceed with projects within the framework of current law.

Kim Hong-ki, CEO of Ulleung Mineral Co., Ltd., said, “With the National Assembly holding things up, the number of domestic development companies has fallen from about 20 to five.” He added, “Since the Drinking Water Management Act was amended last June to allow drinking water to be made from seawater, we will use that law as the basis for pursuing deep-ocean-water development.”

Local governments along the East Coast—including Gangwon Province, Goseong County, Yangyang County, Gangneung City, Uljin County, and Ulleung County in North Gyeongsang Province—are also eagerly awaiting passage of the bill as they seek to attract businesses, confident in the growth potential of the deep-ocean-water market. They see it as a potential boost for the East Coast’s stagnant local economy.

The current bill would allow deep-ocean-water developers to pay water-use fees as taxes, with the revenue available for local projects.

Professor Jong-ho Lee of Kyungdong University’s Department of Deep Ocean Water Science predicted, “Businesses related to deep ocean water could have a substantial economic impact by creating jobs, attracting tourists, and increasing residents’ incomes.”

Jointly planned by this newspaper and the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries
Goseong — Reporter Gyeong-ho Ahn (Hankook Ilbo, khan@hk.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-195-8372c75064.title: National Oceanographic Research Institute Holds Hearing on Amendments to the Hydrographic Services Act Regulations
ko-news-notices-195-8372c75064.text:
National Oceanographic Research Institute Holds Hearing on Amendments to the Hydrographic Services Act Regulations
2022-03-02
Wide-ranging views sought on key issues, including exemptions from general hydrographic surveys
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director General Jong-rok Park, held a public hearing on amendments to the Enforcement Decree and Enforcement Rules of the Hydrographic Services Act at 3 p.m. on September 1, 2005, in the institute’s main conference room.
The Act had been amended and promulgated on July 29, 2005. The hearing brought together working-level officials from central and local governments and representatives of relevant industry groups to gather a broad range of views on the implementing regulations. Key issues included which marine construction projects should be exempt from the general hydrographic-survey requirement, how to subdivide hydrographic-survey business categories, and how to revise registration criteria.
For marine construction projects extending over several years, participants considered whether to conduct a hydrographic survey at partial completion—taking account of the degree of completion and whether the work could be used—or to conduct a general hydrographic survey after the project was fully completed. The institute said it would reflect an appropriate approach in the regulations.
There was no disagreement about further subdividing the categories for registered hydrographic-survey businesses, an issue of interest to industry. However, participants noted that businesses might have difficulty securing enough qualified technical staff in the short term as the volume of survey work increased.
The institute emphasized revising registration criteria for hydrographic businesses so that eligibility would be limited to people with relevant technical education and work experience, in order to ensure hydrographic surveys met international standards for accuracy.
An institute official said the agency would review the hearing’s discussion and incorporate feasible proposals into the draft amendments.
The draft amendments were scheduled to undergo the necessary procedures, including public notice, around mid-September. If approved by the Cabinet in December, they were expected to take effect at the end of January of the following year.

ko-news-notices-196-8372c75064.title: [News] East Sea Sea-Level Rise Rate Twice the Global Average
ko-news-notices-196-8372c75064.text:
[News] East Sea Sea-Level Rise Rate Twice the Global Average
2022-03-02
The average rate of sea-level rise in the East Sea over the past decade has been far higher than the global average. Analysis of satellite-altimetry observations by Dr. Seok-gu Kang’s team at the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute (KORDI), headed by President Ki-dae Yeom, found an average annual rise of 5.4 ± 0.3 mm over the past nine years. The rate in the southern East Sea was especially high, at 6.6 ± 0.4 mm per year—about twice the global average for a similar period, 2.8 ± 0.4 mm per year. The team was also the first to identify thermal expansion caused by warming in the upper layer of the East Sea as the main driver of the rise there. At a time when researchers were debating whether global sea-level rise over recent decades to a century was mainly caused by the loss of land-based glaciers or by thermal expansion, this study was significant for identifying the primary driver in a semi-enclosed basin such as the East Sea.
The findings came from a KORDI basic research project, “Elemental Technologies for Climate-Change Monitoring and Prediction,” led by Dr. Jae-hak Lee, and were produced in collaboration with a team at a Canadian ocean research institute.
The study drew on TOPEX/Poseidon satellite-altimetry data, East Sea temperature and salinity data, and sea-level observations from tide gauges in Korea and Japan. The paper proposed that thermal-expansion-driven sea-level changes in the East Sea occur over long periods of 10 to 20 years and are closely related to variations in the North Pacific heat budget. The researchers noted that the recent rapid change might be part of a longer-term trend. They called for continued sea-level monitoring in the East Sea and further research into the possibility that the mechanisms driving sea-level rise may change over the long term in connection with ocean variability. The paper was published in the July issue of the Journal of Geophysical Research, a leading geoscience journal published by the American Geophysical Union, and was scheduled to be presented as an invited paper at the 14th meeting of the North Pacific Marine Science Organization (PICES) in Vladivostok in September.
More than two billion people worldwide live within 100 km of a coast, and sea-level change is considered a major indicator of climate change. Understanding the causes and rate of long-term sea-level rise is therefore a matter of interest to scientists and the public alike. Dr. Waleed Abdalati of NASA said, “If sea level rises by one meter, about 100 million people will be affected.” In the 1990s, scientists forecast a rise of about 50 cm over the 21st century—equivalent to 5 mm per year. This study found that the East Sea’s rate had already exceeded that pace during the decade or so since the early 1990s, while the global rate over the same period was about 60% of the forecast rate.
A paper published in Science the previous year by glaciologist Dr. R. Thomas and colleagues reported that ice from the West Antarctic mainland was flowing into the Amundsen Sea and accelerating sea-level rise. They said the glaciers in the Amundsen Sea basin alone contain enough freshwater to raise global sea level by 1.3 m. Given the enormous ice mass in Greenland and Antarctica, global warming could cause sea levels to rise more—or the annual rate to accelerate—beyond current projections. NASA was actively researching the issue, including through ICESat, launched in 2003 to observe the mass balance of the continental ice sheets in Antarctica and Greenland.
Climate change is also expected to increase short-term sea-level fluctuations as well as long-term changes. Warmer oceans, together with other factors, can strengthen typhoons through ocean–typhoon interactions, which is expected to intensify typhoon-driven storm surges. Alongside research into long-term sea-level variability, KORDI planned to launch a national research program on short-term variability, including intensity changes caused by ocean–typhoon interactions, precision storm-surge forecasting, and methods to predict how ocean warming caused by global warming affects typhoon intensity.

ko-news-notices-197-8372c75064.title: National Oceanographic Research Institute Begins Survey of Currents in the East China Sea
ko-news-notices-197-8372c75064.text:
National Oceanographic Research Institute Begins Survey of Currents in the East China Sea
2022-03-02
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director General Jong-rok Park, announced that it would conduct a joint survey with Pusan National University in the East China Sea—the inflow route for the Yellow Sea circulation—from September 8 through September 14 to clarify how water circulates in the Yellow Sea.
Using satellite-tracked drifters and other instruments, the joint survey would measure seawater properties and real-time water movement. For the first time, it would also use a continuous particle-measuring instrument and an acoustic current meter to investigate the distribution of planktonic particles in the East China Sea.
The East China Sea is an important area: it lies along the paths of typhoons approaching Korea, serves as a route for the many vessels traveling to the Yellow Sea, and is where the Ieodo Ocean Research Station is located. Research and practical use of the Yellow Sea circulation require prior investigation and understanding of water circulation in the East China Sea.
A three-dimensional understanding of water movement is especially important for studying the effects on Korean waters of the Three Gorges Dam, the world’s largest dam, built on China’s Yangtze River.
An institute official said, “The survey results are expected to be provided later on our website (www.nori.go.kr) and to serve as important data for understanding marine conditions in the East China Sea following construction of China’s Three Gorges Dam.”

ko-news-notices-198-8372c75064.title: Cultured Pearls to Be Produced Using Nuclear-Plant Warm-Water Effluent
ko-news-notices-198-8372c75064.text:
Cultured Pearls to Be Produced Using Nuclear-Plant Warm-Water Effluent
2022-03-02
(Busan Regional Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Office: Korea’s first pearl-nucleus implantation procedure)
A pilot project to produce cultured pearls using warm water discharged from a nuclear power plant is now moving ahead in earnest.
The Busan Regional Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Office announced on the 21st that, after successfully conducting Korea’s first pearl-oyster cultivation trial using nuclear-plant warm-water effluent, it had implanted cultured-pearl nuclei in the oysters.
The procedure involved 5,000 pearl oysters, each about 7 cm long. In 2003, they had undergone grow-out and overwintering trials using warm-water effluent in the waters off Daebyeon, Gijang-eup, and Wolnae, Jangan-eup, both in Gijang County, Busan.
The implantation was carried out in July at a farm in Tongyeong, South Gyeongsang Province, after preparatory care that included temperature stimulation, depth adjustment, and egg stripping.
The oysters with implanted nuclei were scheduled to be moved back to the waters off Wolnae the following month for overwintering. Producing pearls takes about a year, so the first pearls were expected around October of the following year.
The Busan office plans to disseminate the related pearl-oyster cultivation technology using nuclear-plant warm-water effluent, providing a new source of income for aquaculture operators who mainly farm sea mustard, kelp, and other seaweeds.
Busan — Reporter Gi-hyeon Kim

Yangyang County to Develop Measures to Prevent Coastal Erosion
2022-03-02
County commissions study of coastal conditions
Yangyang County is commissioning a study of coastal conditions to develop measures to prevent increasingly severe coastal erosion.
As it did the previous year, the county plans to spend KRW 30 million this year on a study by the Maritime and Port Technology Research Center at Kwandong University. The study will analyze the extent and causes of coastal erosion in Yangyang and recommend countermeasures.
By the end of the year, the center will conduct interviews and field inquiries along 38.5 km of coastline from Mulchi-ri in Ganghyeon-myeon to Namae-ri in Hyeonnam-myeon. It will also survey a 20-km stretch of shoreline to measure erosion and sedimentation and carry out numerical ocean-modeling experiments.

ko-news-notices-202-8372c75064.title: Korean Coastal Tide Tables Published to Help Mariners Read the Tides
ko-news-notices-202-8372c75064.text:
Korean Coastal Tide Tables Published to Help Mariners Read the Tides
2022-03-02
Korean Coastal Tide Tables Published to Help Mariners Read the Tides
Reporter Soo-kyung Cho (camus0211@nate.com)
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director General Jong-rok Park, announced that it had published the Korean Coastal Tide Tables, containing tide predictions for major Korean ports for 2006.
The tables provide daily high- and low-tide times and predicted sea levels for 47 major ports around the Korean coast, as well as tidal-current predictions for 14 narrow channels. For ports with a large tidal range and heavy vessel traffic—Incheon, Gunsan, and Mokpo on the west coast, and Busan on the south coast—they include hourly predictions.
For about 200 additional coastal locations beyond the 47 standard ports, the tables provide time differences and sea-level ratios relative to a standard port, allowing users to estimate tides along the entire coast at a glance. They also include the latest information on chart-datum benchmarks, which provide vertical reference levels for coastal and port development.
An institute official said, “These tide tables are expected to be useful to navigators, port-construction personnel, the marine industry, and people engaged in marine leisure activities.”
The institute plans to continue gathering the latest domestic and international navigation information promptly and publishing and distributing hydrographic publications. The Korean Coastal Tide Tables can be purchased through the national hydrographic-publication sales network (02-701-9981).
