ko-news-notices-204-8372c75064.text:
Detailed Survey of Hazards at Busan New Port Anchorage Begins
2022-03-02
The South Sea Oceanographic Office of the National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director Jae-seop Lee, announced on the 6th that it had begun a detailed seabed survey at the proposed anchorage east of Gadeokdo Island, in preparation for designating an anchorage for Busan New Port.
The survey vessel Namhae-ro, equipped with advanced instruments including a multibeam echo sounder, GPS, and sound-velocity meter, will measure water depths and check the seabed for navigational hazards and underwater obstructions.
The results will be used to produce seafloor-topography and marine-spatial-information products, including a three-dimensional seafloor map and bathymetric contours. The information on depth changes and underwater obstructions needed to designate the Busan New Port anchorage is intended to support its smooth designation and operation in time for the port’s scheduled opening in January 2006.
An institute official said, “We will continue producing up-to-date marine information—including water depth, seabed topography, currents, and tides—for the new port and nearby waters. By providing safe-navigation information to port users and vessels arriving and departing, we expect to help the port develop into a central hub in Northeast Asia.”

ko-news-notices-205-8372c75064.title: Environmental Concerns Emerge over Gunsan–Janghang Industrial Complex
ko-news-notices-205-8372c75064.text:
Environmental Concerns Emerge over Gunsan–Janghang Industrial Complex
2022-03-02
Environmental concerns are emerging over the Gunsan–Janghang Industrial Complex development project, raising the possibility that they could obstruct its smooth progress.
The National Assembly’s Environment and Labor Committee has called for a comprehensive review, citing serious damage to the tidal-flat ecosystem in the Geum River estuary from development of the Gunsan–Janghang National Industrial Complex.
At a state audit of the Geum River Basin Environmental Office on the 6th, Uri Party lawmaker Kim Young-joo, a proportional-representation member of the National Assembly’s Environment and Labor Committee, said that development of the Janghang district within the Gunjang National Industrial Complex could severely damage the tidal-flat and estuarine ecosystems. She called for the project to be reconsidered in full.
Kim said the area is home to five Class I endangered wildlife species designated by the Ministry of Environment, including the Chinese egret, spoon-billed sandpiper, and black-faced spoonbill, and 14 Class II species, including the Eurasian oystercatcher. She also said more than 30,000 birds inhabit nearby areas such as Daejukdo, and warned that continued development would inevitably destroy the ecosystem.
Kim further argued that the area has exceptionally high conservation value by international standards. She said the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and the Korea Environment Institute had also warned that the Gunsan–Janghang development plan could cause environmental damage and had called for “careful review.”
Geum River Basin Environmental Office head Hee-man Son responded, “We requested one supplement to the environmental impact assessment and received a revised report, but it was still inadequate, so we have requested further revisions.” He added, “We will form a consultation committee on the development-related environmental impact assessment and decide on our position.”
Seoul — Reporter Seung-ryeol Yoo (yous@)

ko-news-notices-206-8372c75064.title: Severe Water Pollution in the Lower Han River
ko-news-notices-206-8372c75064.text:
Severe Water Pollution in the Lower Han River
2022-03-02
It is hardly news that pollution along the Incheon coast has reached a serious level. Water quality has long deteriorated to Class III, making it difficult for fish and shellfish to live there, and fish contaminated with heavy metals have been caught. The situation can no longer be ignored. The root cause of coastal pollution is the large volume of polluted water flowing from the Han River estuary.

According to materials submitted for a parliamentary audit, the Han River accounts for 80% of the pollutants entering Incheon’s coastal waters. Water in the Han River estuary that flows through the Yeomha Channel between Ganghwa Island and Gimpo is even more polluted because large amounts of waste enter it. About one-third of the pollutants carried down the Han River pass through the Yeomha Channel. The scale of the problem is evident from the fact that about 20% of fish caught there are deformed, with bent backs and skin lesions.

A major problem is that no comprehensive management system is in place for the Han River estuary, leaving it almost an administrative blind spot. Around Yudo, an island in the lower Han River on the boundary between Gimpo and Ganghwa, the river to the east is governed by the River Act and falls under the Ministry of Environment, while the area to the west is under the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries. The administrative boundaries are also divided between Incheon and Gyeonggi Province. With responsibilities divided this way, pollution in the estuary cannot be managed effectively. Seoul, Gyeonggi Province, and Incheon share the costs of pollution treatment, but the funding is far from sufficient to address coastal pollution.

The importance of the sea, with its abundant resources, cannot be overstated. Estuaries, where rivers meet the sea, are rich in nutrients and provide habitat and spawning grounds for many species; migratory birds also gather there, creating valuable natural landscapes. When these resources are neglected rather than properly managed, ecosystems continue to deteriorate. If pollution makes the sea so hostile that fish and shellfish cannot survive, and it is allowed to become a dead sea, the ecosystem will inevitably reach a point from which it cannot recover.

Indifference to marine pollution and poor management can ultimately devastate coastal fishing grounds and deplete fish stocks, causing major losses to both fishermen’s livelihoods and the national economy. We must recognize the seriousness of coastal pollution and work to protect the marine environment. Central government ministries and local governments should urgently form a consultative body and establish an organization and comprehensive plan to manage the Han River estuary systematically.

ko-news-notices-207-8372c75064.title: KRW 1 Trillion for Development of Nine New Ports
ko-news-notices-207-8372c75064.text:
KRW 1 Trillion for Development of Nine New Ports
2022-03-02
Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries to increase next year’s new-port facilities budget by 5.2%
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries plans to spend a total of KRW 1.7828 trillion next year on new-port development and facilities at major ports.
On the 28th, the ministry announced that it had budgeted KRW 1.782868 trillion for the port sector next year, up 1.09% from this year’s KRW 1.7635 trillion.
In particular, it plans to allocate KRW 1.0352 trillion to developing nine new ports, including Busan New Port, a 5.2% increase from this year’s KRW 983.8 billion.
The ministry said it needed to expand port-facility projects and urgently improve infrastructure in port hinterland complexes to secure the ports’ position as logistics hubs in Northeast Asia.
It budgeted KRW 468.3 billion for facilities at Busan New Port, up 4.4% from this year, and plans to invest KRW 274 billion at Gwangyang Port.
Planned facility allocations also include KRW 81.6 billion for Pyeongtaek Port, KRW 63.9 billion for Incheon North Port, KRW 90.7 billion for Ulsan New Port, KRW 40.4 billion for Yeongil Bay New Port, and KRW 71.7 billion for Incheon South Outer Port.
A ministry official said, “To establish Northeast Asia as a logistics hub as early as possible, we focused on expanding port infrastructure, improving port-operating efficiency, and strengthening overall competitiveness in attracting transshipment cargo.”
The official added that the ministry would work to supply hinterland sites early to create a basis for attracting multinational logistics companies.
By the end of this year, the Busan New Port project will have received KRW 3.3877 trillion, reaching 37% completion. Next year, construction is to continue on 13 privately financed berths on the north side and five publicly funded berths, including piers on the south side.
At Gwangyang Port, investment is expected to reach KRW 2.7293 trillion by year-end, bringing overall completion to 41%. Next year, priority will be given to building seven berths in Phases 3-1 and 2.
Construction of a 100,000-pyeong logistics complex on the eastern side is under way. The remaining 490,000 pyeong of logistics-complex and functional-facility sites are to be supplied by 2008. The ministry plans to conduct a basic survey and design next year to supply 530,000 pyeong of hinterland land on the western side by 2011.
For major facility projects at six ports, including Busan and Incheon, the ministry budgeted KRW 233.7 billion, down 11.2% from this year.
By port, the allocations are KRW 73.8 billion for Busan, KRW 60.4 billion for Gunsan, KRW 34 billion for Mokpo, KRW 31.9 billion for Jeju, KRW 24 billion for Incheon, and KRW 9.4 billion for Ulsan.
The ministry also budgeted KRW 123 billion for construction at 28 trade ports, up 8.7% from this year, and KRW 36.4 billion for construction at 23 coastal ports, down 30%. It plans to spend KRW 140.7 billion on port-facility maintenance and KRW 211.6 billion on support for the container-terminal corporation.

ko-news-notices-208-8372c75064.title: Work Begins on a National Roadmap for Port Hinterland Complexes
ko-news-notices-208-8372c75064.text:
Work Begins on a National Roadmap for Port Hinterland Complexes
2022-03-02
Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries to commission study this month; plan to be announced in the second half of next year
Prepared: 2005-10-18
A commissioned study to prepare a roadmap setting development scales and priorities for the hinterland complexes of all 28 trade ports will begin in earnest this month.
The comprehensive plan for port hinterland complexes is scheduled to be announced in the second half of next year.
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries said it issued a call for proposals in August for a study to develop a comprehensive plan for hinterland complexes at the nation’s trade ports. It selected Geonil Engineering as the lead contractor, with Kunhwa Engineering and Hangdo Engineering as partner firms.
The ministry also formed a working group that includes its Northeast Asia Logistics Planning Team, the Korea Research Institute for Human Settlements, and the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA).
The plan will set out how to develop, in stages, suitable hinterland complexes on vacant land at the country’s 28 trade ports—including Busan and Pyeongtaek-Dangjin—to support port functions.
The ministry said the study would provide a blueprint covering development needs at each port. It would set target stages for 2011, 2016, and 2020 and identify the required scale of hinterland development in light of each port’s cargo volume and cargo mix.
The ministry will consider diversifying the current approach, which focuses mainly on support complexes for container terminals, to accommodate each region and port’s characteristics, including containers, general cargo, and public waterfront space.
It also plans to shift from uniform, land-development-centered projects to customized port-hinterland logistics complexes that reflect port users’ needs, such as occupancy timing and required floor area. Global shippers and domestic logistics experts will be consulted from the early planning stages.
A port hinterland complex is an area behind a port where value-added activities such as cargo storage, sorting, assembly, distribution, and waterfront uses take place. Major ports such as Rotterdam and Singapore focus not only on cargo handling but also on increasing port value added, an approach described as the “value-ton” concept.
Rotterdam, the gateway to Europe, handled 8.3 million TEU in 2003, ranking seventh worldwide by cargo volume, but generated USD 24.5 billion in annual added value.
Inquiries: Port Bureau, Port Policy Division — Officer Beom-gu Kang; Yoon Du-han, 02-3674-6712 / fax 3674-6716

ko-news-notices-210-8372c75064.title: Can the Causes of Coastal Sand Erosion Be Identified?
ko-news-notices-210-8372c75064.text:
Can the Causes of Coastal Sand Erosion Be Identified?
2022-03-02
Jeju City to establish a monitoring system at Iho Beach
Can science identify the causes of sand erosion occurring at most beaches in the province?
Jeju City has drawn attention by establishing a sand-erosion monitoring system at Iho Beach to identify the causes of beach erosion.
Because erosion affects most beaches in the province, the city hopes the survey results will help identify solutions.
On the 18th, Jeju City announced that it had installed shoreline- and wave-monitoring equipment in a building near Iho Beach.
The system includes three video cameras and network equipment. Observation data are sent in real time to the contractor, GeoSystem Research Co., Ltd.
The city expects the monitoring system will need to operate for at least three to five years to analyze the causes of sand erosion, develop countermeasures, and verify the results afterward.
Based on the findings, Jeju City plans to develop an effective restoration plan and improve the function of Iho Beach.
Bedrock and gravel are exposed in many places on Iho Beach’s sandy shore, which is 250 m long and 120 m wide, because the beach has eroded over several years.
Erosion is also occurring at most of the province’s beaches, including Hamo and Jungmun. The survey is expected to help address problems at those beaches as well.
A Jeju City official said, “This survey is part of the nationwide monitoring-system project that the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries is carrying out at 22 sites to address coastal erosion.”
Reporter Sang-seop Park (2005-10-19)

ko-news-notices-211-8372c75064.title: Wellness Products Made with Deep Ocean Water Soon to Reach the Market
ko-news-notices-211-8372c75064.text:
Wellness Products Made with Deep Ocean Water Soon to Reach the Market
2022-03-02
A range of products made with deep ocean water is expected to reach the market as early as next year.
On the 18th, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries said that research and development results were beginning to emerge and that deep ocean water would be commercialized across several industries, including drinking water and cosmetics, starting next year.
Eight Korean companies are participating in the commercialization project, including Dongwon F&B (green-tea drinks), Kooksoondang (distilled soju), and Aekyung Industrial (cosmetics). The ministry said each company expected to produce prototypes by December this year.
Deep ocean water collected from depths of 200 m or more is a clean water resource rich in nutrients and almost free of organic matter and pathogens. Japan, the United States, and other countries have been producing products using deep ocean water since 1990. In Japan, the market is worth KRW 2 trillion a year.
A Korean pilot project last year used deep ocean water to cultivate laver. The growth rate was up to twice that achieved with ordinary surface water. Deep ocean water is expected to find a range of uses not only in manufacturing but also in agriculture and fisheries.
If developed for drinking, however, deep ocean water would cost about 1.5 times as much as commercially available bottled spring water, so reducing production costs remains a challenge.
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries plans to complete a Deep Ocean Water Research Center in Ohori, Jukwang-myeon, Goseong County, Gangwon Province, by November to support full-scale research and development. The center will bring water from depths of 300–500 m ashore through intake pipes, desalinate it, and supply it to Korean research institutes and companies.
Dr. Hyun-joo Kim, head of the Deep Ocean Water Research Center at the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute, said, “Once deep-ocean-water research gets under way in earnest, Korea too will enter an era of using it as a new source of industrial energy.”
Reporter Byung-tae Choi (cbt@kyunghyang.com)

ko-news-notices-212-8372c75064.title: National Oceanographic Research Institute to Hold Seminar for Its 56th Anniversary
ko-news-notices-212-8372c75064.text:
National Oceanographic Research Institute to Hold Seminar for Its 56th Anniversary
2022-03-02
Institute to discuss how to navigate an era of change
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director General Jong-rok Park, will mark its 56th anniversary on November 1 with a ceremony and a seminar on its future direction at the Paradise Hotel in Incheon. Guests from across the marine sector and senior figures will be invited.
About 100 people are expected to attend, including the Vice Minister of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, oceanographers, association and industry representatives, and institute staff. Experts will present and discuss the institute’s role and importance in the new ocean era and the direction of its organizational development.
Presenters will include Dr. Seok-woo Lee of Marine Science and Technology Co., Ltd.; Professor Im-sang Oh of Seoul National University; Professor Jung-ki Choi of the Korean Society of Oceanography; and Dr. Hoe-su Jeong of the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute. Their topics will include strengthening the institute’s expertise, expanding ocean-observation activities in response to climate change, cooperation among relevant agencies to mitigate storm surges, and the importance of precise hydrographic-survey data for scientifically documenting coastal-environment changes.
An institute official said, “This seminar will help the institute respond to the recently growing demand for ocean surveys and establish a direction for change suited to the new ocean era.”

ko-news-notices-213-8372c75064.title: Plans Under Way for Real-Time Collection of Marine Environmental Data off Jeju
ko-news-notices-213-8372c75064.text:
Plans Under Way for Real-Time Collection of Marine Environmental Data off Jeju
2022-03-02
Plans are under way to build a system that uses a ubiquitous sensor network (USN) to measure marine environmental conditions off Jeju in real time.
On the 23rd, the National Computerization Agency (NCA) said it had begun selecting field-test projects to identify USN application-service models. Eight proposals had been submitted and were under review, including “Building a USN-Based System to Collect Marine Environmental Data off Jeju.”
A USN is a network that wirelessly collects information detected by various sensors. It is foundational infrastructure for accelerating the spread of ubiquitous computing through sensor technology. Four application models are to be selected.
The NCA said projects that demonstrate strong demand for sensors and practical effectiveness in field tests could be selected for future USN pilot programs. The selection process has attracted considerable interest from domestic and foreign businesses involved in radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags.
A proposal submitted by SysNeck Co., Ltd. describes using a 2.45-GHz wireless network along the Jeju coast to collect marine-ecosystem data in real time and continuously monitor seawater temperature and dissolved oxygen.
The proposal calls for installing the U-sensor network along the coast using standard buoys, together with closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras that enable real-time monitoring.
By collecting marine environmental data 24 hours a day, the system is expected to detect changes in seawater temperature and harmful red tides early and track them in real time, helping minimize damage to fisheries.
Reporter Bong-cheol Hyeon (hbc@jejunews.com)

ko-news-notices-214-8372c75064.title: [Hydrographic Survey] Typhoon Changes the Shape of Haeundae Beach
ko-news-notices-214-8372c75064.text:
[Hydrographic Survey] Typhoon Changes the Shape of Haeundae Beach
2022-03-02
Typhoon Nabi changed the shape of Haeundae Beach.
The South Sea Oceanographic Office of the National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director Jae-seop Lee, and the Remote Sensing Center at Pukyong National University, led by Professor Cheol-woong Choi, conducted a joint government–university survey of Haeundae, Korea’s largest beach. They confirmed that the typhoon had affected the beach’s topography.
Using precise GPS positioning, the team surveyed the beach before Typhoon Nabi passed (August 20–21) and after it passed (September 19–20). After combining the measurements with aerial photographs and satellite imagery, they found that sand deposition on the western side of Haeundae, toward Dongbaekseom Island, increased the beach area by 2,509.91 m². On the eastern side near Mipo, sand loss exposed gravel and rocks and eroded 4,316.45 m².
The total sandy-beach area also decreased by 3,096 m², from 56,537 m² before the typhoon to 53,441 m² afterward. The beach slope became gentler after the typhoon passed.
An institute official said, “We will incorporate the findings into the Beach Information Map to improve visitor safety and convenience and provide information needed by local governments to manage beaches. We also plan to continue monitoring changes in beach topography.”

ko-news-notices-215-8372c75064.title: Study and Management Plan for the Marine Environment of Incheon’s Coastal Islands
ko-news-notices-215-8372c75064.text:
Study and Management Plan for the Marine Environment of Incheon’s Coastal Islands
2022-03-02
Work begins on an environmental survey and conservation and management plan for Incheon’s coastal islands
Reporter Sang-hwan Ham
Incheon City commissioned the West Sea Coastal Environment Research Center at Inha University (the Research Center) to develop a marine-environment conservation and management plan for the islands off Incheon and the surrounding coast, with recommendations for conservation and sustainable use.
The Research Center will spend 24 months, through September 25, 2007, surveying the human, social, and natural-ecological conditions of 155 inhabited and uninhabited islands off Incheon and building a research database. The work will define the terrestrial areas of the islands and their surrounding intertidal zones.
The main research tasks are: surveys of the islands’ human and social environments; surveys of natural conditions, including terrestrial and marine topography, geology, landscapes, flora, and fauna; surveys of terrestrial environmental damage, development, current uses, and pollution; surveys of island fisheries and local awareness; creation of a database, GIS, and web service for the survey results; assessment of each island’s ecological carrying capacity; development of marine conservation and use standards for each island; and preparation of a sustainable island and marine-environment conservation and management plan.
The 155 islands will be divided into 20 priority islands and those receiving general surveys, with intensive work on the priority islands. For comparative analysis, the islands will also be grouped into nine areas: Yeongheung, Yeongjong, Deokjeok, Jawol, Jangbong, Baengnyeong, Yeonpyeong, Ganghwa, and Jumun.
Uninhabited islands will be classified as either specially designated islands identified by the Ministry of Environment or general islands. General islands will then be categorized as conservation, semi-conservation, or use islands. Field teams will record positions with GPS for use in the GIS.
To assess the islands, the team will combine its field-survey results with recent data from government agencies and major research institutes, including the Ministry of Environment, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, and Incheon City. The findings will be used to classify islands for conservation or use and develop management and conservation measures.
The 20 priority islands for intensive surveys are Yeongjongdo, Yongyudo, Daemuido, Ganghwado, Gyodongdo, Seokmodo, Boreumdo, Jumundo, Yeongheungdo, Seonjaedo, Jawoldo, Seungbongdo, Daeijakdo, Jangbongdo, Sindo, Sido, Deokjeokdo, Baengnyeongdo, Daecheongdo, and Daeyeonpyeongdo.
Incheon — Reporter Sang-hwan Ham

ko-news-notices-216-8372c75064.title: First Comprehensive Marine Survey in the Gangneung Area Completed
ko-news-notices-216-8372c75064.text:
First Comprehensive Marine Survey in the Gangneung Area Completed
2022-03-02
Continuous observations are needed to understand marine conditions accurately
Reporter Soo-kyung Cho (camus0211@nate.com)
The East Sea Oceanographic Office of the National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director Ki-seok Seo, announced that it had completed a month-long comprehensive survey of currents and other marine conditions offshore of Gyeongpo Beach and in the waters from Sacheon to Anmok, Gangneung. The survey began last September.
This was the first survey of these waters. The team used the state-of-the-art 150-ton survey vessel Donghae-ro and advanced instruments, including an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) and a conductivity–temperature–depth (CTD) instrument. After analysis, the observations are expected to provide baseline data for clarifying marine conditions in the area and supporting a bid to host the Windsurfing World Championships at Gyeongpo Beach the following September.
The results showed that currents in the waters off Gangneung flowed predominantly northward regardless of the time of observation. This agrees with the general northward flow along Korea’s east coast in summer. Current speeds varied by location by around 0.5 knots.
An institute official added, “Because this was the first survey in the Gangneung area, there is not yet enough accumulated observation data. Continued surveys are needed to understand marine conditions more accurately.”
The official also said, “We will continue working to provide a range of marine-information services that meet users’ needs by conducting surveys that reflect their views and the characteristics of each region.”

ko-news-notices-217-8372c75064.title: Oyster Shells Could Replace Sand in Construction
ko-news-notices-217-8372c75064.text:
Oyster Shells Could Replace Sand in Construction
2022-03-02
Korean researchers have developed a technology to use oyster shells—which add to marine and fishing-ground pollution—in place of sand at construction sites or as an environmentally friendly cement-based soil stabilizer.
On the 1st, Dr. Gil-lim Yoon’s team at the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute (KORDI) announced that it had developed a method of mixing oyster shells with sand in a set proportion to stabilize soft ground.
The team tested the mixture in soft-ground improvement work on a road project at Busan Port and confirmed that oyster shells could serve as a sand substitute.
Cement-based soil stabilizers, which are widely used, may contain heavy metals and are increasingly restricted in areas where there is a risk of soil or water pollution. Developing an environmentally friendly substitute had therefore become urgent.
In a separate test, the team used an oyster-shell stabilizer to build a cutoff wall at a waste landfill to prevent leachate. It confirmed that the wall had high strength and effectively blocked leachate.
The team also found no engineering problems with strength or chemical reactions when crushed oyster shells were mixed with cement in place of sand.
Based on the findings, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries plans to supply 24,000 tonnes on a pilot basis next year to construction of the Sihwa District Multi-Techno Valley, which is scheduled to begin then. It plans to incorporate the material into port and fishing-port design technology and construction specifications.
Korea generates about 300,000 tonnes of oyster shells each year. About 200,000 tonnes are recycled, while the remaining 100,000 tonnes become a serious source of marine pollution through illegal dumping or landfilling.
Reporter Seong-gi Jin

ko-news-notices-218-8372c75064.title: National Oceanographic Research Institute Needs to Improve Its Marine Information Services
ko-news-notices-218-8372c75064.text:
National Oceanographic Research Institute Needs to Improve Its Marine Information Services
2022-03-02
The National Oceanographic Research Institute’s marine-information services—which produce, analyze, and process oceanographic data—need improvement, researchers said.
On the 31st of the previous month, Dr. Seok-woo Lee of Marine Science and Technology Co., Ltd. argued in a paper titled “Future Tasks for the National Oceanographic Research Institute” that observations should be analyzed statistically and theoretically so they can support predictions of future marine conditions. He said the institute should strengthen its services by turning the results into useful marine data and information for specialists in the marine industry.
Dr. Lee emphasized that data from standard tide-gauge stations should support a broad program of research and surveys, including analysis of storm surges and sea-level changes and prediction of ocean currents.
In a paper titled “Desirable Directions for the Institute’s Work,” Professor Im-sang Oh of Seoul National University’s School of Earth and Environmental Sciences proposed that the institute establish a system to predict ocean conditions and issue real-time forecasts, take over and operate the Ieodo Ocean Research Station efficiently, and conduct coordinated, wide-area ocean observations.
Professor Oh argued that Korea needed a proposed Ocean Survey and Forecasting Administration, comparable to the Korea Meteorological Administration, to conduct research and coordinate responses to marine and coastal disasters and address long-term phenomena such as global warming, El Niño, La Niña, and sea-level rise.
Professor Jung-ki Choi of Inha University, president of the Korean Society of Oceanography, said the institute’s systems for managing, providing, and using survey data were weak and that its data collection, organization, analysis, forecasting, and service functions were inadequate. He called for specialized survey work and stronger research functions, including the continued production, accumulation, and provision of baseline data for coastal-environment management.
Today, to mark its 56th anniversary, the National Oceanographic Research Institute will invite marine-sector leaders and senior figures to a ceremony and a seminar at the Paradise Hotel in Incheon, where the presentations above will inform discussion of the institute’s future direction.
Reporter Won-yong Kim (wykim@joongboo.com)

ko-news-notices-220-8372c75064.title: “Beach Sand Is Disappearing”
ko-news-notices-220-8372c75064.text:
“Beach Sand Is Disappearing”
2022-03-02
“Beach Sand Is Disappearing”
[YTN, 2005-11-08 15:51]
[Reporter Jong-su Lee]
The area of sandy beach used for bathing and other recreation is gradually shrinking.
A joint report by the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and GeoSystem Research measured erosion since 2003 along beaches on 13 coasts nationwide. It found a gradual erosion trend in seven areas.
The beaches narrowing because of erosion are Haeundae in Busan; Daecheon in Boryeong; Gangmun in Gangneung; Myeongsasimni in Wando; Kkotji in Taean; Hosan in Samcheok; and Iho in Jeju.
By contrast, Gyeongpo Beach in Gangneung, Gwangalli in Busan, Bongpyeong-ri in Uljin, Jinha in Ulju, and Janggol Beach in Ongjin were found to be relatively stable.
The report attributed coastal erosion to human causes, including indiscriminate coastal-development projects, and natural factors, including sea-level rise associated with climate change and frequent typhoon landfalls.

ko-news-notices-221-8372c75064.title: [Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries] Symposium to Discuss Creating Value from Coastal Areas
ko-news-notices-221-8372c75064.text:
[Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries] Symposium to Discuss Creating Value from Coastal Areas
2022-03-02
[Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries] Symposium to Discuss Creating Value from Coastal Areas
[ Yonhap News press release, 2005-11-03 13:05 ]
— About 300 Korean and international coastal experts to attend at Dong-Eui University in Busan on the 4th
A symposium on creating value from coastal areas and developing coastal policy will be held at the International Hall of Dong-Eui University in Busan on the afternoon of the 4th. About 300 Korean and international participants from industry, academia, research institutes, central government, and local governments are expected to attend.
The presentations will include four Korean topics, among them “Long-Term Changes in Japan’s Coastal-Zone Policy and Future Prospects,” by Toru Takamatsu, executive director of Japan’s Port and Harbor Space Advanced Environment Research Center, and “The Current State and Future Tasks of Coastal-Erosion Monitoring in Korea,” by Dr. Su-yong Nam of GeoSystem Research. Panelists and participants will then discuss the presentations.
A ministry official said, “Coastal areas, where the sea meets the land, have high ecological diversity and economic productivity, but are also environmentally sensitive. For years, we failed to recognize the importance of coastal-zone management and pursued development- and growth-oriented policies. This has damaged natural environments and spread problems such as coastal erosion, which is why we are holding this symposium.”
The ministry plans to use the symposium to raise awareness of the importance of coastal areas, carefully review the issues raised, and reflect them in coastal-development policy.

ko-news-notices-224-8372c75064.title: Fine Sand at Wando’s Myeongsasimni Beach Is Shrinking
ko-news-notices-224-8372c75064.text:
Fine Sand at Wando’s Myeongsasimni Beach Is Shrinking
2022-03-02
The sandy-beach area at Myeongsasimni Beach in Wando is gradually decreasing.
On the 8th, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and GeoSystem Research said a report they prepared jointly, “Status and Plan for Monitoring Coastal Erosion in Korea,” found a gradual erosion trend at Myeongsasimni Beach. Since 2004, GeoSystem Research and its partners have monitored erosion there using two video towers behind the beach. Seven cameras observe the shoreline and one observes waves.
An interim analysis found that erosion at Myeongsasimni was proceeding very slowly. The causes were assessed as unregulated development, including the coastal road behind the beach; a decrease in sand sources; and high waves associated with climate change.
Tae-soon Kang, deputy director at GeoSystem Research, said, “We have only been monitoring the beach for two years, so it is difficult to draw conclusions about long-term trends, such as how long the sand will remain. Coastal erosion is not merely a loss of sand; it is also a problem for coastal ecosystems and the loss of land. We will continue monitoring for at least five more years.”
Reporter Ju-jeong Kim (jjnews@kwangju.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-225-8372c75064.title: Marine Survey of the Han River Estuary and Ganghwa Island after 38 Years
ko-news-notices-225-8372c75064.text:
Marine Survey of the Han River Estuary and Ganghwa Island after 38 Years
2022-03-02
A marine survey of the Han River estuary is being conducted for the first time in 38 years.
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), headed by Director General Jong-rok Park, announced on the 10th that it would conduct a month-long marine survey beginning on the 14th in the waters from the Han River estuary to Ganghwa and Yeongjong Islands.
The Han River estuary has a large tidal range and receives substantial amounts of freshwater and sediment from the Han and Imjin rivers into Gyeonggi Bay. It is one of the world’s natural estuaries whose ecosystems remain well preserved.
Marine surveys are essential to understanding the oceanographic conditions of Gyeonggi Bay, including the waters near Incheon.
Access to the area is difficult, and strong currents and extensive tidal flats have long constrained surveys. Since the Navy’s comprehensive survey in 1967, only partial and fragmentary surveys had been conducted.
Data from the Han River estuary remain seriously insufficient for understanding how coastal development is changing the marine environment and related oceanographic conditions.
The survey will be conducted jointly by NORI, Inha University, and industry and academic partners. At six stations in the Han River estuary and around Ganghwa Island, the team will install current meters, conductivity–temperature–depth (CTD) profilers, and pressure-operated tide gauges for continuous monitoring.
An institute official said, “We expect this survey to clarify how seawater and freshwater mix in the Han River estuary, provide accurate tidal-current forecasts around Ganghwa Island, and supply important marine data for future development of the Han River waterway.”
Reporter Beom-jin Baek

ko-news-notices-226-8372c75064.title: Research Cooperation for the Deep Ocean Water Industry
ko-news-notices-226-8372c75064.text:
Research Cooperation for the Deep Ocean Water Industry
2022-03-02
The Gyeongbuk Marine Bioindustry Research Institute, headed by Director Kuk-hwan Ahn, and the East Sea Fisheries Research Institute of the National Fisheries Research and Development Institute (NFRDI), headed by Director Jong-deuk Bang, signed an agreement on research and technical cooperation. The agreement aims to advance marine-bio and deep-ocean-water industries in the East Sea. <Photo>
On the 21st, the two organizations held a signing ceremony in the county office’s main conference room. They agreed to maintain an ongoing, close partnership through joint research on marine biotechnology and the deep-ocean-water industry; joint academic events and seminars; shared use of research facilities and equipment; and exchanges of technical information.
They also agreed to strengthen research cooperation that uses the East Sea’s clean, healthy marine environment and diverse marine life to develop marine biotechnology and the deep-ocean-water industry.
The Gyeongbuk institute expects that close cooperation will expand research on the deep-ocean-water industry in waters under Gyeongbuk’s jurisdiction, as the East Sea Fisheries Research Institute begins full-scale research on the East Sea deep-sea ecosystem this year.

ko-news-notices-227-8372c75064.title: Marine Environmental Surveys around Nuclear Power Plants
ko-news-notices-227-8372c75064.text:
Marine Environmental Surveys around Nuclear Power Plants
2022-03-02
Surveys cover nearby land and sea areas
Biological and chemical studies conducted alongside physical surveys
Since 1986, general environmental surveys have been conducted on land and in the waters around every operating nuclear power plant to assess the plants’ effects on the surrounding environment. The work follows the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Energy’s Notice No. 1996-330, “Guidelines for Environmental Surveys around Nuclear Power Plants,” and includes biological, chemical, and physical investigations.
Seasonal biological surveys record the species composition and abundance of phytoplankton, zooplankton, benthic organisms, seaweeds, and fish. They also record the species, number, and weight of organisms that collide with intake screens and the species and number of organisms drawn into cooling systems.
At Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant, surveys assess damage to cold-water seaweeds such as wakame and laver living near the discharge outlet, and compensation has been provided. Measures to reduce the effects of warm-water discharge are also being pursued.
To improve the reliability of the surveys, the plant reportedly shares about half of the survey items with the Korea Electric Power Research Institute and local universities in the surrounding area, with the aim of ensuring transparency.
Annual water-quality data collected around Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant show that the reported value was 7.03 mg/L in 1991 and remained at a similar level through 1995. It rose to 10.10 in 1997, then gradually declined; by 2001 and 2002, it was back near the level recorded in the early 1990s, with no major overall change.
Chemical oxygen demand around the plant rose somewhat, from 0.78 in 1991 to 1.56 in 2003, but remained broadly similar to levels when the plant first began operating.
Environmental groups, however, are calling for stricter environmental management, arguing that even a small increase in chemical oxygen demand can have a significant environmental effect.
Total nitrogen has also fluctuated regularly between 0.01 and 0.1, with no clear indication of environmental change.
The number of seaweed species recorded around the plant fluctuated from 51 in 1989 and stood at 33 in 2003. By contrast, the number of marine benthic-animal species increased substantially, from 45 in 1988 to 87 in 2003.
An official at Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant said, “Taken together, the results of 18 years of surveys show no concerning changes in the surrounding environment attributable to plant operations. The overall community structure resembles that of the surrounding natural ecosystem, suggesting little impact.”
Yeonggwang — Reporter Hyeong-jin Kim

ko-news-notices-228-8372c75064.title: Comprehensive Monitoring of Radiation Levels and Environmental Changes
ko-news-notices-228-8372c75064.text:
Comprehensive Monitoring of Radiation Levels and Environmental Changes
2022-03-02
Comprehensive Monitoring of Radiation Levels and Environmental Changes
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Published: 2005-11-30 00:00
Review of Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant’s environmental-management system
Now that Gyeongju has been selected as the site for the long-delayed radioactive-waste facility, the public and local residents are paying close attention to nuclear-plant environmental management and safety.
Interest is also growing in how nuclear-plant operators verify safety and manage residents’ radiation doses from radioactive substances discharged by operating plants, including Yeonggwang.
This article reviews the environmental-management system at Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant and other operating plants.

● Environmental surveys and assessment
Before a power plant is built, environmental management focuses on predicting and assessing the project’s environmental effects so that construction and operation can be environmentally sound and sustainable and the surrounding area can remain pleasant to live in.
Environmental-impact assessments conducted before and during construction, as well as post-construction environmental monitoring, are based on the Act on Assessment of Impacts of Projects on Environment, Traffic, Disasters, etc.
A specialist organization conducts the pre-construction assessment. It predicts and assesses the effects of plant construction and operation on nearby areas and prepares a draft assessment report. Information sessions or public hearings are then held to gather residents’ views from the assessment area, and those views are incorporated into the report.
Assessment subjects include meteorology; topography and geology; flora and fauna; the marine environment; water and soil quality; waste; noise, vibration, odors, and other aspects of the living environment; population; housing; industry; and transportation. The assessment also covers direct and indirect radiation effects on residents and effects of plant cooling-water discharge on marine life and fishery resources.
Monitoring sites are selected based on local weather, population distribution, and topography. At each site, surveys measure the radiation dose rate one meter above ground and radioactivity in air, water, surface soil, seafood, other foods, and pine needles, according to established standards. Baseline data for assessing the effects of plant operations are collected through environmental-radioactivity surveys conducted several years before operation begins. Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant said, “We establish an environmental-radioactivity monitoring plan to assess the effects on residents and the environment of the small amounts of radioactive gases and liquids discharged from a nuclear power plant, and survey and assess radioactivity concentrations and radiation doses around the plant.”

● Environmental monitoring system
The operator, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power Co. (KHNP), conducts environmental monitoring at nuclear power plants.
Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant said, “To build confidence in environmental monitoring and improve the objectivity of the data, a civilian environmental-monitoring committee for the plant—with participants from the government, regulatory bodies, research institutes, local universities and residents, academic experts, and legislative representatives—conducts surveys, assessments, inspections, consultations, and verifications of the environment around the plant.”

● Radiation management
At a nuclear power plant, radioactive materials generated in the reactor and their routes of movement are contained behind multiple barriers. Depending on their type, the materials are also treated through processes such as radioactive decay, solidification, filtration, and evaporation.
Most radioactive materials generated during plant operation are removed or treated through these processes. Only very small amounts that do not pose an environmental hazard are released.
Environmental-radiation management therefore verifies that releases comply with regulations and that the health and safety of nearby residents are protected. Under the “Regulations on Environmental Radiation Surveys and Environmental Radiological Impact Assessments around Nuclear Facilities,” monitoring checks whether radiation doses received by residents remain below the prescribed limits.

● Marine-environment management
To monitor marine conditions continuously, Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant operates continuous seawater-temperature monitors at 11 sites offshore of the plant, along with multiparameter water-quality analyzers and current-direction and current-speed meters at its intake and discharge outlets. The readings are monitored remotely via a wireless transmission system and are also made available online.
To map the spread of warm-water discharge more precisely, the plant commissioned the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources (KIGAM) to conduct aircraft-based remote infrared surveys of nearby waters from September 1997 through November 2001. The plant also conducted an aerial remote-infrared survey of nearby waters four months earlier. Beginning in August 2002, the plant commissioned the same institute for a three-year study using satellite observations to assess the discharge plume’s extent.
Nuclear-plant operators predict and seek to minimize the effects of construction and operation on residents and the surrounding environment. They carry out a range of environmental-management activities before construction and throughout the construction and operating periods.

● Conclusion and measures
Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant officials said measurements taken in 2003—including cumulative environmental radiation dose and ambient dose rate—showed no significant change around the plant compared with previous measurements or general areas, and were not different from natural-background radiation levels.
Radioactivity detected in environmental samples, as in previous years, was attributed to residual effects of past nuclear tests. The detected amounts were below levels found elsewhere across Korea.
A plant official added that the radiation levels in the surrounding environment were assessed to be sufficiently safe.
In a further statement, officials said that the 2003 measurements of cumulative dose and ambient dose rate showed no significant difference from past levels or general areas and remained comparable to natural-background radiation.
Yeonggwang — Reporter Hyeong-jin Kim

ko-news-notices-229-8372c75064.title: Deep-Ocean-Water Use Fees to Generate Revenue for Local Governments
ko-news-notices-229-8372c75064.text:
Deep-Ocean-Water Use Fees to Generate Revenue for Local Governments
2022-03-02
Marine-environment impact-survey provision removed; water-use-right term tied to license period
The government prepared a bill to support research and development of deep ocean water, a process that had been under way for more than a year, and planned to submit it to the National Assembly in December.
On the 16th, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and Goseong County said the government had issued advance notice of the “Act on the Development and Management of Deep Ocean Water” and, after gathering comments from other ministries, prepared a final draft. The bill defines deep ocean water and sets out water-use rights and fees, quality standards and specifications, and methods for processing and preserving the water.
In revising the draft, the government removed a licensing provision for deep-ocean-water distributors and a marine-environment impact-survey provision that would have required applicants to submit assessments of effects on surrounding environments and restoration plans. It also replaced a disputed, fixed 10-year term for water-use rights with the term of the water-use business license.
The bill gives the state authority to grant rights to develop deep ocean water, including by drawing and using it. Individuals, companies, and local governments may draw deep ocean water after obtaining a water-use right from the Minister of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries.
The minister may impose and collect a water-use fee based on the quantity withdrawn from each licensee. The collected fees are to become revenue for the city, county, or autonomous district where the intake is located.
A city or provincial governor’s permission will be required to manufacture or process deep ocean water for drinking. The Minister of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries will set and announce standards for its composition, manufacturing, and preservation in consultation with the Minister of Environment on water-quality standards.
Separately, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries had submitted a total of KRW 2.7 billion to the National Assembly for next year’s deep-ocean-water development program: KRW 700 million for spray and facility technology to increase and cultivate fishery resources; KRW 800 million to operate a research center and build a resource and environmental-management system; and KRW 1.2 billion for fisheries-sector research on uses and applications.
A ministry official said, “Next year’s national budget will be used for research at the center established in Goseong. The government considers deep-ocean-water development commercially promising, but public-sector research and review are also needed, separately from commercialization.”
Seoul — Reporter Jeong-rok Song
Article published: 2005-11-16 20:13

ko-news-notices-230-8372c75064.title: Saemangeum Is in Turmoil
ko-news-notices-230-8372c75064.text:
Saemangeum Is in Turmoil
2022-03-02
[The Hankyoreh] “Final seawall-closure work to begin next March”
As the appeal ruling in the Saemangeum lawsuit, scheduled for next month, and the final closure of the Saemangeum seawall, scheduled for March next year, draw closer, the area around Saemangeum is visibly abuzz.

It is clam season, when fishers should be out raking the mudflats. Instead, fishers from Gyehwa-ri in Gyehwa-myeon, Buan County, North Jeolla Province, have taken turns traveling to the Blue House since the 24th of last month to hold individual protests calling for the Saemangeum reclamation project to be halted. For more than a month, fishers from Haje Village in Seonyeon-ri, Okseo-myeon, Gunsan, have also camped at the entrance to a nearby golf course, demanding action on pollution in the Saemangeum mudflats. They say the seawall altered water circulation and made the water shallower, while wastewater discharged from the golf course compounded the problem and wiped out the hard clams on the mudflat in front of their village.

Environmental groups and leaders of the life-respecting movement left Saemangeum after a court of first instance ruled in February that the project should be canceled or changed. Their decision to hold an “emergency dialogue” about Saemangeum at Jogyesa Temple in Seoul on the 18th appears connected to the renewed activity around the bay. Having attached great significance to the partial victory in the first ruling, some had returned to anti-radioactive-waste-site protests or their daily lives. At the meeting, they reflected that “our complacent response could cost Saemangeum its lifeline” and vowed to reunite and work to save it.

At 7 p.m. on the 23rd, about 20 fishermen with grave expressions gathered at the volunteer crime-prevention patrol office in Gyehwa-ri, Buan County. They included village heads, fishing-cooperative leaders, and youth-association heads from fishing communities in Buan, Gimje, and Gunsan, whose livelihoods depend on the sea and mudflats around Saemangeum. A letter sent earlier that month to fishing-cooperative leaders had brought them together. The Saemangeum Project Group of the Korea Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation asked them to move fishing boats from inside the seawall to waters outside it, because the final seawall-closure work was scheduled to begin on March 24 of the following year.

“The final closure is tightening around our fishermen’s livelihoods. We felt we couldn’t just sit by, so we arranged this meeting to discuss what to do together.” Kim Jin-tae, head of the Gyehwado Fishing Cooperative, opened the discussion. “Final closure” means closing the two remaining openings, totaling 2.7 km, north of Garyeokdo and south of Shinsido. Those gaps are part of the 33-km seawall, divided into four construction sections. For the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, the Jeonbuk Provincial Government, and the Korea Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation, the work would bring a 15-year project to completion. For the mudflats and the life they support, however, it would close the last narrow passage through which they could breathe.

Fishers are leaving the clam beds during harvest season and taking turns protesting in Seoul
The appeal court’s final hearing is also approaching next month … a dimly moonlit evening
Even fishermen who had stood by are now gathering

While fierce public debate and court battles over the reclamation project continued outside the Saemangeum site, construction proceeded as planned inside the restricted area, apparently unaffected by the controversy. Strictly speaking, the final closure had not been delayed; work was waiting for the lock gates needed before closure could begin. When the reporter visited the seawall construction site north of Garyeokdo on the 23rd, trucks were busy hauling rocks for the final closure.

“The seawall project has been completely halted only once so far, for the three days immediately after the first Saemangeum court ruling,” said Kim Hak-won, head of the civil-engineering team at the Korea Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation’s Saemangeum Project Group. “We plan to finish the lock gates by March and begin the final closure, aiming to complete it on April 24, when the tidal range is smallest.” His words conveyed confidence that the Saemangeum project would continue regardless of outside criticism.

Although fishermen around Saemangeum share opposition to a project that threatens their livelihoods, their actions have differed considerably. Those in villages first harmed by the seawall—through rapid changes in mudflat fishing conditions and falling catches of fish and shellfish—were also the first to recognize the project’s problems. They therefore became active in the opposition movement. In villages not yet seriously affected by the seawall, many fishermen were busy making a living and paid little attention to Saemangeum. The meeting was also a chance to clear any resentment that may have grown between the groups.

Leaders from fishing villages that had not actively joined the opposition movement reached out first, saying, “We are ashamed that we didn’t even know you had gone all the way to the Blue House and were facing such criticism.” Leaders who had spearheaded the opposition joined hands with them and replied, “Politicians using Saemangeum to win votes have taken advantage of all of us. We are truly grateful that you are stepping forward now.” Those at the meeting agreed that “Saemangeum must be protected to the end, with hope,” and decided to join forces by forming a response organization.

Joo Yong-ki, co-executive chair of the Saemangeum Life and Peace Jeonbuk Solidarity, said, “Fishing cooperatives, which organize fishermen in the three cities and counties around Saemangeum, have now decided to take organized part in the opposition movement that has been led by environmental groups and some fishermen. This could kindle a new spark in efforts to save Saemangeum.”

Buan–Gunsan / Text and photos by Jeong-su Kim (jsk21@hani.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-231-8372c75064.title: Deep Ocean Water Research Complex Moves Ahead
ko-news-notices-231-8372c75064.text:
Deep Ocean Water Research Complex Moves Ahead
2022-03-02
Intake pipe installation progressing smoothly; Phase 1 expected to finish around the 10th of next month
Korea’s first pilot complex for deep-ocean-water research is taking shape.
On the 29th, the Deep Ocean Water Research Group at the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute (KORDI) said that construction of the intake pipeline, which began in earnest last month, had finished laying pipe as far as 2 km offshore. Work to bury the pipeline is now under way.
If construction continues at the current pace, Phase 1 is expected to be completed around the 10th of next month. The team then plans to conduct a test run and analyze water quality, which is expected to accelerate research projects using deep ocean water.
With installation of the intake pipeline nearing completion, Goseong County plans to establish an industrial complex through a public–private joint venture and begin full-scale production of bottled water, desalinated salt, and beverages, seeking ways to revitalize the local economy through deep ocean water.
Hyun-joo Kim, head of KORDI’s Deep Ocean Water Research Group, said, “Construction started about a month later than originally planned, but favorable weather has allowed it to proceed as scheduled. Completing the intake pipeline will mean that the research infrastructure is in place.”
Goseong — Reporter Hoon Choi

ko-news-notices-232-8372c75064.title: Government Neglect Leaves Coastal Fishing Grounds Seriously Polluted (Full Report)
ko-news-notices-232-8372c75064.text:
Government Neglect Leaves Coastal Fishing Grounds Seriously Polluted (Full Report)
2022-03-02
(Seoul—Yonhap News) Reporter Beom-hyeon Kim — A Board of Audit and Inspection report released on the 1st found that lax management and inadequate oversight by the central and local governments are allowing pollution to worsen in fishing grounds and coastal marine ecosystems.

An audit conducted late last year of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, the Ministry of Environment, and other agencies examined marine-pollution prevention and fishing-ground cleanup programs. It found that long-term continuous cultivation of aquaculture grounds, overcrowding, and failure to carry out voluntary cleanups were worsening pollution and reducing fishery productivity.

The Fishing Grounds Management Act requires each fishing ground to be cleaned voluntarily once every three years. If the requirement is not met, the responsible fishing-ground operator or organization may be fined by the competent city, county, or district.

Yet weak local-government oversight meant that many fishing grounds, including aquaculture sites, were not being cleaned as required. In 2003, these sites covered 74,307 hectares, or 53% of the total area of fishing grounds.

In Incheon, voluntary cleanup had been carried out on only 30 of the 3,901 hectares of fishing grounds. In Gangwon Province, it had been carried out on only 240 of 5,650 hectares, further worsening pollution.

The Board also said the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries should make aquaculture licenses conditional on completing required cleanup. It urged the ministry to amend the Fishing Grounds Management Act and related rules to link aquaculture licenses with mandatory cleanup.

As of December 31 of the previous year, 925 of the 8,625 licensed aquaculture sites—covering 10,256 hectares—had been continuously cultivated for more than 10 years. In Yeosu, authorities issued extension or development licenses to 157 sites that had been continuously cultivated, but failed to verify cleanup compliance at 92 of them.

Heavy-metal pollution in sediments beneath aquaculture grounds was serious in two coastal areas, including Tongyeong in South Gyeongsang Province. Sediment samples from farms off Tongyeong contained 291.44 mg/kg of copper, above the ERM benchmark of 270 mg/kg. The ERM level is the concentration at which adverse effects may occur in 50% of benthic organisms.

An audit of land-based pollution sources flowing into the sea also found that sewage-system coverage in watersheds draining into four environmental-conservation areas, including Wando and Doam Bay, was only 0.52%–21.68% as of December 30, 2003—far below the national average of 78.75%. As a result, untreated sewage was flowing into nearby coastal waters.

Nine rivers flowing into Masan Bay had water quality worse than Class V. Nevertheless, Masan City did not know the discharge routes used by 73 industrial wastewater facilities. The city also had not identified 1,015 high-volume wastewater-generating businesses that were discharging sewage into five rivers without connecting their pipes to interceptor sewers.

In 2000, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries designated four areas, including Hampyeong Bay, as environmental-conservation areas and five areas, including Sihwa Lake and the Incheon coast, as special-management areas. However, it prepared a master management plan only for Sihwa Lake and none for the other eight areas, leaving them exposed to land-based pollution.

As a result, the number of the 53 monitoring sites in environmental-conservation and special-management areas that exceeded the water-quality standards under the Framework Act on Environmental Policy rose from 18 in 2000 to 30 in 2003. All 19 sites classified as Class I waters had deteriorated to Class II by 2003.

Sediment testing also found more than twice the target level of hexavalent chromium in Gwangyang Bay: 123 mg/kg, compared with the 52.3 mg/kg target set by the National Fisheries Research and Development Institute (NFRDI). At least two types of heavy metals exceeded their targets in each of the areas tested.

Unlike standards for rice paddies, fields, and rivers, Korea had no criteria for heavy-metal contamination in marine sediments. The Board therefore asked the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries to establish and publish such standards.

The Board also urged the Minister of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries to develop a marine-pollution prevention plan for environmental-conservation and special-management areas; the Minister of Environment to expand basic environmental facilities and strengthen oversight of businesses illegally discharging sewage or wastewater; and the Mayor of Masan to require high-volume wastewater generators to connect drainage systems to interceptor sewers.
