ko-news-notices-233-8372c75064.title: Coastal Erosion Leaves No Room to Retreat
ko-news-notices-233-8372c75064.text:
Coastal Erosion Leaves No Room to Retreat
2022-03-02
Traffic halted in Sacheonjin-ri, Gangneung, after erosion washed away a military fence and beach
Coastal erosion is washing away beaches at well-known seaside resorts and damaging infrastructure, including military perimeter fencing and roads.
From the night of the 29th through the early morning of the 30th of last month, high waves washed away a 50-meter section of military coastal fencing in Sacheonjin-ri, Sacheon-myeon, Gangneung, and covered the adjacent road. As of the 1st, traffic in the area was completely halted. At the time, a high-wave advisory, with waves reaching up to 6 m, and a strong-wind advisory, with gusts up to 18 m/s, were in effect along the East Coast.
In September of the previous year, an 80-meter section of military perimeter fencing only about 200 m north of the newly damaged area was also washed away. Gangneung City and military units carried out emergency repairs.
At Anmok Beach in Gyeonso-dong, Gangneung, erosion over the past several months has washed away a roughly 300-meter stretch of beach. The resulting decline in visitors is affecting local businesses.
Despite serious erosion damage in Gangneung and elsewhere, government and other authorities have relied on one-off measures such as groynes and training dikes.
Professor Gyu-han Kim, 44, of Kwandong University said, “To identify and address the causes of coastal erosion, we urgently need long-term data-gathering plans. Instead, the authorities are showing the limits of a ‘put out today’s fire and move on’ approach.” He said Korea urgently needed measures such as developing specialist research groups at the national level.
Gangneung — Jeong-min Gu (jungmkoo@kado.net)

ko-news-notices-234-8372c75064.title: Netherlands Shifts from Building Dikes to Working with Nature
ko-news-notices-234-8372c75064.text:
Netherlands Shifts from Building Dikes to Working with Nature
2022-03-02
(Seoul—Yonhap News) Reporter Se-jin Kim — After centuries of fighting water to secure land, the Netherlands appears ready to abandon its hard-line strategy of building dikes and shift toward a softer, nature-friendly approach to flood management.

As global warming makes it increasingly difficult to predict how severe natural disasters could become, the urgent need to prepare for the worst is pushing the Netherlands to rethink its relationship with water and learn to live alongside it.

The International Herald Tribune (IHT) reported on the 6th that, as part of this effort, the Dutch government was buying millions of square meters of farmland and industrial land near major canals. The land would be kept available as floodplains in an emergency.

The government’s idea is that these areas would absorb floodwaters and act as buffers, preventing even greater damage from inundation.

The designated floodplains could still be used as farmland or developed with floating factories or homes. However, the dikes that have protected these areas could be lowered or removed entirely.

The Netherlands also plans to rely more on “natural barriers” against flooding, including sand dunes, marshes, and tidal flats, in addition to floodplains.

Builders are promoting “amphibious” houses that are fixed on the ground in ordinary conditions but can float when floodwaters rise.

Some architects and engineers are going further, proposing ambitious plans for floating farms, factories, and even apartment buildings.

Concern that global warming could pose a much larger and longer-term threat to the Netherlands has driven the government away from the simple idea of building dikes higher and larger.

Since 1990, precipitation in northern Europe has increased by 40%, significantly increasing winter river flows. In recent years, water rising to the tops of dikes has forced hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate on two occasions. These events have accelerated the Netherlands’ shift in flood-management strategy.

The Netherlands hopes its new approach to water management will be able to handle an exceptionally severe flood that occurs once every 10,000 years.

By contrast, New Orleans, which recently suffered extensive hurricane damage, had been protected by infrastructure designed to withstand floods expected once every 30 to 100 years.

In the Netherlands, cities, factories, and greenhouse-growing areas that generate 70% of gross domestic product are currently located below sea level.

smile@yna.co.kr
(End)

ko-news-notices-236-8372c75064.title: [Goseong] Foundations in Place for the Deep Ocean Water Industry
ko-news-notices-236-8372c75064.text:
[Goseong] Foundations in Place for the Deep Ocean Water Industry
2022-03-02
Goseong County is opening a center to conduct full-scale research on deep ocean water, the first development of its kind in Korea. The county announced that it will open the Deep Ocean Water Research Center on the 21st, jointly established with the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, and begin full-scale testing and research.
The county said it had invested KRW 13.9 billion in the research complex in Ohori, Jukwang-myeon, including a research-and-development building and a fisheries-experiment building. The center can draw an average of 1,000 tonnes of deep ocean water per day.
At the opening and first water-intake ceremony, Goseong County and the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute (KORDI) will sign a memorandum of understanding on building and operating the research center to support research and commercialization of deep ocean water.
Eight companies working on joint research and practical applications will move into the center and begin developing prototypes. The eight products are distilled soju by Kooksoondang; cosmetics by Aekyung Industrial; fermented sauces by Sempio Foods; green-tea drinks by Dongwon F&B; ion drinks by Hyeonnae Pharmaceutical Industry; tofu by Gangneung Chodang Tofu; rice wine by Doosan; and fermented drinks by Daehakchon.
A Goseong County official said, “Although work on burying the intake pipeline began somewhat later than planned, favorable weather has allowed it to proceed smoothly, and the deep-ocean-water development project is now on schedule.” The official added, “We expect this to provide a new way to revitalize the deep-ocean-water industry and the county’s stagnant local economy.”
Reporter Gyeong-ung Lee (kwlee@kwnews.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-237-8372c75064.title: Pohang Uses Seaweed-Forest Reefs to Fight Barren Grounds
ko-news-notices-237-8372c75064.text:
Pohang Uses Seaweed-Forest Reefs to Fight Barren Grounds
2022-03-02
Pohang City in North Gyeongsang Province has drawn attention for deploying seaweed-forest artificial reefs to combat “barren grounds,” a whitening phenomenon that is devastating coastal fishing grounds.
Barren grounds form when changes in the marine environment turn the surfaces of underwater rocks white, resembling desertification on land. The condition is highly damaging to the habitat of fish and shellfish, including sea urchins, abalone, and sea cucumbers.
Since the 1980s, when steel complexes and coastal tourism and recreation facilities were built indiscriminately along the East Coast of North Gyeongsang Province, large amounts of wastewater have flowed into the sea and become a major cause of damage to fishing grounds.
The seaweed-forest reefs are square concrete or steel structures measuring 3 m by 3 m. They are deployed on white, barren rocky areas of the seabed and allowed to settle. The idea is that seaweed spores, including those of wakame and kelp, will take hold on the submerged reefs and grow into dense underwater “forests,” creating better habitat for marine life.
These seaweed forests provide effective protection and nursery habitat for marine life. Fish use them as spawning grounds, and juvenile fish and shellfish can use them as nursery areas.
Pohang has 3,070 hectares of coastal fishing grounds, but catches and harvests have declined, causing hardship. The city identified barren grounds as a major cause of the drop in fishermen’s income.
This year, for the first time, the city spent KRW 140 million to deploy seaweed-forest reefs on a pilot basis at five fishing grounds, including the coastal grounds off Jigyeong-ri, Songna-myeon, in Buk-gu. An effectiveness survey by the East Sea Fisheries Research Institute found that the reefs had greatly supported spawning and propagation of fish and shellfish.
Next year, Pohang plans to spend KRW 600 million to designate three barren-ground sites along the East Coast and deploy about 200 reefs, beginning a full-scale, phased restoration of the marine ecosystem.
Oh Yeong-seok, a fisheries-resources officer in Pohang City’s Fisheries Department, said, “Once seaweed forests have formed around the reefs submerged from early next year, we expect the marine ecosystem degraded by barren grounds to be fully restored after 2008.”
Pohang — Reporter Sang-jo Kim (sangjo@kmib.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-238-8372c75064.title: Yeongheung and Seonjae Tidal Flats to Become a Wetland Conservation Area
ko-news-notices-238-8372c75064.text:
Yeongheung and Seonjae Tidal Flats to Become a Wetland Conservation Area
2022-03-02
[Seoul Newspaper] Despite earlier opposition from residents that had prevented the designation, 49.4 km² of tidal flats around Yeongheung and Seonjae Islands in Ongjin County, Incheon, will be designated as a wetland conservation area by the end of this month.
On the 9th, Incheon City said the designation would cover the tidal flats along Yeongheung and Seonjae Islands, excluding Janggyeong-ri and Sippori beaches, pond-style aquaculture sites, and the youth marine training center.
Infrastructure needed for fishing on the tidal flats, such as access roads to fishing grounds and small landing quays, is expected to be permitted in the area.
The city and the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries accepted residents’ requests to exclude four areas from the protected zone and allow such infrastructure to be built.
In November 2003, Incheon City had asked the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries to designate the tidal flats around Yeongheung and Seonjae Islands as a wetland conservation area, but resident opposition prevented the designation.
Based on the revised designation plan, the city held a final public hearing for residents that day in the Ongjin County Office conference room.
Incheon — Reporter Hak-jun Kim

ko-news-notices-239-8372c75064.title: 3D Visualization Produced of the East Sea Seafloor
ko-news-notices-239-8372c75064.text:
3D Visualization Produced of the East Sea Seafloor
2022-03-02
A three-dimensional visualization of the underwater terrain around the East Sea and Dokdo is expected to help people understand the seafloor off Korea’s east coast.
On the 23rd, the National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI) said it had completed a project, begun the previous April with a budget of KRW 100 million, to create 3D imagery of the seafloor in the East Sea and around Dokdo.
The project covered 99,000 km² of the East Sea. It visualizes seafloor topography in waters under Korea’s jurisdiction and around major trade ports, and is expected to help clarify the underwater geography of the East Sea and Dokdo.
For the 3D visualization, the institute drew on precise surveys conducted over two years beginning in 1996 to produce the National Basic Ocean Map. The surveys used advanced marine-observation equipment, including differential GPS (DGPS).
The visualization will also provide baseline data for assigning names to East Sea seafloor features, as announced by the Marine Geographical Names Committee of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries. The institute is discussing with the Ministry of Education and Human Resources Development how to include the material in elementary, middle, and high-school textbooks.
An institute official said, “This visualization will help people understand the East Sea and Dokdo and provide information that can clearly communicate Korea’s position internationally. Because it makes seafloor features easy to see in detail, it will also help raise public awareness of the ocean.”
Donghae — Reporter Seong-bae Hong (sbhong@kado.net)

ko-news-notices-240-8372c75064.title: [Goseong] “Goseong County Should Pursue the Deep Ocean Water Project Independently”
ko-news-notices-240-8372c75064.text:
[Goseong] “Goseong County Should Pursue the Deep Ocean Water Project Independently”
2022-03-02
The Goseong County Council urged the county to pursue development of a deep-ocean-water industrial complex as an independent county project.
At its 152nd administrative-affairs audit review on the 23rd, the council said Gangwon Province had entered a deep-ocean-water project that Goseong County and the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries were pursuing jointly, citing foreign-investment attraction as its rationale. The council said the province had spent more than two years without progress on the industrial-complex project.
It criticized the province for wasting time and budget by choosing foreign partners such as IBM and Arcadia whose financial resources and ability to carry out the project had not been verified. It also said the province had offered neither an apology nor an alternative.
The council urged Goseong County to become the sole developer of the deep-ocean-water industrial complex, actively attract domestic private investors, invalidate the agreement between the county and the province, and demand compensation from the province for losses caused by delays.
To promote marine biotechnology using deep ocean water, the council also called for developing an industrial complex, creating jobs, and expanding the county’s tax base. It urged the county to prepare a detailed, feasible comprehensive tourism-development plan linked to tourism to Mount Geumgang.
Reporter Gyeong-ung Lee (kwlee@kwnews.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-242-8372c75064.title: [Marine Observation] 2006 East Sea Marine Survey Program Announced
ko-news-notices-242-8372c75064.text:
[Marine Observation] 2006 East Sea Marine Survey Program Announced
2022-03-02
The East Sea Oceanographic Survey Office of the National Oceanographic Research Institute (Director Kim Jeong-gi) announced its 2006 marine survey program for Korea’s East Sea.
The main projects planned for 2006 include tide observations to measure sea-level highs and lows at six sites along the East Sea coast; tidal-current observations near Sokcho Port; surveys of Korean coastal currents off Donghae, Jukbyeon, and Hupo; surveys of tidal bench marks along the East Sea coast; short-term tide observations at Jumunjin and Ganggu to verify the vertical datum; a hydrographic survey of the waterway south of Jukbyeon Port; coastal-route surveys at 44 ports, including Ulsan Port; and a marine-characteristics survey of the anchorage at Donghae Port.
In particular, after Uljin County in North Gyeongsang Province was selected to host the first National Marine Sports Festival, organized by the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries that August, the office planned to observe seawater movement during the event and provide organizers and athletes with real-time data on the direction and speed of the flow. It said the program would be centered on local communities and users.
An agency official said, “We will promptly analyze and process the observations and provide them through our website (www.nori.go.kr). They will also be promptly incorporated into publications such as charts and other hydrographic publications. The data are expected to be widely used for safe vessel operations, port construction, understanding the marine environment, disaster-prevention support, and fishing activities.”

ko-news-notices-243-8372c75064.title: Yangyang’s Jeongam Beach Has Become a Gravel Beach
ko-news-notices-243-8372c75064.text:
Yangyang’s Jeongam Beach Has Become a Gravel Beach
2022-03-02
At Jeongam Beach in Ganghyeon-myeon, Yangyang County, sand has been washed off the beach for a long time, leaving it covered with gravel.
The sand-scouring (sand being washed away) at Jeongam Beach has continued for more than a decade. During that time, the roughly one-meter-thick sandy beach disappeared, exposing the gravel that had been buried beneath it. As a result, it is uncertain whether the beach can operate this year.
The sand loss, once confined to some sections, has recently spread across the entire beach. Gravel is now exposed along a one-kilometer stretch, prompting calls for urgent countermeasures.
Residents said, “All the sand on Jeongam Beach has disappeared, leaving gravel, and we are not even sure the beach can operate this summer.” They added, “Measures are needed to address this sand-scouring as well as coastal erosion along the East Coast.”
Yangyang County plans to temporarily stockpile sand generated by dredging the nearby Jeonjin Port and use it to restore the beach for the summer holiday season. However, the sand poured onto the beach continues to be washed away by waves, and no fundamental measure to prevent the loss of sand has been established.
A county official said, “The sand loss at Jeongam Beach is thought to result either from artificial structures such as breakwaters or from large buildings along the coast disrupting the flow of sea breezes. We plan to develop and implement long-term measures addressing sand-scouring as well as coastal erosion.”
Yangyang / Nam Jin-cheon

ko-news-notices-244-8372c75064.title: Sihwa Lake’s Fourth Main Drainage Channel to Flow Again
ko-news-notices-244-8372c75064.text:
Sihwa Lake’s Fourth Main Drainage Channel to Flow Again
2022-03-02
Water quality in the Fourth Main Drainage Channel, one of the major pollution sources affecting Sihwa Lake, has improved enough for its water to flow into the lake again after two years.
The Sihwa Regional Sustainable Development Council said on the 18th that, since the second half of last year, the channel’s COD (chemical oxygen demand) level had fallen below 20 ppm and remained there for more than six months.
That level is about one-hundredth of the 1,970 ppm recorded in March 2004 and meets the legal limit of 40 ppm.
Accordingly, the council decided to remove the 40-meter-long weir installed in the Fourth Main Drainage Channel and hold a ceremony to restore the channel’s flow into Sihwa Lake at about 1 p.m. on the 19th on the northern reclaimed tidal flat.
After water quality in the Fourth Main Drainage Channel was found to be extremely poor in early 2004, weirs were installed on it and the First Main Drainage Channel to prevent their water from flowing into Sihwa Lake. The water was instead routed through collection sewers and treated at the Sihwa Sewage Treatment Plant.
Beginning this year, the council decided to gradually expand water-quality improvement work to the First Main Drainage Channel, where a weir is installed, and to the Second and Third Main Drainage Channels.
A council official said, “Over the past two years, we monitored the water quality of 13 stormwater conduits connected to the Fourth Main Drainage Channel every day, repaired 64 locations where sewer lines had been incorrectly connected, and achieved improvements through ongoing inspections of businesses, education, and outreach.”
The Sihwa Regional Sustainable Development Council was established in February 2004 as a public-private consultative body involving the Ministry of Construction and Transportation, local governments, local civic groups and residents, experts, and the Korea Water Resources Corporation. It has worked to improve water quality in the Fourth Main Drainage Channel—the most polluted of the four main drainage channels—and to prepare a comprehensive development plan for the Sihwa District.
Siheung — Reporter Kim Shin-seop (blog: sskim)

ko-news-notices-245-8372c75064.title: Seogwipo Tourism Harbor Project to Move Forward
ko-news-notices-245-8372c75064.text:
Seogwipo Tourism Harbor Project to Move Forward
2022-03-02
The Seogwipo Tourism Harbor development project, one of the seven flagship projects of Jeju Free International City, is set to move forward at a site in the sea 400 meters east of its originally planned location. The Wellbeing Theme Town, once reported as a replacement for the tourism harbor, is being pursued separately as a follow-up project to the seven flagship projects. Infrastructure work for the Yerae-dong resort-style residential complex in Seogwipo is to begin in the second half of this year, while sales at the Jeju High-Tech Science and Technology Complex are expected to begin around May. This article looks at how the seven projects are taking shape.
◆ Tourism Harbor and Wellbeing Theme Town
According to Seogwipo City and the Jeju Free International City Development Center on the 25th, the Seogwipo Tourism Harbor project had been at risk of being canceled after the Cultural Heritage Administration denied permission for an alteration, citing concerns about impacts on soft-coral colonies offshore from Seogwipo Port and the habitat of giant mottled eels downstream from Cheonjiyeon Falls. The Development Center had reportedly planned to build a Wellbeing Theme Town in Seogwipo as a replacement if the tourism harbor project fell through.
However, Seogwipo City and the Development Center are reportedly in talks to continue the tourism-harbor project at a different location. They concluded that reclaiming the Jaguri Coast for the original plan would be difficult and are considering a marine leisure and tourism complex in the waters about 400 meters east of the coast, covering roughly 64,000 pyeong. The proposed facilities include berths for cruise ships of 30,000 to 80,000 tons, moorings incorporating a marina, water-sports facilities, and a visitor center. The city and the Development Center say this approach would allow development while minimizing environmental damage.
The Wellbeing Theme Town, which has been pursued since 2004, will therefore proceed entirely separately from the tourism harbor. The Development Center initially planned a “Health and Beauty Town,” then expanded the concept into a Wellbeing Theme Town with vocational training institutions, specialized nursing facilities for older people, and alternative-medicine treatment facilities. Because it is not a replacement project for the tourism harbor, it is unclear whether the town will be built in downtown Seogwipo. Inland mid-mountain areas, hot-spring sites, and coastal areas are under consideration.
◆ High-Tech Science Complex sales expected around May
The resort-style residential complex received approval for its development project and implementation plan last October. Construction is expected to begin after the detailed-design service results are released at the end of August. Consent to sell has been obtained from owners of 71 percent of the land, and land-compensation work is proceeding relatively smoothly.
For the Jeju High-Tech Science and Technology Complex, land compensation—the most difficult task—was completed last December, and sales are expected to begin around May. The complex is drawing interest from companies in Seoul and other parts of the capital region with substantial incentives for incoming businesses, including a 100-percent corporate-tax exemption for three years and a 50-percent reduction in property tax and comprehensive land tax for five years. Purchase contracts have also been signed for 70 percent of the total area of Shinhwa Historical Park, and approval for its development project is expected this year.
◆ Shopping outlets and other projects expected to lag
Three projects—the Jeju High-Tech Science and Technology Complex, the Yerae-dong resort-style residential complex, and Shinhwa Historical Park—are progressing smoothly. It remains uncertain, however, whether the shopping outlet, Seogwipo Tourism Harbor, expansion of the Jungmun Complex, and designation of Jeju Airport as a free-trade zone can proceed as originally planned. The airport free-trade-zone designation failed to materialize late last year.
Jin Cheol-hoon, chairman of the Jeju Free International City Development Center, said, “This year, we will focus our efforts on three key projects: the high-tech science and technology complex, the resort-style residential complex, and Shinhwa Historical Park.” He added, “In particular, for 2006 Visit Jeju Year, we will step up promotion and marketing of Jeju development projects and devote our efforts to attracting domestic and international investors.”
Reporter Lim Hyeong-gyun (hyim@chosun.com)

ko-news-notices-246-8372c75064.title: Busan Plans an Underwater Park off Dadaepo
ko-news-notices-246-8372c75064.text:
Busan Plans an Underwater Park off Dadaepo
2022-03-02
A project is under way to create Korea’s first underwater park, where visitors can experience the world beneath the sea off the coast of Busan.
On the 25th, Busan City announced plans to establish a 7,000-hectare “underwater fish park” in the waters around Namu Island and Hyeongje Islands, southeast of Dadaepo Port in Saha-gu. The city has secured KRW 100 million in municipal funding and plans to commission a study in February to prepare the basic plan.
The study will outline the park’s proposed location and direction, construction costs, and facilities. The city will then decide whether to proceed with full-scale implementation. If the study is completed at the end of this year and the project advances as planned, the park is expected to be completed around 2010.
The plan is to establish aquaculture sites equipped with artificial reefs and let visitors experience diverse fish and underwater environments through scuba diving, snorkeling, an underwater observation tower, and glass-bottom boats. The city is also considering an ocean-viewing platform and fishing area on Namu Island.
A Busan City official said, “As Busan aspires to become a marine-tourism city, we are pursuing an environmentally friendly underwater park to create attractions and activities that make use of the underwater world.”
Reporter Son Young-sin (zero@)

ko-news-notices-247-8372c75064.title: Ministry Launches Tidal-Flat Ecosystem Website
ko-news-notices-247-8372c75064.text:
Ministry Launches Tidal-Flat Ecosystem Website
2022-03-02
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries will begin full operation on the 23rd of an information website on tidal-flat ecosystems (tidalflat.go.kr). Visitors can view major tidal flats across the country at a glance and take a virtual tour of a tidal flat.
The site offers a range of information, including definitions and types of tidal flats, well-known tidal flats in Korea and abroad, tidal information, and related international conventions.
It also provides information on five wetland-protection areas, including Muan Tidal Flat, designated for tidal-flat ecosystem conservation, and four ecosystem-conservation areas, including the Sinduri Coastal Dune area. The site’s tidal-flat information center includes a virtual tidal-flat experience, a marine-terms dictionary, and an open forum.
Reporter Lee Dong-hyeon
Busan Ilbo / Entered: 2006-01-23 11:03

ko-news-notices-248-8372c75064.title: Saemangeum Seawall Gap-Closing Work to Finish in April
ko-news-notices-248-8372c75064.text:
Saemangeum Seawall Gap-Closing Work to Finish in April
2022-03-02
After 15 years of work on the world’s longest seawall, the final gap-closing work on the 33-kilometer Saemangeum Seawall resumed in March following a two-year-and-nine-month pause and is scheduled to finish in April.
The Saemangeum Project Office of the Korea Rural Community Corporation said on the 30th, “After preparing earth, rock, and other materials beginning in February, we will start closing the two remaining gaps, a combined 2.7 kilometers, on March 24 and expect to finish in late April.”
Once the gaps are closed, the 33-kilometer seawall will connect Buan, Gimje, and Gunsan in North Jeolla Province. Behind it, 28,300 hectares of reclaimed land—about 140 times the area of Yeouido—and an 11,800-hectare freshwater lake will be created.
Work will take place in late March, when tidal exchange is at its lowest during the year. Crews will remove the temporary cofferdam and use large barges and trucks to dump rock-filled gabion baskets weighing at least three tons into the sea to close the gaps. The project will require 1.17 million cubic meters of stone, equivalent to 180,000 large dump-truck loads.
The average daily advance will be 105 meters. Barges at sea will dump 600 cubic meters of stone at a time, while dump trucks on the seawall will extend the embankment to a height of 5 meters above sea level and a top width of 9 meters. During the final week, 210 dump trucks, 43 pieces of heavy equipment, and 14 barges will be mobilized. Currents reach 6 to 7 meters per second, so crews will continuously place gabions designed to withstand the strong currents and individual rock blocks weighing 3 to 5 tons to join the seawall.
This is the final gap-closing operation. Paving the roadway for public and vehicle access is expected to be completed by the end of 2008.
The project office will hold an on-site briefing on the overall final-stage work on the 2nd of next month, attended by government officials including Minister of Agriculture and Forestry Park Hong-soo and Korea Rural Community Corporation President Ahn Jong-un.
The project office said, “Closing the 2.7-kilometer gap requires a level of technical skill incomparable to the seawall work completed so far. Foreign experts, including those from the Netherlands, have expressed interest in visiting to observe this project, described as an exceptionally difficult undertaking in architecture and civil engineering.”
Construction of the Saemangeum Seawall began in 1991, and 27.3 kilometers had been completed. After a joint public-private investigation and lawsuits, forward construction had been halted for two years and seven months, with only reinforcement work continuing. Of the total project cost of KRW 3.4756 trillion, KRW 2.1604 trillion was for the seawall, and 88 percent of that seawall budget had been spent by the previous year.
Buan — Reporter Kim Yong-gwon (ygkim@kmib.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-249-8372c75064.title: “Introduce Coastal Total Pollutant Load Management off Busan”
ko-news-notices-249-8372c75064.text:
“Introduce Coastal Total Pollutant Load Management off Busan”
2022-03-02
A proposal has been made to introduce a coastal total pollutant load management system to protect water quality in Busan’s coastal waters. Rather than relying on the current concentration-based regulation of pollution sources, the proposal would manage total pollutant loads within the environmental capacity of each coastal water area.
The proposal appeared in a report titled “Basic Research for Implementing Coastal Total Pollutant Load Management in Busan,” released on the 1st by Baek Gyeong-hoon, associate research fellow at the Busan Development Institute.
The report says water-quality management would be more effective if the Busan coast were divided into three types of area for pollutant-load management: ecological coasts, which have rich biodiversity and high ecological value; environmental-management coasts, where water quality needs improvement because land-based pollutants are entering the sea in significant amounts; and water-oriented recreational coasts, which have high scenic and cultural value. It expects load management in each area to help prevent indiscriminate development along the coast.
As prerequisites for applying the system, the report calls for surveys and research on pollutant discharges from marine aquaculture farms, contamination levels and pollutant release from seabed sediments, and pollutant discharges from ships.
It also says that several years of baseline data on the marine environment must be accumulated for the coastal waters covered by the system, including patterns of human use, geographic location, tidal-current patterns, and ocean-current circulation.
Reporter Kim Jong-gyun (kjg11@busanilbo.com)

ko-news-notices-250-8372c75064.title: Hydrographic Surveys Mandatory After Marine Construction from This Year
ko-news-notices-250-8372c75064.text:
Hydrographic Surveys Mandatory After Marine Construction from This Year
2022-03-02
Amendments to the Hydrographic Survey Act take effect January 30.
Beginning January 30, any marine construction work related to vessel navigation safety must be followed by a hydrographic survey, paid for by the party responsible for the construction.
Under the amended Hydrographic Survey Act, the project owner must conduct a hydrographic survey for work that alters the existing coastline or seabed topography. This includes most port construction, channel dredging, coastal reclamation, marine-sand extraction, and installation of artificial reefs. The survey results must be submitted to the government for review.
An official from the National Oceanographic Research Institute said, “With the amendments taking effect, changes in the marine environment can be communicated promptly to mariners. This will contribute to navigational safety and provide baseline information that will help the government develop more reasonable coastal-management measures based on scientific understanding of unexpected coastal erosion and sedimentation.”
The amended Hydrographic Survey Act was promulgated on July 29, 2005. Amendments to its subordinate regulations were approved at a Cabinet meeting on January 24, and the provisions took effect on January 30.

ko-news-notices-251-8372c75064.title: [Coastal Management] Coastal-Disaster Prevention Policy Featured Abroad
ko-news-notices-251-8372c75064.text:
[Coastal Management] Coastal-Disaster Prevention Policy Featured Abroad
2022-03-02
Storm-surge warning system selected as a featured policy for February and presented in an English-language government magazine
A project to establish a warning system to reduce damage from coastal surges, carried out by the National Oceanographic Research Institute as a key 2005 initiative, was featured internationally in the February issue of Korea Policy Review, an English-language government policy magazine.
The article describes comprehensive, coordinated marine monitoring for natural hazards originating at sea, such as storm surges and tsunamis; sharing observational information; and promptly assessing and disseminating information about developing situations. It presents the institute’s overall policy for preventing coastal disasters.
Korea Policy Review (KPR), published monthly by the Korean Overseas Information Service under the Government Information Agency, is an English-language guide to government policy. It is produced to introduce major Korean government policies and the country’s development to experts around the world and to strengthen international confidence in Korea. The article can be found under “Multimedia” and “Magazines” at http://www.korea.net.
An institute official said, “Taking this overseas coverage as an opportunity, we will work harder to publicize the institute’s activities internationally, in step with the government’s efforts to actively promote its policies abroad in an increasingly globalized world.”

ko-news-notices-252-8372c75064.title: Dedicated Marine Environmental Assessment Center Established
ko-news-notices-252-8372c75064.text:
Dedicated Marine Environmental Assessment Center Established
2022-03-02
A dedicated body will handle environmental impact assessments for development projects that use the sea, including marine-aggregate extraction.
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries said it had established a Marine Environmental Impact Assessment Center at the National Fisheries Research and Development Institute to systematically manage the effects of steadily increasing marine-development activities on the marine environment. The center began operations on the 17th.
To ensure expertise and impartiality in its assessments, the center has an assessment review committee and has appointed 35 marine-environment experts from universities, research institutes, and environmental organizations to serve as expert members. It will operate five subcommittees covering water quality, sediment, prediction and mitigation, socioeconomic matters, and marine life.
The center is expected to strengthen specialized analysis and assessment of the marine-environment impacts of activities such as marine-aggregate extraction. It will also strengthen the marine-environment consultation component of environmental impact assessments and preliminary environmental reviews conducted by the Ministry of Environment.
The ministry also plans to build assessment capacity systematically by developing methods for reviewing marine environmental impact assessment reports and guidelines for different types of activities, training officials responsible for the work, and creating a database of assessment materials.
Until now, marine-environment surveys had been divided between the National Fisheries Research and Development Institute and the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute.
As a result, the fisheries institute took over management of automatic marine water-quality monitoring stations that had been operated by the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute at eight locations nationwide, including the Nakdong River and Masan Bay.
However, some in marine science and industry have objected to consolidating marine environmental impact assessment at the fisheries institute, saying, “It is hard to understand why the institute responsible for fisheries resources and aquaculture has been put in charge of marine environmental assessment.”
Reporter Lee Dong-hyeon / Busan Ilbo

ko-news-notices-253-8372c75064.title: Incheon Coastal Water Quality Deteriorating Rapidly
ko-news-notices-253-8372c75064.text:
Incheon Coastal Water Quality Deteriorating Rapidly
2022-03-02
Incheon City is preparing countermeasures after reports showed that coastal water quality is worsening and the volume of waste collected along the Incheon coast is increasing.
According to the city on the 21st, the coastal COD (chemical oxygen demand) level rose sharply over the past four years, from 1.32 mg/L in 2002 to 1.71 mg/L in 2004 and 1.69 mg/L last year.
Last year, 19,916 metric tons of waste were collected along the coast, up 14.9 percent from 17,330 tons in 2004 and nearly 2.5 times the 7,980 tons collected in 2002.
By type, midwater debris rose more than tenfold, from 380 tons in 2002 to 4,481 tons last year. Coastal debris also increased nearly sixfold, from 2,663 to 13,370 tons.
Over the same period, however, floating marine debris fell by about half, from 1,290 to 692 tons, while debris accumulated on the seafloor declined by about two-thirds, from 3,647 to 1,373 tons.
The city plans to draw up comprehensive measures to improve coastal water quality and protect marine ecosystems, with a budget of about KRW 9.4 billion this year.
To monitor pollution, the city will spend KRW 24 million to install a real-time automatic marine water-quality monitoring network in waters near Palmido. It also plans to spend KRW 1 billion and, by the end of this year, install a dedicated incinerator and volume-reduction machine on Socheongdo and Ganghwa, each capable of processing 100 kilograms of marine waste per hour.
The city will also expand and designate a 153-square-kilometer wetland-protection area covering the tidal flats of Yeongjongdo and Yeongheungdo. It plans to develop a 55.7-square-kilometer area around Daeijakdo in Jawol-myeon as a pilot site for native-plant communities.
Reporter Park In-gwon / Incheon Ilbo

ko-news-notices-258-8372c75064.title: Supreme Court Ruling Allows Saemangeum Project to Proceed, a Victory for Government
ko-news-notices-258-8372c75064.text:
Supreme Court Ruling Allows Saemangeum Project to Proceed, a Victory for Government
2022-03-02
[Edaily, Reporter Cho Yong-cheol] In the dispute over the Saemangeum project between environmental groups seeking to preserve tidal flats and the government seeking to develop high-quality farmland, the Supreme Court ruled in the government’s favor. The government’s position was to close the seawall, create reclaimed land, and develop high-quality farmland.
On the 16th, the Supreme Court sitting en banc affirmed the lower court’s ruling against 3,538 residents of North Jeolla Province and environmental groups who had sued the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, Jeollabuk-do Province, and others to cancel the Saemangeum project plan.
In its opinion, the court said, “Although there are differing views, the joint public-private investigation team’s economic analysis found the Saemangeum master plan to be economically viable. The lower court was therefore correct to find no clear evidence supporting the claims of environmental groups and others that the project was not economically viable.”
The court explained, “In light of increased demand for land, the need to develop replacement farmland for marginal farmland, and changes in domestic and international conditions—including the risk of future food shortages due to the opening of rice imports and the reunification of North and South Korea—the Saemangeum project is an important national undertaking.”
The court also said, “Environmental groups and others claim that the government concealed the purpose of the Saemangeum project and conducted a deficient environmental impact assessment. However, the evidence is insufficient, and the assessment was lawful under the statutes in force at the time and followed the procedure for gathering residents’ opinions.”
On environmental concerns, the court added, “The water-quality standards for the freshwater lake are expected to be met through a phased development approach that separates the Dongjin and Mangyeong water areas and circulates seawater through the Mangyeong area to gradually convert it to freshwater. It is therefore difficult to find that a material change in circumstances has occurred.”
Supreme Court Justices Kim Young-ran and Park Si-hwan dissented, saying, “The need to secure farmland has diminished considerably, even at the cost of sacrificing the Saemangeum tidal flats, a valuable resource for both present and future generations. Given also that the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry’s environmental impact assessment and economic review were deficient or overstated, the Saemangeum project should be canceled.”
Their dissent added, “The demands of our time require protecting the living and natural environments from infringement and damage, and ensuring that everyone can enjoy a healthy and pleasant environment and live with human dignity.”

ko-news-notices-260-8372c75064.title: Comprehensive Observations of Seawater Movement from Yeosu to Mokpo
ko-news-notices-260-8372c75064.text:
Comprehensive Observations of Seawater Movement from Yeosu to Mokpo
2022-03-02
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (Director Jeong Yu-seop) announced that it will conduct observations of seawater movement in the waters from Yeosu to around Mokpo from the 21st of this month through the end of October.
Observation sites were selected with advice from about 20 marine-related organizations and around 10 university professors. The seven-month survey will continuously measure tides, tidal currents, and ocean currents in both horizontal and vertical dimensions, using real-time wide-area sea-level observation equipment, seabed-mounted current meters at multiple depths, and sea-level gauges.
The waters are part of Dadohaehaesang National Park. The many islands make water movement complex, and strong currents have contributed to frequent vessel accidents. The area is also a source of harmful algal blooms that repeatedly damage nearby aquaculture, making information on seawater movement essential.
An institute official said, “Once the observations are complete, they will reveal the complex characteristics of seawater movement and allow us to calculate constants for tidal-current forecasts. We expect accurate seawater-movement information for this area to help improve maritime traffic safety and support harmful-algal-bloom response.”
The institute plans to begin providing seawater-movement forecast information through its website (www.nori.go.kr) next year.

ko-news-notices-261-8372c75064.title: Marine Engineering Tank for Experiments Completed
ko-news-notices-261-8372c75064.text:
Marine Engineering Tank for Experiments Completed
2022-03-02
A world-class marine-engineering tank, described as a “small sea,” has been completed in Korea and is beginning full-scale operation.
The Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute said on the 26th that it had held a completion ceremony for installation of a large Computerized Planar Motion Carriage (CPMC) at the Marine Engineering Tank of its Marine System Safety Research Center in the Daedeok Research Complex in Daejeon. The facility is now in full operation.
The institute’s marine-engineering tank, in operation since 1998, is a comprehensive test facility for reproducing sea states found in real waters. It is 56 meters long, 30 meters wide, and 4.5 meters deep. It also has a high-performance deep-sea pit, 5 meters in diameter and 12 meters deep, for simulating deep water.
With the CPMC now installed, the tank has equipment for reproducing irregular waves from multiple directions, uniform currents, and wind with specified spectral characteristics, as well as a vertically movable wave maker. It can reproduce a range of wave conditions close to those at sea.
Tests that previously had to be carried out overseas—including ship seakeeping tests, maneuvering tests of ships and underwater objects, and transport, installation, and motion tests of various marine structures—can now be conducted in Korea. This is expected to help protect domestic technology and strengthen the international competitiveness of Korea’s shipbuilding and marine industries.
At the ceremony, KORDI President Yeom Ki-dae said, “Now that Korea has an advanced facility for marine research and testing, it will greatly help advance shipbuilding and marine technology.”
Reporter Cho Jin-man

ko-news-notices-262-8372c75064.title: Sand-Price Dispute Stalls Busan New Port’s South Container Terminal Works
ko-news-notices-262-8372c75064.text:
Sand-Price Dispute Stalls Busan New Port’s South Container Terminal Works
2022-03-02
Construction of Phase 2-2 of the South Container Terminal at Busan New Port continues to be disrupted by a “sand war.” The Busan Regional Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Office, the ordering agency, has responded cautiously, saying the work is not on the project’s critical path and will not affect the overall schedule. Dado Shipping, the company contracted to extract and transport sand, must extract by July the volume originally authorized by the government. If it fails to do so and its permit lapses, the entire new port could lose its source of sand, making a severe supply crisis difficult to avoid.
▲ Price talks remain deadlocked
Daelim Industrial, responsible for building Phase 2-2 of the South Container Terminal, and sand-extraction company Dado Shipping have continued price negotiations but have yet to reach an agreement. Daelim planned to begin sand-fill work on December 15 last year, but has been unable to buy sand and cannot proceed with reclamation work beyond the SCP (sand-compaction-pile) work. Daelim manager Ko Gwang-guk said, “When we won the contract, we set the sand price at about KRW 6,000 per cubic meter. It now exceeds KRW 10,000, which we cannot accept. From the 3rd of next month, we will have to secure sand and start construction, no matter how high the price.”
Dado Shipping says it cannot lower the price because it supplied sand at the same price to Daewoo Engineering & Construction for the new port’s multi-purpose terminal and to Daelim at the Gwangyang Port construction site. Dado argues that cutting the price only for Daelim would prompt objections from other companies on grounds of unfair treatment and could harm small and midsize transport companies.
▲ Outlook
There is no clear way to mediate or resolve the standoff between the two companies. The dispute is increasingly likely to delay the new-port construction project, a national undertaking, and weaken Busan Port’s competitiveness. The Busan Regional Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Office says it will not intervene in individual companies’ pricing disputes. It is considering combining the first- and second-phase reclamation work sections, but that could increase the total sand requirement, and it remains uncertain whether the contractor would accept the plan.
There are also concerns that the permit for sand extraction off the south coast could lapse. Because sand extraction and supply had been delayed, Dado Shipping received an extension from the Ministry of Construction and Transportation through July to extract sand in waters 50 kilometers southeast of Yokjido off the south coast. The permit period can be extended only once; if extraction still does not take place, the permit for the Yokjido waters could lapse. If that happens, the new-port project could be seriously disrupted because at least 40 million cubic meters of sand would be unavailable for Phase 2-2, future Phases 2-3 and 2-4, the West Container Terminal, and development of the port’s hinterland.
Cho Jong-hwan, director of the Busan Port Construction Office, said, “Sand reclamation is not a critical-path activity that will delay the overall construction schedule, so there should be no major problem completing the terminal in 2008.”
Reporter Cho Jin-man (jmcho@kookje.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-263-8372c75064.title: U.S. FDA Praises Sanitary Conditions in Yeosu’s Gamak Bay
ko-news-notices-263-8372c75064.text:
U.S. FDA Praises Sanitary Conditions in Yeosu’s Gamak Bay
2022-03-02
Sanitary conditions in the waters around Gamak Bay on the south coast of South Jeolla Province have been found to be good.
South Jeolla Province said on the 27th that, after an on-site inspection of the 4,188-hectare Gamak Bay area near Yeosu, two U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) employees, including a shellfish-sanitation specialist, rated the sanitary conditions in the waters very highly.
After the inspection, FDA employee Michael Anti said at an assessment meeting at Yeosu City Hall, “Satisfactory standards were met in maintaining a suitable distance between the designated shellfish-growing waters and fish farms, keeping the offshore area and shoreline clean, marking the boundaries of the designated waters, and preventing discharges of land-based pollutants.” He added, “The area is managed very systematically and well.”
The FDA employees also expressed satisfaction with measures to reduce water pollution through thorough recordkeeping on antibiotic use at offshore fish farms using net cages.
From the 22nd through the 24th, the FDA conducted an on-site review of sanitation management in designated waters in South Jeolla Province, including Gamak Bay near Yeosu and the waters around Narodo in Goheung. Inspections are conducted every two years under the 1972 Korea–U.S. Shellfish Sanitation Agreement and a memorandum of understanding exchanged by the two countries in 2003. They focus primarily on sanitation in Gamak Bay, including how pollution sources are managed.
FDA recognition of the designated waters’ safety has wider effects, lending international recognition to the safety of fisheries products from South Jeolla waters and significantly influencing future seafood exports. Gamak Bay produces about 7,000 tons of shellfish a year, including oysters, ark shells, and Manila clams; 2,000 tons of oysters are exported to the United States.
A South Jeolla Province official said, “In preparation for the FDA inspection, we conducted three rounds of management checks in the designated waters with the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, Yeosu City, and Goheung County.” The official added, “Now that the safety of the designated waters has been recognized, we expect access to the U.S. export market without a separate, more stringent procedure.”
Mokpo — Kookmin Ilbo Cookie News Reporter Lee Sang-il (silee062@kmib.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-264-8372c75064.title: Korea’s Tidal-Flat Area Projected to Halve in 32 Years
ko-news-notices-264-8372c75064.text:
Korea’s Tidal-Flat Area Projected to Halve in 32 Years
2022-03-02
A study has projected that the area of Korea’s tidal flats, often called a repository of marine life, will have fallen by half over the 32 years from 1964 through the year of the study.
On the 30th, the Korea Environment Institute (KEI) said that the “Korean Marine Handbook” recorded 3,905 square kilometers of tidal flats in Korea in 1964. Taking west-coast reclamation into account, the area was expected to shrink to 2,000 square kilometers in the study year and to less than 1,500 square kilometers by 2015.
From 1987, when development of the west coast began in earnest, through the study year, 810.5 square kilometers of tidal flats had officially been reclaimed. The Saemangeum project (208 square kilometers) and Sihwa Lake project (180 square kilometers) accounted for 48 percent of that area and were identified as major drivers of tidal-flat loss.
Of Korea’s tidal flats, South Jeolla Province has the largest share at 44 percent, followed by Gyeonggi Province at 35 percent, South Chungcheong Province at 13 percent, North Jeolla Province at 5 percent, and South Gyeongsang Province—including Busan—at 3 percent. South Jeolla and Gyeonggi, both on the west coast, together account for about 80 percent.
The institute said that over the past decade coastal tidal flats had declined sharply—by 30 to 40 percent, especially along the west coast—because of large-scale reclamation projects. It also noted frequent cases in which marine reclamation work was halted, reduced, or modified because of indiscriminate development and environmental damage.
Of 51 marine-reclamation projects that completed environmental-impact-assessment consultations during the three years beginning in 2002, 15 (30 percent) were reduced or canceled because of environmental concerns—in other words, three out of ten were held up.
To prevent suspended sediment from spreading during reclamation and dredging, the institute proposed installing silt curtains during construction and classifying reclamation areas as conservation, development-management, or development-improvement areas as part of an environmentally sound management system.
Reporter Kim Seong-yong (ksy@yna.co.kr) / Yonhap News (Seoul)

ko-news-notices-265-8372c75064.title: “Saemangeum Can Meet Agricultural-Water Standard by 2012” — Seoul National University College of Agriculture
ko-news-notices-265-8372c75064.text:
“Saemangeum Can Meet Agricultural-Water Standard by 2012” — Seoul National University College of Agriculture
2022-03-02
A study has found that Saemangeum Lake, which has been at the center of water-pollution concerns, is expected to meet the Class IV lake-water standard for agricultural use by 2012, when construction is scheduled to be completed.
On the 2nd, a research team led by Professor Park Seung-woo of Seoul National University’s College of Agriculture said that, after six months of research commissioned by the Saemangeum Environmental Measures Working Committee in August last year, it projected total phosphorus (TP) in the Mangyeong waters of Saemangeum Lake would be 0.094 mg/L in 2012. This would meet the Class IV lake-water standard of 0.1 mg/L or less.
A 2001 water-quality forecast by the Ministry of Environment and a joint public-private investigation team had concluded that, even with the government’s water-quality conservation measures, TP in the Mangyeong waters would reach 0.103 mg/L in 2012, making the Class IV target difficult to meet.
The research team said that since August 2002, about 300 million tons of water released annually from nearby Yongdam Dam for power generation had flowed into the upper reaches of the Mangyeong River, producing a clear dilution of pollutants. It also attributed the lower pollutant output to demographic and livestock changes: Jeollabuk-do’s population fell by about 52,000 between 1998 and 2002, while the numbers of Korean native cattle and dairy cows declined by 8.9 percent and 2.7 percent, respectively.
The team added that, since the Ministry of Environment’s 2001 survey, the government had implemented stronger water-quality conservation measures that substantially reduced pollutant inputs to the Mangyeong waters, further supporting the projected result.
Professor Park said, “Since 2003, major water-quality indicators such as biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and total phosphorus have improved considerably. If the original water-quality measures are carried out as planned, we expect water quality to improve beyond the target.”
Kookmin Ilbo Cookie News — Reporter Noh Yong-taek (nyt@kmib.co.kr)

ko-news-notices-267-8372c75064.title: Proposed Dredging off Sinseondae Pier Sparks Controversy
ko-news-notices-267-8372c75064.text:
Proposed Dredging off Sinseondae Pier Sparks Controversy
2022-03-02
Government port policy has appeared inconsistent over a proposed dredging project in the waters in front of Sinseondae Pier, one of Busan’s major container terminals.
On the 11th, the Busan Regional Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Office said it would commission experts to assess economic feasibility and other issues before carrying out a deepening-dredging project there under the non-management-authority port-construction scheme. This put the immediate project on hold at a recent meeting of the office, Busan Port Authority (BPA), and Sinseondae Container Terminal Co. (PECT), after the office had announced its intention to proceed.
As a result, the dredging project requested by PECT has been delayed again. The article describes non-management-authority port construction as a scheme in which a port project that would ordinarily use government funds is first carried out with private capital, with the construction costs later recovered through measures such as reductions in port-use charges.
The Busan Regional Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Office had previously made a tentative decision to deepen the channels in the approach/departure and turning areas at Sinseondae Pier from the current depth of 14.5 to 15 meters to 16 meters, so that very large container ships could berth without difficulty. The work was to proceed under the same non-management-authority port-construction scheme.
Differences between the office’s Port Logistics Division and the Busan Port Construction Office are reportedly behind the loss of consistency in Busan Port’s facility-improvement policy. The Port Logistics Division announced its intention to approve the dredging, citing sufficient social justification. The Busan Port Construction Office, however, argues that because the project would ultimately involve substantial government funding, an expert study should first establish whether the work is warranted and forecast vessel demand.
PECT is pursuing the deepening project under this scheme, investing KRW 14 billion because fully loaded, very large vessels have difficulty using the pier. A similar plan fell through last year after BPA refused to reimburse the investment costs.
Reporter Cho Jin-man (jmcho@kookje.co.kr)

ko-news-press-1415-c14319c1ac.title: Coastal Erosion Accelerating at 178 Beach Sites Nationwide
ko-news-press-1415-c14319c1ac.text:
Coastal Erosion Accelerating at 178 Beach Sites Nationwide
2022-03-25
Coastal erosion is accelerating at 178 beach sites nationwide
Ports and road construction among the causes; sand loss and pebble exposure underway
GeoSystem Research team led by Dr. Nam Soo-yong
More than 178 sandy coastal sites across the country are experiencing erosion.
The team led by Dr. Nam Soo-yong of GeoSystem Research presented the findings at a symposium on “Efficient Use and Conservation of the Coast” in Gangneung on the 7th and stressed that effective countermeasures are urgently needed.
Dr. Nam said the 178 sites where coastal erosion was occurring comprised 92 sites with shoreline-soil erosion or slope collapse, 36 with revetment failure, 35 with beach erosion, and 15 with coastal-dune erosion.
The cited causes differed by region: installation of coastal structures such as ports on the east coast; reduced sediment supply and typhoons on the south coast; and coastal-road construction and storms on the west coast.
At Hosan Beach in Samcheok, large-scale sand extraction has led to sand loss and increasing pebble exposure since 2001. At Haeundae in Busan, ongoing coastal erosion has been associated with a coastal road built on a revetment in the late 1960s and development of the backshore area.
Busan’s Songdo Beach, Songdo Beach in Pohang, and Gujora Beach in South Gyeongsang Province have already lost their function as bathing beaches or are at risk of doing so. At Manripo Beach in South Chungcheong Province, more gravel has become exposed since breakwaters were installed.
Reporter Kim Won-hak (environment@bosa.co.kr)
Article entered: 2004-10-07, 4:23 p.m.

ko-news-press-1419-c14319c1ac.title: Beach-Water Test Results Vary with Sampling Location and Method
ko-news-press-1419-c14319c1ac.text:
Beach-Water Test Results Vary with Sampling Location and Method — Reporter Park Jeong-hwan
2022-03-25
Beach-water test results vary widely with the sampling location and method, undermining their reliability.
This has prompted calls for clear guidelines on where and how beach-water samples should be collected.
Rep. Kim Young-ju of the National Assembly’s Environment and Labor Committee announced on the 3rd the results of water-quality tests at Eulwangri Beach on Yongyu Island, Jung-gu, Incheon. The tests were conducted on the 5th and 6th of the previous month at Rep. Kim’s request by the National Institute of Marine and Fisheries Science.
The tests found total coliform counts ranging from 2,400 to 9,200 per 100 mL in seawater collected at three locations at Eulwangri Beach. The highest result was more than three times the wastewater-treatment-plant effluent standard of 3,000 per 100 mL.
Fecal coliform counts—bacteria associated with feces and sewage—ranged from 1,100 to 2,400 per 100 mL of seawater.
Rep. Kim said, “Eulwangri Beach is so seriously contaminated with coliform bacteria that swimming should be prohibited.”
Water-quality test results for the same beach, collected at nearly the same time by the Incheon City Public Health and Environment Research Institute, were entirely different.
The total coliform count in samples taken at Eulwangri Beach on the 13th of the previous month was 20 per 100 mL.
That result was classified as “suitable” for swimming and was completely different from the result of the test commissioned by Rep. Kim from the National Institute of Marine and Fisheries Science.
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries classified beach water as “suitable” for swimming when total coliform counts were no more than 1,000 per 100 mL of seawater.
The different results from the same beach were attributed to different sampling methods.
An employee of the Jung-gu Tourism Promotion Division who collected samples for both Rep. Kim’s test and the city research institute’s test said the two institutions used different methods.
For the test commissioned by Rep. Kim, samples were taken during the rainy season at low tide, when the water had receded, from a point about 30 meters offshore. The sample was collected when rainwater was washing household wastewater from land into the sea, a time when coliform bacteria were abundant.
When the city’s Public Health and Environment Research Institute collected samples through Jung-gu, it was high tide and the site was about 100 meters offshore. Domestic wastewater, including sewage, had been diluted by seawater, so pollution indicators such as coliform counts would inevitably be lower.
The problem is that the method for collecting samples for beach-water tests is not clearly specified.
For beach-water sampling sites, the rules define a water depth of 0.5 to 1.5 meters (within 15 centimeters of the surface) but do not prescribe a specific method.
Consequently, even samples taken under the same conditions can show considerable water-quality variation between the East and South Seas, where the tidal range is not large, and the West Sea, where it is pronounced.
A 45-year-old merchant identified as K, who runs a business at Eulwangri Beach, said, “The city’s water-quality survey said there was ‘no problem,’ so vacationers flocked here. But after the National Institute of Marine and Fisheries Science announced its test results, visitors suddenly dwindled. As someone who runs a business near the beach, I’m disconcerted.”
Reporter Park Jeong-hwan / blog.itimes.co.kr / hi21

ko-news-press-1424-c14319c1ac.title: “The Beach Could Disappear at This Rate”
ko-news-press-1424-c14319c1ac.text:
“The Beach Could Disappear at This Rate”
2022-03-25
[Hankyoreh] Erosion is progressing to a worrying degree along nearly half of the country’s sandy beaches and coastal dunes. The problem is especially severe on the east coast, where typhoon damage compounds the effects of reckless coastal development, including roads, seawalls, and aggregate extraction.
A report commissioned by the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries from GeoSystem Research and others surveyed erosion histories at 62 beaches and dunes nationwide the previous year and assigned severity grades. The report, released on the 16th, classified 21 sites as “Concern” and 6 as “Severe”; 44 percent of all sites showed erosion at or above the “Concern” level.
Beaches graded “Concern” included Gwangalli and Haeundae in Busan, Gyeongpodae and Jeongdongjin in Gangwon Province, and Kkotji Beach in Anmyeon-eup, South Chungcheong Province.
At Jeongdongjin, the beach slope has become steeper since the coastal road was widened and the river was improved. At Kkotji Beach, the dune area behind the beach was developed and a concrete retaining wall was built; afterward, erosion affected 3.4 kilometers of coast and gravel began to replace the sandy beach.
At the Namhangjin-ri coast in Seongdeok-dong, Gangneung, Gangwon Province, which was rated “Severe” and requires urgent action, erosion is occurring along a 1.85-kilometer stretch. Since a breakwater was built, the military’s coastal security fence has also collapsed. Hosan Beach in Wondeok-eup, Samcheok, has lost 1.3 kilometers of coast as aggregate extraction and construction of Hosan Port disrupted the sediment-supply balance.
At Unyeo Beach in Gonam-myeon, Taean County, South Chungcheong Province, erosion became severe after large-scale silica-sand extraction and revetment construction, putting the newly built revetment at risk of collapse.
Erosion is particularly severe on the east coast. Of 16 survey sites in Gangwon Province, 8 were graded “Concern” and 4 “Severe.” In North Gyeongsang Province, 4 of 6 coastal sites—including Songdo Beach in Pohang—were graded “Concern,” while the coast at Bongpyeong-ri, Jukbyeon-myeon, was rated “Severe.”
Kim Mu-hong, an official in the Coastal Planning Division of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, said, “Coastal erosion is mainly caused by human activities such as reclamation, road construction, and seawalls undertaken without assessing their combined effects. We are building a long-term monitoring system to identify the precise causes of erosion.”
Environmental affairs reporter Cho Hong-seop (ecothink@hani.co.kr)

ko-news-press-1427-c14319c1ac.title: [Emerging Growth Company] GeoSystem Research
ko-news-press-1427-c14319c1ac.text:
[Emerging Growth Company] GeoSystem Research
2022-03-25
GeoSystem Research (CEO Kim Hong-seon; www.geosr.com), a company specializing in marine and aquatic-environment engineering services, is recognized for achieving a high level of technical capability in Korea through bold investment in advanced equipment and continuous research and development.
The company works in marine physical surveys; water-quality and seabed-sediment analysis; surveying and exploration; coastal-erosion monitoring systems; and GIS and software development. By training specialists in these fields, it is expanding into marine remote-monitoring systems and remote management of aids to navigation. Since its establishment in 2000, GeoSystem Research has undertaken a range of government-funded research projects. Recently, it has focused on direct and remote monitoring, surveying and exploration, and numerical modeling and simulation.
Numerical modeling and simulation use computer programs to solve differential equations describing water movement in the sea, rivers, and lakes, as well as the transport, diffusion, and interactions of materials. The programs can reproduce observed results and simulate future changes or past conditions. GeoSystem Research has hundreds of domestic and international applications of its work and a broad suite of current software for simulating tides, currents, waves, material transport and diffusion, topographic change, and ecosystem change in marine and aquatic environments. It also has a distinctive capability to develop storm-surge-height data for different typhoon scenarios and rapidly forecast coastal inundation, helping reduce coastal-disaster impacts.
A company representative said, “As green growth and natural-disaster risk reduction become major concerns, and renewable energy industries that can replace fossil fuels gain prominence, it is increasingly important to accurately simulate the many processes occurring in marine and aquatic environments.” Through multidisciplinary approaches to research and operational projects, the company identifies processes and develops alternatives. This is expected to sustain its leading position in numerical modeling and simulation. CEO Kim Hong-seon said, “As a leading company in marine research and technical services, we will work to contribute to the development of Korea’s marine science and technology and to have our capabilities recognized globally.”

ko-news-press-1428-c14319c1ac.title: Eco-Friendly Green-Growth Technology Cooperation Symposium
ko-news-press-1428-c14319c1ac.text:
Eco-Friendly Green-Growth Technology Cooperation Symposium
2022-03-25
Symposium on cooperation in eco-friendly green-growth technology
Industry, academia, research, and government experts in green-growth technology will gather
The Korea Coast Guard, headed by Commissioner General Lee Gil-beom, will hold a joint research symposium bringing together industry, academia, research institutes, and government at 3 p.m. on September 25 in its second-floor main conference room. The event aims to respond proactively to rapidly changing marine conditions at home and abroad and strengthen cooperation on eco-friendly green-growth technology.
Experts will present and discuss eight marine-environment research projects, including “Distribution of Alkylphenols in Sediments from Ocean-Dumping Sites” by Professor Shin Kyung-hoon of Hanyang University and “The Fate of Oil and Its Effects on Pelagic Ecosystems Using Mesocosms” by Dr. Shim Won-jun of the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute.
The symposium will focus on scientific support for oil-spill response in the wake of the Hebei Spirit oil spill off Taean. Topics include how oil spilled at sea changes over time and how tar forms, with the aim of minimizing environmental damage in a major pollution incident.
The Industry–Academia–Research–Government Joint Research Council was established in June 2004, centered on the Korea Coast Guard, with marine experts appointed from the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute, Inha University, SK Energy, and other organizations. It seeks to strengthen the Coast Guard’s expertise by building active public-private cooperation, jointly address problems, and discuss future development directions.
This year the council added the Korea General Environmental Research Institute and GeoSystem Research, expanding participation by specialized marine organizations. Ten institutions and organizations are conducting joint research in four fields, including marine-pollution response technology and ecotoxicology.
Through regular council meetings, the Coast Guard plans to promote academic advice and information exchange, make up for gaps in research through measures such as shared use of facilities, and strengthen technical cooperation. It is also pursuing ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation as a testing laboratory so that its test results will gain international recognition. The initiative is expected to contribute substantially to the expertise of industry, academia, research, and government.

ko-news-press-1430-c14319c1ac.title: East Coast Beaches Are Shrinking, and Solutions Remain Elusive
ko-news-press-1430-c14319c1ac.text:
East Coast Beaches Are Shrinking, and Solutions Remain Elusive
2022-03-25
Coastal erosion severe at 6 of 25 sites; artificial structures are the leading cause
Local governments face limits in finding solutions; stronger national support is needed
20110619002108
Coastal erosion along the East Coast of North Gyeongsang Province is worsening, making countermeasures urgent.
According to North Gyeongsang Province and local governments including Pohang and Gyeongju on the 19th, the province commissioned GeoSystem Research Co., Ltd. and Ara Technology Co., Ltd. to monitor sandy beaches along the East Coast as part of a comprehensive erosion-management effort. Six of the 25 surveyed sites received a Grade D, indicating severe erosion, for a severe-erosion rate of 24 percent. This was a marked increase from 22.7 percent in 2009 and 18.2 percent in 2008.
The survey found no Grade A sites (Good); 8 were Grade B (Normal), 11 Grade C (Concern), and 6 Grade D (Severe). Seventeen sites, or 68 percent, were at the Concern or Severe level.
Photo caption: Erosion is severe along the coast near Oryu Beach in Gampo-eup, Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, and countermeasures are needed.
Gyeongju — Reporter Jang Young-tae
At Grade C and D sites, erosion has become severe: beaches are disappearing, and sand has been eroded from beneath roads. These sites include Jeonchon, Najeong, and Oryu in Gyeongju; Songdo in Pohang; Daetan in Yeongdeok; and Bongpyeong, Wolsongjeong, Deoksin, Geumeum, and Hujeong in Uljin.
Sandy beaches are important parts of the coastal environment and serve functions such as natural filtration. Despite the seriousness of the problem, countermeasures have made little progress.
At Songdo Beach in Nam-gu, Pohang, the sandy beach once averaged 70 to 80 meters in width. Only a small portion remains, and the beach has lost its function as a bathing beach.
At Samjeong Beach in Guryongpo, Nam-gu, Pohang, and along the coast near Hajeong-ri, sand loss has turned beaches into gravel. Concrete wave-dissipating blocks were installed offshore to keep sand from being washed away, but the measure has not been sufficient.
Experts identify coastal artificial structures as a leading cause of erosion, including changes in wave direction caused by breakwaters and development of areas behind the coast.
They say an integrated management strategy is needed, combining active coastal-erosion prevention measures with enforcement against indiscriminate development.
North Gyeongsang Province plans to spend KRW 430 million this year on coastal-erosion monitoring at 23 East Coast sites, from March through the end of the year, to assess erosion and carry out science-based, environmentally sound coastal-improvement projects.
Detailed monitoring is planned at two sites: the coast of Sadong 1-ri in Ulleung County and the coast from Gusan to Wolsong-ri in Uljin County.
Jang Du-wook, a member of the North Gyeongsang Provincial Council, said, “Local governments have limits in fully addressing coastal erosion, so it must be treated as a national issue. The province should actively explain the seriousness of East Coast erosion to the relevant ministries and call for comprehensive support.”
Pohang — Reporter Jang Young-tae (3678jyt@segye.com)

ko-news-press-1435-c14319c1ac.title: Fiji Newspapers Cover On-Site Activities of Experts Deployed for a KOICA Project
ko-news-press-1435-c14319c1ac.text:
Fiji Newspapers Cover On-Site Activities of Experts Deployed for a KOICA Project
2022-03-25
Activities in Fiji related to our company’s ongoing KOICA [South Pacific Renewable Energy Support] project were covered by local newspapers, the Fiji Times and Fiji Sun, on December 9, 2011.
